knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cost Circulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear minimum-cost circulation with lower and upper arc bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph. For each arc \(a\in A\), let \(c_a\in\mathbb R\) and \(-\infty<\ell_a\le u_a\le+\infty\). A feasible circulation is a vector \(x\in\mathbb R^A\) satisfying \(\ell_a\le x_a\le u_a\) for every arc and \[\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_a=0\qquad(v\in V).\] The minimum-cost circulation problem is \[\min\left\{\sum_{a\in A}c_ax_a:x\text{ is a feasible circulation}\right\}.\] An instance is infeasible if no such \(x\) exists and unbounded below if feasible circulations have arbitrarily negative cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimum-cost circulation minimizes linear arc cost subject to flow conservation at every vertex and prescribed lower and upper arc bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite.
\(c_a\in\mathbb R\) and \(\ell_a\le u_a\) for every \(a\in A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}=\inf\{c^\top x:Bx=0,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cost Transshipment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear transshipment with the convention that positive balance denotes supply.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be finite, with arc costs \(c\in\mathbb R^A\), bounds \(\ell\le u\), and balances \(b\in\mathbb R^V\) satisfying \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\). A feasible transshipment is \(x\in\mathbb R^A\) such that \(\ell\le x\le u\) and \[\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_a=b_v\qquad(v\in V).\] The minimum-cost transshipment problem minimizes \(c^\top x\) over these vectors. Thus \(b_v>0\) specifies net supply, \(b_v<0\) specifies net demand, and \(b_v=0\) imposes ordinary flow conservation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimum-cost transshipment sends specified supplies to specified demands at minimum linear cost while respecting all arc bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph.
\(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\).
\(\ell_a\le u_a\) for every \(a\in A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}=\inf\{c^\top x:Bx=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Prescribed-Value Minimum-Cost Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-source, single-sink flow with fixed throughput.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph, let \(s,t\in V\) be distinct, and fix \(F\ge 0\). Let \(c\in\mathbb R^A\), and let the arc bounds satisfy \(-\infty<\ell_a\le u_a\le+\infty\) for every \(a\in A\). If \(B\) is the node-arc incidence matrix using net outflow, a feasible flow of prescribed value \(F\) is a vector \(x\in\mathbb R^A\) satisfying \[Bx=F\mathbf e_s-F\mathbf e_t,\qquad \ell\le x\le u.\] The prescribed-value minimum-cost flow problem has extended optimal value \[\operatorname{OPT}=\inf\{c^\top x:Bx=F\mathbf e_s-F\mathbf e_t,\ \ell\le x\le u\}.\] It is the transshipment instance with supply \(F\) at \(s\), demand \(F\) at \(t\), and zero balance elsewhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among all bounded source-to-sink flows having exactly the prescribed throughput, minimize linear arc cost; the instance may be infeasible or unbounded below.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite and \(s\ne t\).
\(c\in\mathbb R^A\) and \(-\infty<\ell_a\le u_a\le+\infty\) for every \(a\in A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}=\inf\{c^\top x:Bx=F\mathbf e_s-F\mathbf e_t,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\).

children.title: Minimum-Cost Maximum Flow
children.top_down_role: Throughput optimization followed by cost minimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cost Maximum Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lexicographic optimization of throughput first and cost second.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph, let \(s,t\in V\) be distinct, let \(u\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^A\) be finite arc capacities, and let \(c\in\mathbb R^A\) be arc costs. With \(B\) denoting the node-arc incidence matrix using net outflow, define \[\mathcal F=\{x\in\mathbb R^A:0\le x\le u,\ (Bx)_v=0\text{ for every }v\in V\setminus\{s,t\}\}.\] For \(x\in\mathcal F\), define \(|x|=(Bx)_s=-(Bx)_t\), and let \[F^*=\max\{|x|:x\in\mathcal F\}.\] A minimum-cost maximum flow is any \[x^*\in\arg\min\{c^\top x:x\in\mathcal F,\ |x|=F^*\}.\] Thus throughput is maximized first, and cost is minimized only among maximum-value flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: First maximize source-to-sink throughput under finite arc capacities; among all maximum flows, select one having minimum linear cost.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite and \(s\ne t\).
\(u\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^A\) has finite components.
\(c\in\mathbb R^A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((|x^*|,c^\top x^*)\) is lexicographically optimal with throughput ordered decreasingly and cost increasingly.

notation.meaning: Net flow value from source s to sink t.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cost-preserving reduction of the fixed-maximum-value cost phase to minimum-cost circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: After determining \(F^*\), add a zero-cost return arc \(a_0=(t,s)\) with \(\ell_{a_0}=u_{a_0}=F^*\). A flow \(x\) on the original arcs has value \(F^*\) if and only if its extension with \(x_{a_0}=F^*\) is a feasible circulation. The extension preserves objective value, so minimum-cost maximum flows correspond bijectively to minimum-cost circulations in the augmented network.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed zero-cost return arc from the sink to the source converts the maximum-value cost phase into an equivalent minimum-cost circulation.
assumptions_latex: \(F^*\) is the maximum feasible source-to-sink flow value.
The return arc \(a_0=(t,s)\) has zero cost and fixed flow \(F^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\longleftrightarrow (x,x_{a_0}=F^*)\text{ is a cost-preserving bijection between value-}F^*\text{ flows and feasible augmented circulations.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Node–Arc and Return-Arc Formulations of Maximum Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-capacity, single-commodity directed maximum flow with zero lower bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a directed network with source $1$, sink $m$, and arc capacities $u_{ij}$, maximum flow is formulated by maximizing $f$ subject to $\sum_j x_{ij}-\sum_k x_{ki}=f$ for $i=1$, $0$ for $i\notin\{1,m\}$, and $-f$ for $i=m$, with $0\le x_{ij}\le u_{ij}$. Equivalently, introducing a return arc $(m,1)$ with flow $x_{m1}=f$, lower bound $0$, and cost $-1$ converts the problem into a zero-balance minimum-cost circulation with all other arc costs zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum flow maximizes the source-to-sink flow value subject to node conservation and arc capacities. Treating that value as flow on a return arc from the sink to the source gives an equivalent zero-balance circulation formulation, with cost −1 on the return arc and zero cost elsewhere.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a directed single-commodity network with source }1\text{ and sink }m.
0\le x_{ij}\le u_{ij}\quad((i,j)\in E),\qquad u_{ij}\in\mathbb Z_{<\infty}.
\ell_{ij}=0\quad((i,j)\in E).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max f\ \text{subject to flow conservation and capacities is equivalently represented by a circulation with }x_{m1}=f\text{ and }c_{m1}=-1.

children.title: Lower-Bound Normalization
children.top_down_role: Transformations removing nonzero lower arc bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Bound Normalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine substitution converting finite lower bounds to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min\{c^\top x:Bx=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\) with finite \(\ell\). Set \(y=x-\ell\), \(b'=b-B\ell\), and \(u'=u-\ell\). Then \[Bx=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad By=b',\ 0\le y\le u'.\] The objectives satisfy \(c^\top x=c^\top y+c^\top\ell\). Consequently the substitution is a bijection between feasible sets, preserves the ordering of feasible solutions, and changes the optimal value only by the known constant \(c^\top\ell\). If the original data are integral, the map also preserves integrality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtract each arc's lower bound, adjust vertex balances by its incidence, and retain costs; feasibility and optimal solutions correspond up to a constant cost.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is the node-arc incidence matrix.
\(\ell\in\mathbb R^A\) is finite and \(\ell\le u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\leftrightarrow y=x-\ell\) bijects the two feasible regions and \(\operatorname{OPT}_{x}=\operatorname{OPT}_{y}+c^\top\ell\).

notation.meaning: Net outflow induced by the vector of lower bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Upper-Bound Elimination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arc-reversal substitution eliminating finite upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an arc \(a=(i,j)\) constrained by \(0\le x_a\le u_a<\infty\), introduce the reverse arc \(\bar a=(j,i)\) with unbounded nonnegative flow \(y_{\bar a}=u_a-x_a\) and cost \(-c_a\). Delete \(a\), replace balances by \(b'_i=b_i-u_a\), \(b'_j=b_j+u_a\), and leave other balances unchanged. Then feasible solutions correspond bijectively through \(x_a=u_a-y_{\bar a}\), and \[c_ax_a=c_au_a-c_ay_{\bar a}.\] Applying this independently to every finitely upper-bounded arc removes all such upper bounds, while preserving minimizers after adding the known constant \(\sum_a c_au_a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace a bounded arc by an unbounded reverse arc carrying unused capacity, adjust endpoint balances, and account for a constant objective shift.
assumptions_latex: The balance convention is \(Bx=b\) with net outflow positive.
Each transformed arc satisfies \(0\le x_a\le u_a<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_a\leftrightarrow y_{\bar a}=u_a-x_a\) preserves feasibility and changes cost by the constant \(c_au_a\).

notation.meaning: Reverse arc replacing the original finitely capacitated arc.
Unused capacity of the original arc.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of unbounded reverse-arc complementation for an originally nonnegative capacitated arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(0\le x_a\le u_a<\infty\), the substitution \(y_{\bar a}=u_a-x_a\) implies \(0\le y_{\bar a}\le u_a\), not merely \(y_{\bar a}\ge0\). For example, if \(u_a=1\), the allowed value \(y_{\bar a}=2\) in the proposed unbounded replacement maps to \(x_a=-1\), violating \(x_a\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unused-capacity reversal retains an upper bound when the original flow has a finite lower bound; dropping it destroys equivalence.

\(y_{\bar a}=u_a-x_a\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Valid reverse-arc complementation when the original variable has no finite lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If an arc variable is constrained only by \(x_a\le u_a<\infty\), with no finite lower bound, then \(y_{\bar a}=u_a-x_a\ge0\) on the reverse arc gives a bijection. Under the net-outflow convention, replace \(b_i\) by \(b_i-u_a\), replace \(b_j\) by \(b_j+u_a\), and replace cost \(c_a x_a\) by \(-c_a y_{\bar a}\) plus the constant \(c_a u_a\).

knowledge_statements.title: Circulation Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of balanced transshipment to circulation using fixed-flow auxiliary arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Bx=b\) be a transshipment instance with \(\sum_v b_v=0\), where positive \(b_v\) denotes supply. Add a new vertex \(r\). For each \(v\) with \(b_v>0\), add a zero-cost arc \((r,v)\) whose lower and upper bounds both equal \(b_v\); for each \(v\) with \(b_v<0\), add a zero-cost arc \((v,r)\) fixed at \(-b_v\). Retain every original arc and require zero balance at every vertex. Restriction to the original arcs bijects feasible circulations with feasible transshipments and preserves their costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Attach fixed zero-cost arcs to a new vertex so prescribed supplies and demands become ordinary circulation conservation equations.
assumptions_latex: \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\).
Fixed-flow arcs are permitted through equal lower and upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Bx=b\) on original arcs holds exactly when the augmented flow is a circulation.

children.title: Transshipment Reductions

knowledge_statements.title: Transshipment Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Viewing circulation as the zero-balance transshipment case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a minimum-cost circulation instance \(Bx=0\) with bounds \(\ell\le x\le u\), form a transshipment instance on the same graph, with the same bounds and costs, by setting \(b_v=0\) for every vertex. The feasible regions and objective functions are identical. More generally, after fixing auxiliary arcs in a circulation reduction, deleting those arcs and moving their incidence contributions to the right-hand side produces \(Bx=b\). Thus circulation and balanced transshipment formulations convert into one another without changing the original decision variables or their costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A circulation is exactly a transshipment with zero balances; deleting fixed auxiliary arcs conversely recovers nonzero prescribed balances.
assumptions_latex: The same outflow-minus-inflow incidence convention is used in both formulations.
Any deleted auxiliary arc has a fixed flow value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:Bx=0,\ \ell\le x\le u\}=\{x:Bx=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\) when \(b=0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower-Bound Shifting from Circulation to Transshipment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conversion of a lower-bounded circulation to a zero-lower-bound transshipment on the same graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a circulation \(Bx=0\) with bounds \(\ell\le x\le u\) and cost \(c^{\mathsf T}x\), set \(y=x-\ell\). Then \(0\le y\le u-\ell\) and \(By=-B\ell\). Thus \(y\) is a transshipment with balance \(b'=-B\ell\). The objective is \(c^{\mathsf T}y+c^{\mathsf T}\ell\), so \(x=y+\ell\) is a feasible-solution bijection and preserves minimizers up to the constant \(c^{\mathsf T}\ell\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subtracting lower bounds turns a circulation into a zero-lower-bound transshipment, adjusts balances, and adds only a constant to the objective.
assumptions_latex: The same outflow-minus-inflow incidence convention is used throughout.
\(\ell\le u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x:Bx=0,\ \ell\le x\le u\}=\ell+\{y:By=-B\ell,\ 0\le y\le u-\ell\}.

children.title: Canonical-Form Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Preservation of feasibility, objective values, capacities, and recoverable solutions across the two forms.

knowledge_statements.title: Canonical-Form Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization equivalence of circulation and balanced transshipment canonical forms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every finite balanced transshipment instance with \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\), fixed-arc augmentation produces a circulation instance whose feasible circulations restrict bijectively to the original feasible transshipments and have equal cost. Conversely, every circulation instance is a transshipment instance with \(b=0\). These reductions preserve feasibility, finite optimal values, minimizers, and unboundedness. When bounds and balances are integral, the reductions use only integral fixed flows and preserve integral feasible solutions. The augmentation adds one vertex and at most \(|V|\) arcs and is computable in time linear in the augmented instance description.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Balanced transshipment and circulation are mutually reducible while preserving costs, feasibility, optimality, integrality, and linear instance growth.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph.
\(b\in\mathbb R^V\) satisfies \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\).
Equal lower and upper bounds may encode fixed auxiliary flows.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{transshipment}}=\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{augmented\ circulation}}\), with a cost-preserving bijection of feasible solutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Transportation Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transportation as minimum-cost flow on a layered bipartite network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For supplies \(a_i\ge0\), demands \(b_j\ge0\), and costs \(c_{ij}\), assume \(\sum_i a_i=\sum_j b_j\). Construct a network with source \(s\), supply vertices \(i\), demand vertices \(j\), and sink \(t\). Give \((s,i)\) capacity \(a_i\), \((i,j)\) cost \(c_{ij}\) and sufficient capacity, and \((j,t)\) capacity \(b_j\); all other costs are zero. A flow of value \(\sum_i a_i\) corresponds to the transportation plan \(x_{ij}=x_{(i,j)}\), satisfying \(\sum_jx_{ij}=a_i\) and \(\sum_ix_{ij}=b_j\), with identical cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Represent a transportation table as flow through source, supply, demand, and sink layers; transportation quantities are the middle-arc flows.
assumptions_latex: \(a_i,b_j\ge0\) and \(\sum_i a_i=\sum_j b_j\).
Every permitted shipment pair has a corresponding middle arc.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}x_{ij}=c^\top x\), and feasible transportation plans biject with full-value network flows.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\sum_{i\in I}s_i\) and \(D=\sum_{j\in J}d_j\). If \(S>D\), add a dummy demand node \(j_0\) of demand \(S-D\) and zero-cost arcs \((i,j_0)\) from every origin. If \(D>S\), add a dummy supply node \(i_0\) of supply \(D-S\) and zero-cost arcs \((i_0,j)\) to every destination. Deleting dummy shipments gives a cost-preserving correspondence with the variant in which all margins on the smaller-total side are met exactly and margins on the larger-total side are upper bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Assignment Reductions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Assignment as unit-supply, unit-demand transportation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) and \(J\) be finite sets with \(|I|=|J|\), and let \(c_{ij}\in\mathbb R\) be the cost of assigning \(i\in I\) to \(j\in J\). Form the transportation problem with \(a_i=1\) for every \(i\in I\), \(b_j=1\) for every \(j\in J\), and variables \(x_{ij}\ge0\). Its constraints are \[\sum_{j\in J}x_{ij}=1\quad(i\in I),\qquad \sum_{i\in I}x_{ij}=1\quad(j\in J).\] Its integral feasible points are precisely perfect assignments, with \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\). The bipartite transportation constraint matrix is totally unimodular, so with the integral right-hand side the linear relaxation has an integral optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Set every transportation supply and demand to one; perfect assignments are the integral feasible plans, and total unimodularity makes the linear relaxation exact.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) and \(J\) are finite and \(|I|=|J|\).
\(c_{ij}\in\mathbb R\) for every \((i,j)\in I\times J\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min\{\sum_{i\in I,\,j\in J}c_{ij}x_{ij}:x\text{ is a perfect assignment}\}\) equals the unit-transportation linear-programming optimum.

knowledge_statements.title: Bipartite Network Expansions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Clone expansion from integral transportation to assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an integral transportation instance with \(a_i,b_j\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) and total mass \(N=\sum_i a_i=\sum_j b_j\). Replace each supply vertex \(i\) by \(a_i\) clones and each demand vertex \(j\) by \(b_j\) clones. Join every permitted supply clone of \(i\) to every permitted demand clone of \(j\), assigning each such edge cost \(c_{ij}\). A perfect assignment of clones induces \(x_{ij}\) equal to the number of matched clone pairs of types \((i,j)\). Conversely, every integral transportation plan expands to such a perfect assignment, with equal total cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Clone each origin and destination according to its integral multiplicity; perfect assignments between clones encode integral transportation plans with unchanged cost.
assumptions_latex: \(a_i,b_j\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\) and \(\sum_i a_i=\sum_j b_j=N\).
Clone edges reproduce exactly the permitted transportation pairs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Integral transportation plans and perfect clone assignments correspond cost-preservingly, although the expanded graph may have size polynomial in \(N\), not its bit length.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite directed graph \(G=(V,A)\), let \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\) prescribe node supplies, with positive entries denoting net production. The supply regime is balanced precisely when
\[\sum_{v\in V} b_v=0.\]
If a flow satisfies the conservation equations
\[\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_a=b_v\qquad(v\in V),\]
then its prescribed supplies are balanced. Supply balance is necessary but, in the presence of arc bounds or missing connections, not sufficient for feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Supplies are balanced when their total is zero. This is necessary for flow conservation, although capacity restrictions or network connectivity may still make the model infeasible.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V=\{s,t\}\), prescribe \(b_s=1\) and \(b_t=-1\), and give the arcs leaving \(s\) total upper capacity strictly less than \(1\). Then \(b_s+b_t=0\), but no capacity-feasible flow satisfies \(Bx=b\).

assumptions_latex: The outflow-minus-inflow convention is used.
Flows are nonnegative and the total upper capacity leaving \(s\) is less than one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\quad\text{but}\quad\{x:Bx=b,\ 0\le x\le u\}=\varnothing.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Componentwise Characterization of Unrestricted Balance Solvability

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,A)\) have weakly connected components \(C_1,\ldots,C_k\), and let \(B\) use the outflow-minus-inflow convention. The unrestricted equations \(Bx=b\) admit a solution \(x\in\mathbb R^A\) if and only if \(\sum_{v\in C_h}b_v=0\) for every component \(C_h\). For a weakly connected graph this reduces to \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\). Nonnegativity and arc bounds can create additional obstructions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With unrestricted signed arc variables, prescribed balances are realizable exactly when they sum to zero in every weak component.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite directed graph.
Arc variables are unrestricted real numbers in this incidence-image statement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists x\in\mathbb R^A:Bx=b\iff \sum_{v\in C}b_v=0\quad\text{for every weak component }C.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines feasible flows, records aggregate balance as necessary but not sufficient for feasibility, and distinguishes capacitated from uncapacitated minimum-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G=(\mathcal N,\mathcal A) be directed, with supplies b_i, capacities u_{ij}\in[0,+\infty], and costs c_{ij}. A flow f is feasible if b_i+\sum_{j\in I(i)}f_{ji}=\sum_{j\in O(i)}f_{ij} for every i and 0\leq f_{ij}\leq u_{ij} for every arc. Every feasible flow satisfies \sum_i b_i=0; hence \sum_i b_i\neq0 implies infeasibility. Assuming \sum_i b_i=0, minimum-cost flow minimizes \sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal A}c_{ij}f_{ij} over feasible flows. It is uncapacitated if all u_{ij}=+\infty and capacitated otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible flow satisfies node conservation and its nonnegative arc-capacity bounds. Aggregate supply must equal aggregate demand, although this condition alone need not ensure feasibility. Minimum-cost flow minimizes total linear arc cost; it is uncapacitated exactly when every upper capacity is infinite.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a capacitated flow realizing balanced vertex supplies and demands, together with the circulation and vertex-role terminology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $G$ be a digraph, $u:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}_{+}$, and $b:V(G)\to\mathbb{R}$ with $\sum_{v\in V(G)}b(v)=0$. A $b$-flow in $(G,u)$ is a function $f:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}_{+}$ such that $f(e)\leq u(e)$ for every $e\in E(G)$ and $\sum_{e\in\delta^{+}(v)}f(e)-\sum_{e\in\delta^{-}(v)}f(e)=b(v)$ for every $v\in V(G)$. A $b$-flow with $b\equiv0$ is a circulation. If $b(v)>0$, then $v$ is a source and $b(v)$ is its supply; if $b(v)<0$, then $v$ is a sink and $|b(v)|$ is its demand.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a directed graph with nonnegative arc capacities and vertex balances summing to zero, a b-flow is a nonnegative capacity-feasible arc flow whose net outflow at each vertex equals that vertex's balance. Zero balances yield a circulation; positive-balance vertices are sources and negative-balance vertices are sinks.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be finite and let \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\). If
\[\sum_{v\in V}b_v\ne0,\]
then no vector \(x\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) can satisfy
\[\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_a=b_v\qquad(v\in V).\]
Thus an unbalanced supply vector makes the standard equality-constrained flow model infeasible, independently of costs and arc bounds. The converse fails: a balanced vector may remain infeasible because of lower bounds, upper bounds, or network cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero total supply makes exact node conservation impossible, regardless of costs or capacities. Zero total supply removes this obstruction but does not guarantee feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Node Balancing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Star augmentation that converts arbitrary supplies into a balanced extended instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\), set \(B=\sum_{v\in V}b_v\) and add an auxiliary node \(r\) with supply \(b_r=-B\). Add an artificial arc \((v,r)\) for every \(b_v>0\) and \((r,v)\) for every \(b_v<0\), each with zero lower bound and capacity at least \(|b_v|\). Then
\[\sum_{v\in V\cup\{r\}}b_v=0,\]
and the artificial flow \(x_{vr}=b_v\) for \(b_v>0\), \(x_{rv}=-b_v\) for \(b_v<0\), with original arcs set to zero, satisfies every augmented balance equation. Artificial costs may be assigned separately to penalize their use.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding one node with the opposite aggregate supply and suitable star arcs produces a balanced, feasible augmented instance; penalties can discourage artificial flow.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite.
\(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\) is arbitrary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The augmented supply vector is balanced and admits the displayed artificial-star flow.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the auxiliary-node construction, the augmented balances require \(\operatorname{div}x(r)=-B\), where \(B=\sum_{v\in V}b_v\). If \(B\ne0\), every augmented feasible flow therefore uses nonzero net artificial flow incident with \(r\), and its restriction to the original arcs cannot satisfy all original balance equations. Thus auxiliary-node balancing changes the model. If \(B=0\) and \(x\) is augmented-feasible, then all artificial arcs being zero is equivalent to the restriction \(x_A\) satisfying the original balances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The auxiliary star balances the enlarged model but does not repair the original closed model: nonzero aggregate supply forces artificial flow, while zero artificial flow recovers an original feasible flow in the balanced case.

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Circulation Feasibility Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hoffman-type cut certificate under the outflow-minus-inflow balance convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be finite, let \(l,u\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) satisfy \(l\le u\), and let \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\) satisfy \(b(V)=0\). A flow \(x\) with \(l\le x\le u\) and \(\operatorname{div}x=b\) exists if and only if, for every \(S\subseteq V\),
\[l(\delta^+(S))-u(\delta^-(S))\le b(S)\le u(\delta^+(S))-l(\delta^-(S)).\]
Consequently, any set \(S\) violating either inequality is a directly checkable infeasibility certificate; if no set violates them, the bounded-flow system is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded flow exists exactly when every vertex cut can carry its required net supply. Any cut violating the displayed lower or upper inequality certifies infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite and directed.
\(l,u\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) with \(l\le u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility is equivalent to the two cut inequalities for every \(S\subseteq V\).

knowledge_statements.title: Network-Flow Integrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral-vertex theorem for a finite capacitated network-flow polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a finite directed graph. Suppose \(b\in\mathbb{Z}^{V}\) and \(l,u\in\mathbb{Z}^{A}\) with \(l\le u\), and define
\[P=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{A}:\operatorname{div}x=b,\ l\le x\le u\}.\]
If \(P\ne\varnothing\), then every vertex of \(P\) is integral. Hence, for every \(c\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\), whenever \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\in P\}\) is finite, it has an optimal solution in \(\mathbb{Z}^{A}\). In particular, continuous relaxation does not destroy the existence of an integral optimum for integral network data.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With integral supplies and arc bounds, every vertex of the feasible flow polytope is integral, so every finite linear-cost optimum has an integral representative.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite and directed.
\(b\in\mathbb{Z}^{V}\) and \(l,u\in\mathbb{Z}^{A}\) with \(l\le u\).
\(P\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{vert}(P)\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^{A}\), and every finite linear-cost minimum over \(P\) has an integral optimizer.

The balance equations force \(x_a=\tfrac12\). Hence the feasible flow polytope is the singleton \(\{\tfrac12\}\) and contains no integral flow.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural matrix reason for integrality of bounded network-flow polyhedra.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\) be the node-arc incidence matrix of a finite directed graph. Then \(B\) is totally unimodular, and adjoining signed identity rows preserves total unimodularity. Consequently the equality-and-bound system \[Bx=b,\qquad \ell\le x\le u\] has a totally unimodular coefficient matrix after equalities are written as paired inequalities. For integral \(b,\ell,u\), every basic feasible solution is integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directed incidence matrices remain totally unimodular when arc-bound rows are added, which makes every basic feasible network flow integral for integral data.

\(b\in\mathbb Z^V\) and \(\ell,u\in\mathbb Z^A\) with \(\ell\le u\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For finite \(G=(V,A)\), supplies \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\), and finite bounds \(l,u\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) satisfying \(l\le u\), define \(b(S)=\sum_{v\in S}b_v\) for \(S\subseteq V\), and define \(q(F)=\sum_{a\in F}q_a\) for \(q\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) and \(F\subseteq A\). The system
\[\operatorname{div}x=b,\qquad l\le x\le u\]
is infeasible if and only if either \(b(V)\ne0\), or \(b(V)=0\) and some \(S\subseteq V\) satisfies
\[b(S)<l(\delta^+(S))-u(\delta^-(S))\]
or
\[b(S)>u(\delta^+(S))-l(\delta^-(S)).\]
Thus aggregate imbalance and a violated capacity cut are the two obstruction forms for this model. Costs play no role in determining feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded flow model is infeasible exactly because total supply is nonzero or some cut cannot accommodate its prescribed net supply. Objective costs do not affect this classification.

children.title: Pathology Separation
children.top_down_role: Structural distinctions between absence of feasible flows and absence of finite optimal values.

knowledge_statements.title: Pathology Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mutually exclusive feasibility and boundedness classification for linear minimum-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite directed graph, consider
\[\inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:\operatorname{div}x=b,\ l\le x\le u\},\]
where \(l\) is finite and \(u\) may contain \(+\infty\). Exactly one of the following holds: the feasible set is empty; the feasible set is nonempty and the infimum is \(-\infty\); or the feasible set is nonempty and a finite minimum is attained. Hence infeasibility concerns only the constraints, whereas unboundedness presupposes feasibility and is witnessed by a negative-cost recession circulation. The two pathologies are logically disjoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every linear minimum-cost flow instance is exactly one of infeasible, feasible but unbounded below, or feasible with an attained finite optimum. Infeasibility and unboundedness cannot coincide.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite.
\(l_a\in\mathbb{R}\), \(u_a\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), and \(l_a\le u_a\).
\(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\) and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Uncapacitated Transshipment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear transshipment with nonnegative flows and no finite upper arc capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An uncapacitated transshipment instance consists of a finite directed graph \(G=(V,A)\), costs \(c\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\), and balanced supplies \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\). Its optimization problem is
\[\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{A}}\ \sum_{a\in A}c_ax_a\quad\text{subject to}\quad x_a\ge0\ (a\in A),\qquad \sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_a=b_v\ (v\in V).\]
No arc has a finite upper bound. Nodes may supply, demand, or transship flow according as \(b_v\) is positive, negative, or zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uncapacitated transshipment minimizes linear routing cost subject to nonnegative flows and node balances, with no finite upper arc capacities and zero aggregate supply.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite and directed.
\(c\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\).
\(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed linear program defines the uncapacitated transshipment model.

notation.meaning: Supply, demand, or zero transshipment requirement at v.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(b(S)=\sum_{v\in S}b_v\). With \(\sum_{v\in V}b_v=0\), the system \(Bx=b,\ x\ge0\) is feasible if and only if \[b(S)\le0\qquad\text{for every }S\subseteq V\text{ with }\delta^+(S)=\varnothing.\] In particular, every weakly connected component has total balance zero.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I\) be a finite set of supply nodes, let \(J\) be a finite disjoint set of demand nodes, let \(A\subseteq I\times J\) be the permitted shipping arcs, and let \(c\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\). For supplies \(s_i\ge0\) and demands \(d_j\ge0\), a balanced transportation problem is
\[\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^{A}}\sum_{(i,j)\in A}c_{ij}x_{ij}\quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_{j:(i,j)\in A}x_{ij}=s_i\ (i\in I),\quad \sum_{i:(i,j)\in A}x_{ij}=d_j\ (j\in J),\quad x_{ij}\ge0\ ((i,j)\in A),\]
with \(\sum_{i\in I}s_i=\sum_{j\in J}d_j\). This is transshipment on a bipartite graph whose arcs run from supply nodes to demand nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A transportation network is a bipartite transshipment model shipping prescribed supply to prescribed demand at minimum linear cost, with total supply equal to total demand.

A feasible plan \(x\) and feasible prices are optimal if every used route is tight: \(x_{ij}>0\Rightarrow\alpha_i+\beta_j=c_{ij}\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a balanced transportation network with permitted arcs \(A\subseteq I\times J\), a feasible plan exists if and only if \[\sum_{i\in S}s_i\le\sum_{j\in N(S)}d_j\qquad(S\subseteq I),\] where \(N(S)=\{j\in J:\exists i\in S,(i,j)\in A\}\).

\(A\subseteq I\times J\) is the permitted-route set.

knowledge_statements.title: Assignment Networks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-supply, unit-demand transportation model on a balanced bipartite graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I\) and \(J\) be finite sets with \(|I|=|J|\), and let \(A\subseteq I\times J\) contain the allowed assignments. The linear assignment model is
\[\min\sum_{(i,j)\in A}c_{ij}x_{ij}\quad\text{subject to}\quad \sum_{j:(i,j)\in A}x_{ij}=1\ (i\in I),\quad \sum_{i:(i,j)\in A}x_{ij}=1\ (j\in J),\quad x_{ij}\ge0.\]
It is a transportation problem with every supply and demand equal to one. Whenever feasible, its vertices are incidence vectors of perfect matchings, so a finite optimum has a binary optimal solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An assignment network is unit-supply transportation. Its feasible vertices encode perfect matchings, so the linear relaxation yields a binary optimum whenever one exists.
assumptions_latex: \(I,J\) are finite with \(|I|=|J|\).
\(A\subseteq I\times J\).
\(c\in\mathbb{R}^{A}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The assignment program is unit transportation, and every feasible vertex lies in \(\{0,1\}^{A}\).

notation.meaning: Assignment amount from i to j.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Costed residual network and feasible-increment correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-network representation for capacitated minimum-cost flows, including cycle correspondence and the stated per-iteration search bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a feasible flow $f$ on $G=(\mathcal N,\mathcal A)$ with $0\le f_{ij}\le u_{ij}$, an original arc $(i,j)$ of cost $c_{ij}$ induces a forward residual arc of capacity $u_{ij}-f_{ij}$ and cost $c_{ij}$ and a reverse residual arc of capacity $f_{ij}$ and cost $-c_{ij}$; zero-capacity arcs are deleted and residual supplies are zero. If $f+\bar f$ is another feasible flow, then $\bar f$ admits a representation as a nonnegative feasible residual circulation $\widetilde f$ of equal cost. Conversely, every feasible residual circulation induces an increment $\bar f$ for which $f+\bar f$ is feasible and costs are equal. Unsaturated cycles correspond, with equal cost, to directed residual cycles whose arcs have positive capacity. Consequently, negative unsaturated-cycle search reduces to negative directed-cycle search, giving $O(n^3)$ work per cycle-canceling iteration when the latter search is implemented in $O(n^3)$ time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible flow produces forward residual arcs for allowable increases and reverse residual arcs for allowable decreases, with the corresponding capacities and opposite costs. Every feasible flow change can be represented by a feasible residual circulation of the same cost, and every feasible residual circulation induces such a change; this need not be a unique representation. Unsaturated cycles correspond cost-preservingly to positive-capacity residual cycles, so an O(n^3) negative-cycle search gives O(n^3) work per cycle-canceling iteration.
assumptions_latex: $G=(\mathcal N,\mathcal A)$ is a capacitated costed network with the standard bounds $0\le f_{ij}\le u_{ij}$.
$f$ is feasible; for the forward construction, $f+\bar f$ is also feasible.
The directed negative-cycle subroutine has running time $O(n^3)$ for the stated iteration bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f+\bar f\text{ feasible}\Rightarrow\exists\widetilde f\text{ feasible in the residual network with }c^{\mathsf T}\bar f=\widetilde c^{\mathsf T}\widetilde f;\quad \widetilde f\text{ feasible residual}\Rightarrow\exists\bar f:\ f+\bar f\text{ feasible and }c^{\mathsf T}\bar f=\widetilde c^{\mathsf T}\widetilde f.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Path Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Endpoint imbalance transfer induced by augmenting along a residual path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a feasible bounded flow \(x\), form its residual network by assigning a forward residual arc capacity \(u_a-x_a\) and cost \(c_a\), and a reverse residual arc capacity \(x_a-l_a\) and cost \(-c_a\), whenever the respective capacity is positive. If \(P\) is a directed residual path from \(s\) to \(t\) and
\[0<\varepsilon\le\min_{e\in P}r_e,\]
augmenting \(\varepsilon\) along \(P\) preserves all arc bounds and every internal node balance, increases divergence at \(s\) by \(\varepsilon\), decreases divergence at \(t\) by \(\varepsilon\), and changes cost by \(\varepsilon\sum_{e\in P}\bar c_e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Augmenting within a residual path transfers a chosen flow amount from its start to its end, preserves internal balances and bounds, and changes cost by path cost times the amount.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) satisfies \(l\le x\le u\).
\(P\) is a directed residual path from \(s\) to \(t\).
\(0<\varepsilon\le\min_{e\in P}r_e\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Residual-path augmentation preserves bounds and internal balances while changing endpoint divergences by \(+\varepsilon\) and \(-\varepsilon\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a directed cycle in the residual network of \(x\), and let \(r_e>0\) be the residual capacity of each \(e\in C\). For any \(0<\theta\le \min_{e\in C}r_e\), augment \(\theta\) on forward residual arcs of \(C\) and subtract \(\theta\) on reverse residual arcs. The resulting flow \(x'=x+\theta\chi_C\) satisfies \(Bx'=Bx=b\) and \(l\le x'\le u\). Moreover, \[c^{\mathsf T}x'-c^{\mathsf T}x=\theta\sum_{e\in C}c_e^R=\theta c^R(C).\] Thus residual-cycle augmentation is circulation-preserving, and a negative-cost residual cycle gives a feasible strict cost decrease.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Augmenting within residual capacities around a directed residual cycle preserves feasibility; its cost change equals the augmentation amount times the cycle's residual cost.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A conformal path component of \(d\) is a vector \(h=\theta\chi_P\), where \(\theta>0\) and \(P\) is a simple directed path from \(s\) to \(t\) using only residual arcs selected by the sign of \(d\): a forward residual copy of \(a\) may occur only if \(d_a>0\), and a reverse copy only if \(d_a<0\). It must satisfy \(|h_a|\le |d_a|\) for every original arc \(a\). Consequently, \(h_a d_a\ge0\), \(|h_a|\le|d_a|\), and \[Bh=\theta(\mathbf e_t-\mathbf e_s).\]

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A conformal cycle component of \(d\) is a vector \(h=\theta\chi_C\), where \(\theta>0\) and \(C\) is a simple directed cycle in the signed residual support of \(d\). Thus a forward residual copy of an original arc \(a\) can occur only when \(d_a>0\), and a reverse copy only when \(d_a<0\); additionally, \(|h_a|\le |d_a|\) for every \(a\). Since \(C\) is a cycle, \[Bh=0.\] Hence the component is a circulation and is conformal to \(d\) arcwise.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exist finitely many conformal path components \(p^1,\ldots,p^k\) and conformal cycle components \(z^1,\ldots,z^m\) such that \[d=\sum_{i=1}^k p^i+\sum_{j=1}^m z^j.\] Every component \(h\) is sign-compatible with \(d\), meaning \(h_a d_a\ge0\) and \(|h_a|\le|d_a|\) for all \(a\in A\). Each \(z^j\) satisfies \(Bz^j=0\), while the path boundaries sum to the total imbalance: \[\sum_{i=1}^k Bp^i=Bd.\] If \(Bd=0\), the decomposition may be chosen with cycle components only.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite signed arc adjustment decomposes into arcwise sign-compatible path and cycle flows; paths realize its node imbalance, while cycles are circulations.

source_witnesses.locator: 1.1.3 Path Flows and Conformal Decomposition p. 7

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructive decomposition in the finite directed signed-support graph, with component-count, runtime, and integrality guarantees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Orient one copy of every arc \(a\) with \(d_a\ne0\) according to the sign of \(d_a\), and give it amount \(y_a=|d_a|\). Repeatedly subtract the bottleneck amount from a directed simple cycle in the positive support. After the support becomes acyclic, repeatedly subtract the bottleneck amount from a maximal directed path in the positive support. Each extracted vector is conformal to \(d\), and every extraction deletes at least one currently positive arc. Thus \[d=\sum_{i=1}^{q}h^i,\qquad q\le |\operatorname{supp}(d)|,\qquad h^i\sqsubseteq d.\] A direct implementation that searches the current support for each component runs in \(O(|\operatorname{supp}(d)|(|V|+|A|))\) time. If \(d\in\mathbb Z^A\), every bottleneck and component can be chosen integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated bottleneck extraction of supported cycles and then maximal paths constructs a conformal decomposition, removes an arc at every step, uses at most one component per initially nonzero arc, and preserves integrality.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is finite and \(d\in\mathbb R^A\).
Each nonzero coordinate of \(d\) is represented by a nonnegative arc in its signed direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d=\sum_{i=1}^{q}h^i,\quad q\le |\operatorname{supp}(d)|,\quad h^i\sqsubseteq d;\qquad d\in\mathbb Z^A\Longrightarrow h^i\in\mathbb Z^A.

h is sign-compatible with and coordinatewise dominated by d
set of arcs where d is nonzero

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational algorithm for a capacitated minimum-cost flow problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize with a feasible flow $f$. While there is an unsaturated negative-cost cycle $C$, let $\delta(C)$ be its augmentation limit. If $\delta(C)<\infty$, replace $f$ by $f+\delta(C)h^C$ and repeat. If $\delta(C)=\infty$, terminate with optimal value $-\infty$. If no unsaturated negative-cost cycle exists, terminate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start from a feasible flow and repeatedly augment as far as possible around an unsaturated negative-cost cycle. A finite augmentation produces another feasible flow; an infinite augmentation limit certifies cost unbounded below; absence of such a cycle terminates the method.
assumptions_latex: $f$ is a feasible flow in a capacitated costed network.
$C$ is an unsaturated cycle of negative cost when an augmentation is performed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta(C)<\infty\Rightarrow f+\delta(C)h^C\text{ is the next feasible iterate};\quad \delta(C)=\infty\Rightarrow \inf c^{\mathsf T}f=-\infty.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Difference of Two b-Flows as a Residual Circulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For two feasible b-flows, records their signed arcwise difference on the bidirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(G,u,b,c)$ be a minimum-cost-flow instance and let $f,f'$ be $b$-flows in $(G,u)$. For each $e\in E(G)$, define $g(e)=\max\{0,f'(e)-f(e)\}$ and $g(\overleftarrow e)=\max\{0,f(e)-f'(e)\}$. Then $g$ is a circulation on $\overleftrightarrow G$, $g(a)=0$ for every $a\notin E(G_f)$, and $c(g)=c(f')-c(f)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given two feasible b-flows, their positive arcwise differences in each direction form a circulation supported on the residual network, whose cost equals the cost difference between the flows.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A node-potential certificate for \(x\) is a vector \(\pi\in\mathbb R^V\) satisfying \[\bar c_e^R:=c_e^R+\pi_v-\pi_w\ge0\qquad\text{for every residual arc }e=(v,w).\] The inequalities are invariant under adding a common constant to all potentials. They are finitely checkable from \(x\), the arc data, and \(\pi\). Because potentials telescope around every directed residual cycle, the inequalities imply that every such cycle has nonnegative total residual cost and therefore certify optimality of \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Node potentials certify optimality when adding each tail potential and subtracting each head potential makes every residual arc cost nonnegative.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an original arc \(a=(v,w)\), define \(\bar c_a=c_a+\pi_v-\pi_w\). Its forward residual copy, present when \(x_a<u_a\), has reduced cost \(\bar c_a\); its reverse copy, present when \(x_a>l_a\), has reduced cost \(-\bar c_a\). Hence a residual reduced-cost certificate consists of the verifiable inequalities \[x_a<u_a\Rightarrow\bar c_a\ge0,\qquad x_a>l_a\Rightarrow\bar c_a\le0.\] Equivalently, \(\bar c_e^R\ge0\) for every residual arc \(e\), which certifies that \(x\) is minimum-cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute reduced costs on every available forward and reverse residual arc; their nonnegativity is an arcwise certificate that the feasible flow is optimal.

knowledge_statements.title: Network Complementary Slackness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded linear-flow complementary slackness in reduced-cost form.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each nonfixed arc \(a\) with \(l_a<u_a\), network complementary slackness requires \[x_a=l_a\Rightarrow\bar c_a\ge0,\qquad l_a<x_a<u_a\Rightarrow\bar c_a=0,\qquad x_a=u_a\Rightarrow\bar c_a\le0.\] If \(l_a=u_a\), that fixed arc imposes no reduced-cost sign restriction. A feasible flow \(x\) is minimum-cost if and only if there exists \(\pi\in\mathbb R^V\) satisfying these conditions. Equivalently, every residual arc has nonnegative reduced cost under \(\pi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible flow is optimal exactly when suitable node potentials make reduced costs nonnegative at lower bounds, zero in arc interiors, and nonpositive at upper bounds on nonfixed arcs; fixed arcs impose no sign restriction.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is feasible for \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Bx=b,\ l\le x\le u\}\).
For \(a=(v,w)\), define \(\bar c_a=c_a+\pi_v-\pi_w\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) and \(\pi\) certify optimality exactly when the reduced-cost sign matches each nonfixed arc's bound status, while fixed arcs impose no sign restriction.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient primal-dual optimality conditions for uncapacitated minimum-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any uncapacitated minimum-cost flow problem, \(\mathbf f\) and \(\mathbf p\) are respectively optimal primal and dual solutions if and only if \(\mathbf A\mathbf f=\mathbf b\), \(\mathbf f\ge0\), and, for every arc \((i,j)\in\mathcal A\), \(p_i-p_j\le c_{ij}\) and \(f_{ij}(c_{ij}-p_i+p_j)=0\). Equivalently, every positive-flow arc satisfies \(p_i-p_j=c_{ij}\), while an arc with \(p_i-p_j<c_{ij}\) carries zero flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible flow and feasible node-potential vector are jointly optimal exactly when every positive-flow arc has zero reduced cost, or equivalently every arc with positive reduced cost carries no flow.

\(\mathbf f\) and \(\mathbf p\) have the primal-flow and dual-potential dimensions of the problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Node–Arc Incidence Matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Head-positive incidence convention for finite directed networks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The node–arc incidence matrix of \(G\) is \(B\in\{-1,0,1\}^{V\times A}\). For a nonloop arc \(a\), its entries are \[B_{v,a}=\begin{cases}-1,&v=\operatorname{tail}(a),\\1,&v=\operatorname{head}(a),\\0,&\text{otherwise},\end{cases}\] while a loop has a zero column. Thus, for every arc-flow vector \(x\in\mathbb R^A\), \((Bx)_v\) is total inflow minus total outflow at \(v\), and \(\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}B=0\). If the underlying undirected graph has \(q\) connected components, then \(\operatorname{rank}(B)=|V|-q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonloop directed incidence column has minus one at its tail and plus one at its head, while a loop has a zero column. Matrix multiplication gives inflow minus outflow, all columns sum to zero, and a graph with q weakly connected components has incidence-matrix rank |V|-q.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph, and loops are represented by zero columns.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x\in\mathbb R^A\), \((Bx)_v\) equals inflow minus outflow at node \(v\), \(\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}B=0\), and \(\operatorname{rank}(B)=|V|-q\) when \(G\) has \(q\) weakly connected components.

notation.meaning: tail and head of arc a

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the weak components of \(G\) have vertex sets \(V_1,\ldots,V_q\), then \[\operatorname{im}B=\left\{b\in\mathbb R^V:\sum_{v\in V_i}b_v=0\text{ for every }i\right\}.\] Its kernel \(\ker B=\{x:Bx=0\}\) is the signed circulation space, and \[\dim\ker B=|A|-|V|+q.\] Zero loop columns contribute independent circulation coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The image consists exactly of balance vectors summing to zero on every weak component, while the kernel is the circulation space of dimension arcs minus vertices plus components.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a finite directed graph with \(q\) weakly connected components.
\(B\) has minus one at each nonloop arc tail and plus one at its head.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{im}B=\{b:\sum_{v\in V_i}b_v=0\ \forall i\}\) and \(\dim\ker B=|A|-|V|+q\).

notation.meaning: vertex set of the ith weak component

knowledge_statements.title: Image and Circulation Spaces of an Incidence Matrix

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Transpose as the Node-Potential Difference Operator
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adjoint representation associated with the head-positive incidence convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every node vector \(\pi\in\mathbb R^V\) and nonloop arc \(a=(v,w)\), \[(B^{\mathsf T}\pi)_a=\pi_w-\pi_v.\] The coordinate of a loop is zero. Moreover, \[\ker B^{\mathsf T}=\{\pi:\pi\text{ is constant on every weak component of }G\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The transpose maps node potentials to head-minus-tail differences, and its kernel consists of potentials constant on each weak component.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is the head-positive incidence matrix of a finite directed graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((B^{\mathsf T}\pi)_{(v,w)}=\pi_w-\pi_v\), and \(B^{\mathsf T}\pi=0\) exactly when \(\pi\) is componentwise constant.
knowledge_statements.title: Transpose as the Node-Potential Difference Operator

children.title: Total Unimodularity Structure
children.top_down_role: Determinantal structure inherited by network matrices and related constraint systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Total Unimodularity Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Total unimodularity of directed node–arc incidence matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every square submatrix \(M\) of the directed node–arc incidence matrix \(B\), \[\det(M)\in\{-1,0,1\}.\] Therefore \(B\) is totally unimodular. Total unimodularity is preserved by deleting rows or columns, transposing, duplicating rows or columns, and multiplying a row or column by \(-1\). In particular, deleting one incidence row from each weakly connected component produces a full-row-rank totally unimodular reduced incidence matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every square minor of a directed node–arc incidence matrix is zero, plus one, or minus one, so the matrix is totally unimodular; deleting one row per weakly connected component yields a full-row-rank totally unimodular reduced incidence matrix.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is the node–arc incidence matrix of a finite directed graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every square subdeterminant of \(B\) belongs to \(\{-1,0,1\}\); hence \(B\) is totally unimodular.

notation.meaning: an arbitrary square submatrix of B

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural total-unimodularity certificate covering directed incidence matrices and their submatrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\in\{0,1,-1\}^{m\times n}\). If every column contains at most one \(+1\) and at most one \(-1\), then \(M\) is totally unimodular. In particular, every directed node–arc incidence matrix and every matrix obtained from it by deleting rows or columns satisfy this condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero-plus-minus-one matrix with at most one plus one and at most one minus one in each column is totally unimodular; directed incidence matrices satisfy this condition.
assumptions_latex: Every column of \(M\) has at most one \(+1\) and at most one \(-1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every square subdeterminant of \(M\) belongs to \(\{-1,0,1\}\).

notation.meaning: signed-column matrix satisfying the stated condition

knowledge_statements.title: Signed-Column Certificate for Total Unimodularity

children.title: Integral Polyhedral Consequences
children.top_down_role: Integrality effects for feasible flow polyhedra with integral network data.

assumptions_latex: The directed graph \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, and \(A\) is its node-arc incidence matrix.
The vectors \(b\in\mathbb Z^V\) and \(\ell,u\in\mathbb Z^E\) satisfy \(\ell\le u\), and the polyhedron \(P\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The polyhedron \(P\) is integral; every vertex of \(P\) belongs to \(\mathbb Z^E\), and every nonempty face of \(P\) contains an integral point.

notation.meaning: Finite directed graph with node set V and arc set E.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite capacitated flows with integral node balances and finite integral lower and upper bounds.

source_refs.locator: Section 3. Counterparts of Network Flow Theorems p. 188
source_refs.source_title: Combinatorial Optimization: Networks and Matroids

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite directed graph with node-arc incidence matrix \(A\). For \(b\in\mathbb Z^V\) and \(\ell,u\in\mathbb Z^E\) satisfying \(\ell\le u\), suppose that \[P=\{x\in\mathbb R^E:Ax=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\] is nonempty. Then \(P\) is an integral polyhedron. In particular, every vertex of \(P\) belongs to \(\mathbb Z^E\), and every nonempty face of \(P\) contains an integral point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite directed graph, integral node balances and finite integral arc bounds define an integral nonempty flow polyhedron: all its vertices are integral, and each nonempty face contains an integral point.
knowledge_statements.title: Integral Polyhedral Consequences

children.title: Flow-Polytope Vertices
children.top_down_role: Combinatorial structure of extreme feasible flows.

assumptions_latex: The flow polytope \(P=\{x:Ax=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\) is nonempty.
The incidence matrix has rank \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible flow \(x\) is a vertex exactly when \(\operatorname{rank}(A_{F(x)})=|F(x)|\).

notation.meaning: Arcs whose flows are strictly between their bounds.
Incidence submatrix indexed by the arc set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex characterization for bounded network-flow polytopes.

source_refs.locator: 5.6 Faces, facets, and vertices p. 63
source_refs.source_title: Combinatorial Optimization: Polyhedra and Efficiency

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in P\), let \(F(x)=\{e\in E:\ell_e<x_e<u_e\}\). Then \(x\) is a vertex of \(P\) if and only if the columns of \(A_{F(x)}\) are linearly independent. For an incidence matrix, this is equivalent to the undirected edge set underlying \(F(x)\) containing no cycle. Thus every vertex has at most \(r\) arcs strictly between their bounds, while all remaining arcs are fixed at lower or upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible flow is a vertex precisely when its strictly non-bound arcs form an incidence-independent set, equivalently an undirected forest.
knowledge_statements.title: Flow-Polytope Vertices

children.title: Flow-Polytope Faces
children.top_down_role: Substructures induced by active capacity or balance restrictions.

assumptions_latex: The bounded flow polytope \(P=\{x:Ax=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every nonempty face equals some nonempty \(F_{L,U}\), and \(\dim F_{L,U}=|R|-\operatorname{rank}(A_R)\).

notation.meaning: Face obtained by fixing arcs at selected bounds.
Arcs not fixed by the selected bounds.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Active-bound representation and dimension of nonempty flow-polytope faces.

source_refs.locator: 5.6 Faces, facets, and vertices p. 63
source_refs.source_title: Combinatorial Optimization: Polyhedra and Efficiency

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For disjoint \(L,U\subseteq E\), define
\[
F_{L,U}=\{x\in P:x_e=\ell_e\text{ for }e\in L,\ x_e=u_e\text{ for }e\in U\}.
\]
Every nonempty face of \(P\) has this form for suitable \(L\) and \(U\). If \(R=E\setminus(L\cup U)\) and the relative interior of the face has all coordinates in \(R\) strictly between their bounds, then
\[
\dim F_{L,U}=|R|-\operatorname{rank}(A_R).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonempty flow-polytope face is obtained by fixing selected arcs at lower or upper bounds; its dimension follows from the remaining incidence rank.
knowledge_statements.title: Flow-Polytope Faces

source_witnesses.locator: 5.6 Faces, facets, and vertices p. 63
source_witnesses.source_title: Combinatorial Optimization: Polyhedra and Efficiency

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Codimension-one criterion for lower- and upper-arc-bound faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) have positive relative dimension \(d\). For an arc \(e\), a nonempty lower-bound face \(F_e^\ell=P\cap\{x_e=\ell_e\}\) is a facet exactly when \(\dim F_e^\ell=d-1\); the same criterion holds for \(F_e^u=P\cap\{x_e=u_e\}\). Using the active-bound dimension formula, this is equivalent to the remaining free incidence columns leaving exactly \(d-1\) feasible degrees of freedom. An empty tight set, a bound tight throughout P, or a tight set of dimension below \(d-1\) does not define a facet.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arc bound defines a facet exactly when its nonempty tight set has codimension one; empty, universally tight, and higher-codimension cases are not facets.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is nonempty and has positive relative dimension d.
Dimensions are taken in \(\operatorname{aff}(P)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_e^\ell\text{ or }F_e^u\text{ is a facet}\iff \dim F=d-1.

notation.meaning: Lower- and upper-bound faces of arc e.

knowledge_statements.title: Arc-Bound Facet Criterion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A linear objective exposing any nonempty face specified by selected arc bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For disjoint \(L,U\subseteq E\), set \[q_e=\begin{cases}1,&e\in L,\\-1,&e\in U,\\0,&e\notin L\cup U.\end{cases}\] If \(F_{L,U}\ne\varnothing\), then \[F_{L,U}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in P}q^{\mathsf T}x.\] Thus every bound-fixed face in the seed representation is explicitly exposed by a linear cost vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign positive coefficients to designated lower-bound arcs and negative coefficients to designated upper-bound arcs to expose their nonempty bound-fixed face.
assumptions_latex: \(P=\{x:Ax=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\) is nonempty.
\(L\cap U=\varnothing\) and \(F_{L,U}\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_{L,U}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in P}q^{\mathsf T}x.

notation.meaning: Cost vector exposing the selected bound-fixed face.

knowledge_statements.title: Explicit Exposure of Bound-Fixed Faces

children.title: Flow-Polytope Adjacency
children.top_down_role: Neighborhood relations among extreme feasible flows.

assumptions_latex: The points \(x\ne y\) are vertices of the flow polytope \(P\).
The dimension \(d=\dim P\) is positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The vertices \(x,y\) are adjacent exactly when \(\dim F(x,y)=1\).

notation.meaning: Smallest face of the polytope containing both vertices.
Constraints active at both vertices, considered within the affine hull.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-skeleton adjacency through common active arc bounds.

source_refs.locator: Section 4.1. Size of Vertices and Faces p. 75
source_refs.source_title: Combinatorial Optimization: Theory and Algorithms

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F(x,y)\) be the intersection of all faces of \(P\) containing distinct vertices \(x\) and \(y\). The vertices are adjacent in the one-skeleton of \(P\) if and only if
\[
\dim F(x,y)=1.
\]
Equivalently, within the \(d\)-dimensional affine hull of \(P\), the lower- and upper-bound constraints active at both \(x\) and \(y\) have rank \(d-1\). These common active bounds therefore leave exactly one feasible degree of freedom.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two flow vertices are adjacent exactly when their smallest common face is one-dimensional, equivalently when common active bounds leave one feasible degree of freedom.
knowledge_statements.title: Flow-Polytope Adjacency

source_witnesses.locator: Section 4.1. Size of Vertices and Faces p. 75
source_witnesses.source_title: Combinatorial Optimization: Theory and Algorithms

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Network-specific representation of one-dimensional flow-polytope faces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x:Ax=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\), where \(A\) is a directed incidence matrix. Every edge direction of \(P\) is a nonzero scalar multiple of a circuit of \(A\). For a loopless directed network, the circuit support is an undirected simple cycle, including a two-edge parallel cycle when applicable, with signs describing a circulation around it. Hence adjacent vertices differ only along one signed cycle. Conversely, if fixing every coordinate outside such a circuit leaves a nondegenerate feasible segment, that segment is a one-dimensional face and its endpoints are adjacent vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every edge of a bounded flow polytope moves along one signed incidence circuit, or network cycle; a nondegenerate feasible circuit section is an edge.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a nonempty bounded flow polytope.
Dimensions and faces are relative to \(\operatorname{aff}(P)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x,y\text{ adjacent}\Longrightarrow y-x=\alpha g_C\text{ for an incidence circuit }g_C\text{ and }\alpha\ne0.
knowledge_statements.title: Circuit Directions of Flow-Polytope Edges

children.title: Tree-Basis Degeneracy Geometry
children.top_down_role: Tree representations, nonuniqueness, and degenerate bases.

children.title: Spanning-Tree Bases
children.top_down_role: Tree-supported basis representations of feasible network flows.

assumptions_latex: The underlying undirected graph is connected and has \(n\) nodes.
One row is deleted from its node-arc incidence matrix \(A\), producing \(\bar A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A set \(B\subseteq E\) is a column basis of \(\bar A\) exactly when \(B\) is a spanning tree.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Column bases of a reduced incidence matrix.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Simplex Methods for Min-Cost Flow p. 169
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a connected graph on \(n\) nodes, the reduced incidence matrix \(\bar A\) has rank \(n-1\). A set \(B\subseteq E\) with \(|B|=n-1\) satisfies
\[
\det(\bar A_B)\ne0
\]
if and only if the underlying undirected arcs in \(B\) form a spanning tree. Consequently, each network-simplex basis can be represented by a spanning tree, with every nonbasic arc assigned to one of its bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The column bases of a reduced incidence matrix are exactly the graph's spanning trees; nonbasic arcs are placed at bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Spanning-Tree Bases

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Simplex Methods for Min-Cost Flow p. 169
source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unique Basic Flow Determined by a Tree and Bound Assignments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic reconstruction associated with a bounded-flow tree basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partition the arcs into a spanning-tree basis \(T\) and nonbasic set \(N\), and prescribe each \(x_e\), \(e\in N\), at either \(\ell_e\) or \(u_e\). For the reduced incidence system \(\bar A x=\bar b\), the balances uniquely determine \[x_T=\bar A_T^{-1}(\bar b-\bar A_Nx_N).\] The resulting basis is primal feasible if and only if \(\ell_T\le x_T\le u_T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A spanning tree and bound assignments on all non-tree arcs uniquely determine the tree flows; the basis is feasible exactly when those flows satisfy their bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar A_T\) is a spanning-tree column basis of a reduced incidence matrix.
Every nonbasic arc is assigned one of its bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The unique basic vector is \(x_T=\bar A_T^{-1}(\bar b-\bar A_Nx_N)\), and it is feasible exactly when \(\ell_T\le x_T\le u_T\).

notation.meaning: basic tree arcs and nonbasic arcs

knowledge_statements.title: Unique Basic Flow Determined by a Tree and Bound Assignments

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise extension of the spanning-tree basis correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite directed graph have \(q\) weakly connected components, and delete one incidence row from each component to obtain \(\bar A\). Then \(\operatorname{rank}(\bar A)=|V|-q\). A set \(F\subseteq E\) of \(|V|-q\) columns is a basis of \(\bar A\) if and only if its underlying undirected edges form a spanning forest containing one spanning tree in every weak component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After deleting one incidence row per weak component, column bases are exactly component-spanning forests and have vertices minus components arcs.
assumptions_latex: The directed graph is finite and has \(q\) weakly connected components.
One incidence row is deleted from each weak component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar A_F\) is nonsingular exactly when \(F\) contains one spanning tree of every weak component.
knowledge_statements.title: Spanning-Forest Bases for Disconnected Networks

children.title: Degenerate Basis Geometry
children.top_down_role: Basic representations containing bound-active or zero-change structural elements.

assumptions_latex: A feasible network-simplex basis consists of a spanning tree \(B\) and nonbasic arcs fixed at bounds.
The associated basic flow is \(x_B\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The basis is degenerate exactly when \(x_e\in\{\ell_e,u_e\}\) for some \(e\in B\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degeneracy of bounded-variable network-simplex bases.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Simplex Methods for Min-Cost Flow p. 169
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B\) be a spanning-tree basis and fix each arc in \(E\setminus B\) at either its lower or upper bound. The balance equations uniquely determine \(x_B\). This feasible basis is degenerate if and only if at least one basic arc also satisfies
\[
x_e=\ell_e\quad\text{or}\quad x_e=u_e.
\]
Geometrically, the represented vertex then lies on more active bound hyperplanes than are required, so a basis pivot may change the tree without moving the flow vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A network basis is degenerate precisely when a tree arc is itself at a bound, allowing basis changes that may leave the represented flow unchanged.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Basis Geometry

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Simplex Methods for Min-Cost Flow p. 169
source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

children.title: Basis Nonuniqueness
children.top_down_role: Multiplicity of tree representations for the same flow-polytope point.

assumptions_latex: The feasible flow \(x\) is a vertex of a bounded network-flow polytope.
A basis representation uses a spanning tree and fixes every non-tree arc at a bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Basis representations of \(x\) are nonunique exactly when two distinct spanning trees satisfy the stated bound assignment and balance equations for \(x\).

notation.meaning: Set of spanning-tree basis representations of the vertex.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Noninjectivity of the map from tree bases to flow vertices.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 5. Simplex Methods for Min-Cost Flow p. 169
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal B(x)\) contain every spanning tree \(B\) such that each arc outside \(B\) is at a bound in \(x\), while the tree equations reproduce \(x_B\). Then the basis representation of \(x\) is nonunique if and only if
\[
|\mathcal B(x)|>1.
\]
Distinct members of \(\mathcal B(x)\) represent the same geometric vertex. Such nonuniqueness can occur only at a degenerate representation, because exchanging a basic arc without changing \(x\) requires a basic arc to be active at a bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A flow vertex has nonunique bases when distinct spanning trees, with their non-tree arcs fixed at bounds, reproduce the same flow; this requires degeneracy.
knowledge_statements.title: Basis Nonuniqueness

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 5. Simplex Methods for Min-Cost Flow p. 169
source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Degeneracy Does Not Imply Basis Nonuniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp converse boundary for the seed's necessary degeneracy condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider two nodes joined by one nonloop arc \(e\), with \(0\le x_e\le1\) and zero balance at both nodes. The only feasible flow is \(x_e=0\), and \(\{e\}\) is the unique spanning tree. Its basis is degenerate because the basic arc is at its lower bound, but the vertex has only one tree-basis representation. Thus basis nonuniqueness implies degeneracy, whereas degeneracy need not imply basis nonuniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A one-arc, two-node network has a unique degenerate tree basis, so degeneracy is necessary but not sufficient for basis nonuniqueness.
assumptions_latex: The graph has two nodes and one directed nonloop arc \(e\).
The bounds are \(0\le x_e\le1\), and both node balances are zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sole feasible vertex has a degenerate but unique tree-basis representation.

notation.meaning: the unique arc and unique spanning-tree edge

knowledge_statements.title: Degeneracy Does Not Imply Basis Nonuniqueness

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basis Forests as Completions of the Free-Arc Forest
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Componentwise combinatorial description of all incidence bases representing one bounded-flow vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) have \(q\) weak components, let \(x\) be a vertex of \(P=\{x:Ax=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\), and put \(F(x)=\{e:\ell_e<x_e<u_e\}\). A component-spanning forest \(T\) represents \(x\) as a bounded-variable incidence basis if and only if \[F(x)\subseteq T.\] Hence \[\mathcal B(x)=\{T:T\text{ contains one spanning tree of each weak component and }F(x)\subseteq T\}.\] In a weakly connected graph these are precisely the spanning-tree completions of \(F(x)\). Basis representations are nonunique exactly when this completion family has more than one member.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All incidence bases representing a flow vertex are exactly the component-spanning forests containing its strictly interior arcs; nonuniqueness is multiplicity of such completions.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite directed graph with \(q\) weakly connected components.
\(x\) is a vertex of the bounded flow polytope \(P\).
One redundant incidence row is removed from each weak component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal B(x)=\{T:T\text{ is component-spanning and }F(x)\subseteq T\}\).

notation.meaning: arcs strictly between their bounds at x

knowledge_statements.title: Basis Forests as Completions of the Free-Arc Forest
