children.title: Arc-Data Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Stability under arc-data changes.

children.title: Arc-Cost Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Stability of optimal flows, prices, and bases under changes to arc costs.

assumptions_latex: The feasible polytope \(P\) is nonempty and independent of the cost vector.
The flow \(x^*\in P\) minimizes \(c^Tx\) over \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The flow \(x^*\) remains optimal under \(c+\delta c\) exactly when \(c+\delta c\in\mathcal C_P(x^*)\).

notation.meaning: Cost vectors for which the flow is optimal.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact optimality region for perturbations of linear arc costs.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 6. Dual Ascent Methods for Min-Cost Flow p. 213
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the minimizing cost cone at \(x^*\) by
\[
\mathcal C_P(x^*)=\{q\in\mathbb R^E:q^T(y-x^*)\ge0\text{ for every }y\in P\}.
\]
For a cost perturbation \(\delta c\), the flow \(x^*\) remains optimal if and only if \(c+\delta c\in\mathcal C_P(x^*)\). Moreover, the optimal value
\[
v(c)=\min_{x\in P}c^Tx
\]
is a concave, piecewise-linear function of \(c\), and every optimal flow at \(c\) is a supergradient of \(v\) there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A flow remains optimal exactly while the perturbed cost stays in its minimizing normal cone; the optimal value is concave and piecewise linear in costs.
knowledge_statements.title: Arc-Cost Sensitivity

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 6. Dual Ascent Methods for Min-Cost Flow p. 213
source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact residual-cycle stability interval for changing one original arc cost while retaining a fixed optimal flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^*\) be optimal and change only the cost of original arc \(a\) from \(c_a\) to \(c_a+\delta\). For each residual directed cycle \(C\), let \(\sigma_a(C)\) be its number of forward residual copies of \(a\) minus its number of reverse residual copies. Define \[L_a:=\sup_{C:\,\sigma_a(C)>0}\frac{-c^R(C)}{\sigma_a(C)},\qquad U_a:=\inf_{C:\,\sigma_a(C)<0}\frac{c^R(C)}{-\sigma_a(C)},\] with an empty supremum equal to \(-\infty\) and an empty infimum equal to \(+\infty\). Then \(x^*\) remains optimal exactly when \(L_a\le\delta\le U_a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact allowable change to one arc cost is the interval imposed by residual cycles using that arc forward or backward.
assumptions_latex: \(x^*\) is feasible and optimal for a finite bounded linear minimum-cost flow problem.
Only the cost of one original arc \(a\) changes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\text{ remains optimal}\iff L_a\le\delta\le U_a.

notation.meaning: signed use of the perturbed original arc by residual cycle C

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Arc Cost Allowable Interval

children.title: Arc-Capacity Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Stability of feasibility and optimal structure under changes to arc capacities.

assumptions_latex: The value \(v(u)=\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ 0\le x\le u\}\) is finite near the capacity vector \(u\).
The set \(D^*(u)\) of optimal dual solutions is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For admissible \(d\), \(v'(u;d)=\max_{(\pi,\beta)\in D^*(u)}(-\beta^Td)\).

notation.meaning: Optimal value as a function of capacities.
Nonnegative dual multiplier for the upper-capacity constraints.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional value sensitivity for upper arc capacities.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 4. The Min-Cost Flow Problem p. 151
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For fixed \(A,b,c\), the finite value function
\[
v(u)=\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ 0\le x\le u\}
\]
is componentwise nonincreasing and convex on each convex region where the problem is feasible. If \(D^*(u)\) is the set of optimal dual solutions and \(\beta\ge0\) denotes the multiplier of \(x\le u\), then every feasible directional derivative satisfies
\[
v'(u;d)=\max_{(\pi,\beta)\in D^*(u)}(-\beta^Td).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual-Cut Characterization of a Feasible Balanced Perturbation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient feasibility test for a simultaneous balanced change of node imbalances, relative to a feasible bounded flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Use the outflow-minus-inflow incidence convention and let \(x\) satisfy \(Ax=b\) and \(\ell\le x\le u\). Form the residual digraph with forward capacity \(u_{ij}-x_{ij}\) and reverse capacity \(x_{ij}-\ell_{ij}\). A perturbation \(d\in\mathbb R^V\) can be realized by some \(x'\) satisfying \(Ax'=b+d\) and \(\ell\le x'\le u\) if and only if \[d(V)=0\quad\text{and}\quad d(S)\le r\bigl(\delta^+(S)\bigr)\quad\text{for every }S\subseteq V,\] where \(r\) denotes residual capacity. Equivalently, the residual network admits a correction flow whose node imbalance is \(d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A balanced node-imbalance change is feasible exactly when every vertex set can send its required net additional outflow through the current residual capacities.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) uses the outflow-minus-inflow convention.
\(Ax=b\) and \(\ell\le x\le u\).
All residual capacities are finite and nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists x'\in[\ell,u]\text{ with }Ax'=b+d\iff d(V)=0\text{ and }d(S)\le r(\delta^+(S))\ \forall S\subseteq V.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fixed-Basis Stability Under Balanced Imbalance Changes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact stability region of an already dual-feasible bounded-variable basis when only node imbalances change.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((B,L,U)\) be an optimal bounded-variable basis for \(Ax=b\), \(\ell\le x\le u\), with nonsingular \(A_B\). Keep costs, bounds, and nonbasic bound statuses fixed, and perturb the balance to \(b+d\). In a full-row-rank incidence representation, the recomputed basic variables are \[x'_B=x_B+A_B^{-1}d.\] Because costs and the basis are unchanged, all reduced costs and hence dual feasibility are unchanged. Therefore the fixed basis remains primal-dual optimal if and only if \[\ell_B\le x_B+A_B^{-1}d\le u_B.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a fixed optimal basis, a compatible balanced imbalance perturbation preserves optimality exactly while the recomputed basic flows remain within their bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(A_B\) is nonsingular in a full-row-rank incidence representation.
The original bounded-variable basis is primal and dual optimal.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Polyhedral Value Function for Balanced Imbalances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint value sensitivity for arbitrary balanced node-imbalance vectors; coordinate supply and demand specializations remain in sibling leaves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed costs and bounds, define \[v(\beta)=\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=\beta,\ \ell\le x\le u\},\] with value \(+\infty\) when infeasible. Then \(v\) is a proper convex polyhedral function on the feasible balance polytope and has the dual representation \[v(\beta)=\max_{p\in\mathbb R^V}\left[p^{\mathsf T}\beta+\sum_{e\in E}\min_{\ell_e\le z\le u_e}\bigl(c_e-(A^{\mathsf T}p)_e\bigr)z\right].\] If \(p^*\) is dual optimal at \(b\), then for every balanced perturbation \(d\), \[v(b+d)\ge v(b)+(p^*)^{\mathsf T}d.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum cost is a convex polyhedral function of the balanced node-imbalance vector, and optimal node prices give a joint subgradient bound for every balanced perturbation.
assumptions_latex: The finite network has fixed linear costs and finite arc bounds.
The balance vector \(b\) is feasible.
Strong linear-programming duality applies.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p^*\in\partial v(b),\qquad v(b+d)\ge v(b)+(p^*)^{\mathsf T}d.

Balanced Imbalance Perturbations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility condition for perturbing node supplies in a capacitated transshipment model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) have node-arc incidence matrix \(A\), with each column containing one \(+1\) and one \(-1\). A perturbation \(d\in\mathbb R^V\) of a balance vector \(b\) is balanced precisely when
\[\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}d=\sum_{v\in V}d_v=0.\]
Thus \(b+d\) preserves the necessary conservation identity \(\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}(b+d)=0\). Balancedness alone does not guarantee feasibility under arc bounds; feasibility additionally requires \(b+d\) to belong to \(\{Ax:\ell\le x\le u\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A node-imbalance change must sum to zero. This preserves global conservation but does not by itself ensure that capacities permit the perturbed balances.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) is the incidence matrix of a directed graph.
\(\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}b=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The perturbation preserves global balance if and only if \(\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}d=0\).

notation.meaning: Original node balances and their perturbation.

children.title: Parametric Flow Structure
children.top_down_role: Changes in optimal network structure across controlled parameter ranges.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Piecewise-affine structure for a scalar affine balance family with fixed costs and bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \[v(\lambda)=\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b^0+\lambda d,\ \ell\le x\le u\},\qquad \mathbf1^{\mathsf T}b^0=\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}d=0,\] with fixed \(A,c,\ell,u\). Its feasible parameter set is an interval, possibly empty or unbounded. On every subinterval where one dual-feasible bounded-flow basis remains primal feasible, its basic flow is affine in \(\lambda\), its nonbasic arcs remain at their bounds, and it is optimal. Because only finitely many bases and statuses occur, the finite value function is convex and piecewise affine on the feasible parameter interval. For a fixed basis, reduced costs are constant; basiswise intervals end through basic-flow bound events, although degeneracy may permit overlapping optimal bases or a basis change without a unique optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With affine node balances and fixed network data, stable bases give affine optimal flows and the value is convex piecewise affine. Reduced costs stay constant for each retained basis, so its interval is limited by primal bound events, subject to degeneracy.
assumptions_latex: The graph, incidence matrix, costs, and finite arc bounds are fixed.
The value is finite on the parameter interval considered.
Balances depend affinely on one scalar parameter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_B(\lambda)\text{ is affine on each stable-basis interval, and }v(\lambda)\text{ is convex piecewise affine}.

notation.meaning: Flow induced by a retained bounded-flow basis.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Right-Hand-Side Parametric Flow Structure
Parametric Flow Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-parameter right-hand-side sensitivity with fixed costs and capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[v(\lambda)=\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b^0+\lambda d,\ \ell\le x\le u\},\]
where \(\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}b^0=\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}d=0\). On every interval of parameters having a common optimal nondegenerate basis, the associated basic flow is affine in \(\lambda\), while its nonbasic arcs remain at bounds. The interval ends when a basic arc reaches a bound or an optimality condition becomes tight. Over any interval on which the problem is feasible, \(v\) is a convex piecewise-affine function of \(\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With affine node balances and fixed network data, each stable optimal basis yields an affine flow; basis events partition the feasible parameter range, and the value is convex piecewise affine.
assumptions_latex: The graph and \(A,c,\ell,u\) are fixed.
The minimum is finite throughout the parameter interval considered.
A basis is interpreted in the bounded network-linear-program sense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Optimal flows are basiswise affine in \(\lambda\), and \(v(\lambda)\) is convex and piecewise affine.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The convex piecewise-affine value claim is standard, but no source is supplied. Moreover, with fixed costs and capacities, reduced costs for a fixed basis do not vary with the right-hand-side parameter, so the claimed optimality-condition breakpoint requires correction or a broader data-variation model.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual Repair of a Primal Warm Start
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact repair after a balanced change in node imbalances with fixed network and bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) satisfy \(Ax=b\) and \(\ell\le x\le u\), and let \(d\) satisfy \(\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}d=0\). Build the capacitated residual network of \(x\) and find a signed residual flow \(y\) satisfying \(Ay=d\). If one exists, \(x'=x+y\) satisfies \(Ax'=b+d\) and the original bounds and is a feasible primal warm start. Such a correction exists if and only if the updated fixed-network, fixed-bound instance is feasible. It may be found by an auxiliary max-flow or feasible-circulation computation, after which any primal-feasible minimum-cost-flow method may reoptimize from \(x'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Route the balance change through the old flow's residual network. A successful correction produces a feasible warm start; under unchanged bounds and network, correction failure exactly means the updated instance is infeasible.
assumptions_latex: \(Ax=b\) and \(\ell\le x\le u\).
The incidence matrix and arc bounds are unchanged.
\(\mathbf1^{\mathsf T}d=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists y\text{ residual with }Ay=d\iff \exists x'\text{ with }Ax'=b+d,\ \ell\le x'\le u.
knowledge_statements.title: Residual Repair of a Primal Warm Start

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact condition for carrying an old flow unchanged into a modified instance on a fixed arc set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be a stored flow and let the updated instance on the same arc set have balances \(b'\) and bounds \(\ell',u'\). The unchanged flow is a valid primal warm start if and only if \[Ax=b',\qquad \ell'\le x\le u'.\] Failure rejects only unchanged reuse; it does not imply that the updated instance is infeasible or that x cannot be repaired.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An old flow is directly reusable exactly when it satisfies every updated balance and bound. Failure means repair or replacement is needed, not that the new problem is infeasible.
assumptions_latex: The incidence matrix and arc-coordinate identification are unchanged.
Updated balances and bounds are known.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ is directly reusable}\iff Ax=b'\text{ and }\ell'\le x\le u'.
knowledge_statements.title: Direct Primal-Flow Reuse Test
Primal Warm Starts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual correction of a previously feasible flow after balanced balance changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a flow \(x\) satisfying \(Ax=b\) and \(\ell\le x\le u\), together with a balanced perturbation \(d\). Construct the residual network of \(x\). Find a residual correction \(y\) whose signed arc flow satisfies \(Ay=d\), respecting every residual capacity. Set \(x'=x+y\). If no such correction exists, report that this warm-start repair failed. Otherwise use \(x'\) as the initial feasible flow for a minimum-cost-flow optimization method and stop when its usual residual optimality certificate holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repair the old feasible flow by routing the changed balances through its residual network, then optimize from the repaired flow; failure to find a correction rejects this warm start.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is feasible for the old balances.
\(\mathbf 1^{\mathsf T}d=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A returned correction produces \(Ax'=b+d\) and \(\ell\le x'\le u\).

knowledge_statements.title: Dual Warm Starts
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reuse of node potentials after costs, capacities, or balances change.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be feasible for the updated instance and let \(\pi\in\mathbb R^V\) be inherited node potentials. For each residual arc \((i,j)\), define its updated reduced cost by \(\bar c_{ij}=c_{ij}-\pi_i+\pi_j\), using the residual arc's signed cost. If \(\bar c_{ij}\ge0\) for every residual arc, then every residual cycle has nonnegative cost, so \((x,\pi)\) certifies optimality for the updated instance. If some inequality fails, this particular reduced-cost test is inconclusive: \(\pi\) may still serve as an initialization, but it does not provide this certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every updated residual reduced cost is nonnegative, the inherited prices certify that the updated feasible flow is optimal. If the test fails, the prices may still initialize dual repair, but this certificate is unavailable.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) satisfies the updated balances and arc bounds.
Residual reverse arcs carry the negatives of their forward costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Residual reduced-cost nonnegativity makes \((x,\pi)\) an updated primal-dual optimality certificate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Right-Hand-Side Preservation of a Dual-Feasible Basis
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual-state reuse when only balances change and a network-simplex tree and bound statuses are retained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix arc costs, bounds, a spanning-tree basis \(T\), and the lower/upper statuses of nonbasic arcs. Potentials satisfying \(c_{ij}-\pi_i+\pi_j=0\) on tree arcs are independent of the balance vector. Consequently, changing only balances leaves all nonbasic reduced costs and their required signs unchanged. An inherited dual-feasible basis remains dual feasible; after recomputing its tree flow, bound feasibility gives immediate optimality, while bound violations leave a dual-feasible initialization for dual network simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changing only node balances preserves the reduced-cost feasibility of a retained tree basis. Its recomputed flow is either optimal immediately or provides a dual-feasible start for primal-feasibility repair.
assumptions_latex: Arc costs and bounds are unchanged.
The tree and nonbasic bound statuses remain structurally valid.
The inherited basis is dual feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Dual feasibility persists, and new primal feasibility implies optimality.}
knowledge_statements.title: Right-Hand-Side Preservation of a Dual-Feasible Basis

children.title: Basis Transfer Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Data changes that preserve or invalidate a reusable network basis.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal and dual inequalities defining where a fixed bounded-flow basis remains optimal under affine data variation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a network-simplex tree basis \(B\), its nonbasic lower/upper statuses, and a parameter interval on which the underlying arcs remain available. Let balances, bounds, and costs vary affinely with \(\lambda\). The basis is an optimal basis exactly at parameters for which its induced basic flow satisfies all current bounds and every nonbasic reduced cost has the sign required by its current lower or upper status. Thus its transfer region is the intersection of the corresponding scalar affine inequalities. An endpoint can occur when a basic flow meets a bound or a nonbasic reduced cost becomes zero; equality may create an alternative optimal basis and does not by itself imply loss of optimality until an inequality is crossed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A retained bounded-flow basis remains optimal exactly while its induced flow is primal feasible and its nonbasic reduced costs have the required signs. Bound hits and zero reduced costs delimit, but need not immediately invalidate, its transfer region.
assumptions_latex: The network structure and retained tree basis remain valid.
Balances, finite bounds, and costs vary affinely with a scalar parameter.
Nonbasic arcs retain specified lower or upper statuses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Lambda_B=\{\lambda:\ell(\lambda)\le x_B(\lambda)\le u(\lambda),\ \bar c_N(\lambda)\text{ has the required bound signs}\}.

notation.meaning: Retained bounded network-flow basis and nonbasic statuses.
Parameter region on which B is an optimal basis.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Basis Transfer Region

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Special boundary regime when only node balances vary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If costs, bounds, the tree, and nonbasic statuses are fixed while only \(b(\lambda)\) varies, the tree-induced potentials and all reduced costs are constant. An initially dual-feasible basis therefore remains dual feasible throughout the parameter range; its optimal-basis transfer can fail only when the affine basic flow violates an arc bound or the retained network structure ceases to be valid. A zero reduced cost may already represent degeneracy, but it is not a newly varying breakpoint in this regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a balance-only change with a fixed tree, costs, bounds, and statuses, reduced costs do not move; only primal bound feasibility or structural validity can end basis transfer.
assumptions_latex: Only the node-balance vector varies.
Costs, bounds, tree arcs, and nonbasic statuses are fixed.
The retained basis is initially dual feasible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar c_N(\lambda)=\bar c_N\quad\text{and transfer persists exactly while }\ell\le x_B(\lambda)\le u.

notation.meaning: Tree-basic flow induced by the varying balances.

knowledge_statements.title: Right-Hand-Side-Only Transfer Boundary
Basis Transfer Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Events at which an inherited bounded network-flow basis ceases to remain optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a network basis and vary the instance data continuously. The basis transfers as an optimal basis while its induced basic flow satisfies every arc bound and the reduced costs of nonbasic arcs have the signs required by their active lower or upper bounds. A transfer boundary occurs when either a basic flow reaches a bound, making primal feasibility tight, or a nonbasic reduced cost reaches zero, making dual optimality tight. Beyond such an event, the inherited basis need not be feasible or optimal and a pivot or reoptimization is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An old basis remains usable only while its basic flows respect bounds and nonbasic reduced costs have correct signs. Bound hits and zero reduced costs mark transfer boundaries.
assumptions_latex: The current basis is initially primal and dual feasible.
Data vary continuously along a scalar parameter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The first violated primal-bound or reduced-cost sign condition ends guaranteed optimal-basis transfer.

notation.meaning: Reduced cost of a nonbasic arc.

children.title: Generic Cycle Canceling
children.top_down_role: The foundational residual-cycle framework.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact feasibility and objective effect of one residual-cycle augmentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be feasible and let \(C\) be a directed cycle in its residual network. For \(0<\delta\le\min_{e\in C}r_e\), augmentation by \(\delta\) around \(C\) produces a feasible flow \(x'\) with \(c^{\mathsf T}x'=c^{\mathsf T}x+\delta c(C)\). If \(\delta=\min_{e\in C}r_e\), at least one residual arc of \(C\) is exhausted; if \(c(C)<0\), the objective strictly decreases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual-cycle augmentation preserves feasibility, changes cost by the augmentation amount times the cycle cost, and at the bottleneck exhausts a residual arc.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is feasible.
\(C\) is a directed residual cycle.
\(0<\delta\le\min_{e\in C}r_e\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x'\text{ is feasible and }c^{\mathsf T}x'-c^{\mathsf T}x=\delta c(C).

notation.meaning: Residual capacity of residual arc e.
Total signed residual cost of C.

knowledge_statements.title: One-Step Cycle-Cancellation Identity
Generic Cycle Canceling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational residual negative-cycle algorithm for a feasible minimum-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a feasible flow \(x\) for \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\). Construct its residual network with residual capacities and signed residual costs. While a directed residual cycle \(C\) has \(c(C)<0\), choose such a cycle, set \(\delta=\min_{e\in C}r_e\), and augment \(\delta\) units around \(C\). Stop when no negative-cost residual cycle exists and output \(x\). The output is optimal; with integral finite data, every augmentation preserves integrality and the procedure terminates after finitely many objective-decreasing iterations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly augment a feasible flow by the bottleneck amount around any negative-cost residual cycle. Absence of such a cycle certifies minimum cost.
assumptions_latex: The initial flow is feasible.
All residual capacities used for the termination claim are finite integers.
Arc costs are integers for the finite-decrease argument.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At termination, \(x\) is a minimum-cost feasible flow.

notation.meaning: Signed residual cost of cycle C.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm and integral finite-termination claim fit the terminal container, but no cycle-canceling source or locator is supplied.

children.title: Cycle-Selection Families
children.top_down_role: Alternative organizations for selecting improving cycles.

knowledge_statements.title: Cycle-Selection Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Admissible and structured rules for choosing an improving residual cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A cycle-selection rule is admissible if, whenever the residual network contains a negative-cost directed cycle, it returns one. Generic selection may return any such cycle. Minimum-total-cost selection minimizes \(c(C)\) over eligible cycles, whereas minimum-mean selection minimizes \(c(C)/|C|\). Each rule preserves feasibility when followed by bottleneck augmentation, and each strictly decreases the objective. Their iteration and running-time guarantees differ because admissibility alone controls neither the magnitude of the decrease nor the number of cancellations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any negative residual cycle gives a valid improvement, but arbitrary, minimum-cost, and minimum-mean selection rules can have substantially different convergence guarantees.
assumptions_latex: The current flow is feasible.
Every selected cycle has positive residual capacity on all its arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bottleneck augmentation along any admissibly selected cycle preserves feasibility and decreases cost.

notation.meaning: Total signed residual cost of cycle C.
Number of arcs in cycle C.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The selection-family distinctions and bottleneck-improvement claim are plausible, but the comparative formulation has no supporting locator.

children.title: Cycle-Canceling Convergence Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Dependence on numeric data, cycle choice, and recession directions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recession certificate for minimum-cost flow with unbounded residual capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a feasible flow's residual network contains a directed cycle of negative total cost whose residual capacity is unbounded on every cycle arc, then the corresponding cycle circulation is a feasible recession direction and the minimum-cost objective is unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative residual cycle with unlimited augmentation capacity certifies that the flow objective is unbounded below.
assumptions_latex: A feasible flow exists.
Every arc of the directed residual cycle has unbounded residual capacity.
The cycle has negative total residual cost.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf\{c^{\mathsf T}x:x\text{ feasible}\}=-\infty.
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Negative-Cycle Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Magnitude-dependent termination bound for bottleneck cancellation under integral data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x^0\) be an integral feasible flow in a finite network with integral finite capacities and integral costs, and suppose the finite optimum value is \(z^*\). If every iteration augments by the residual bottleneck around a negative-cost residual cycle, then all iterates remain integral and the algorithm terminates after at most \(c^{\mathsf T}x^0-z^*\) cancellations. This bound is pseudopolynomial because it depends on numerical objective magnitudes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral bottleneck cycle cancellation terminates within the initial integer objective gap, a magnitude-dependent pseudopolynomial bound.
assumptions_latex: \(x^0\) is an integral feasible flow.
Capacities and costs are finite integers.
The optimum \(z^*\) is finite.
Each selected residual cycle has negative cost and is augmented by its bottleneck.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: N_{\mathrm{cancel}}\le c^{\mathsf T}x^0-z^*.
knowledge_statements.title: Integral Objective-Gap Iteration Bound

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Loss of Unit Progress Without Integrality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the integer objective-descent argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\delta>0\), a residual network may contain a unit-capacity directed cycle of total cost \(-\delta\). Bottleneck cancellation of that cycle decreases the objective by exactly \(\delta\). Therefore, without an integral objective lattice, no uniform unit-decrease bound—and hence no iteration bound derived solely from the unscaled objective gap—follows.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With nonintegral costs, a legal cancellation can improve the objective by an arbitrarily small amount, so integer unit-progress analysis no longer applies.
assumptions_latex: The selected negative cycle has residual bottleneck one and total cost \(-\delta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf\{-\Delta(c^{\mathsf T}x):\text{legal improving cancellation}\}=0\text{ is possible}.
knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Unit Progress Without Integrality
Cycle-Canceling Convergence Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Termination and boundedness limits for residual-cycle cancellation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integral finite capacities and integral costs, bottleneck cycle cancellation keeps flows integral and each iteration lowers the integer objective by at least one; hence it terminates after at most \(c^{\mathsf T}x^0-z^*\) iterations when the optimum \(z^*\) is finite. This bound depends on numerical magnitudes and is therefore only pseudopolynomial. Without integrality, arbitrary cycle choices can yield arbitrarily small decreases, so this argument gives no finite iteration bound. If a negative-cost residual cycle has unbounded residual capacity, it is a recession direction and the objective is unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral data give finite but magnitude-dependent convergence. Real data and arbitrary choices lose that bound, while an unlimited negative residual cycle proves unboundedness.
assumptions_latex: \(x^0\) is a feasible initial flow.
The finite-termination bound assumes finite integral capacities and integral costs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Cycle cancellation is finitely bounded under integral finite data, but the bound is pseudopolynomial; an uncapacitated negative cycle certifies \(z^*=-\infty\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The integral objective-gap bound and unbounded negative-cycle criterion are plausible, but the convergence-boundary record lacks a source, especially for its contrast with arbitrary choices over real data.

children.title: Sequential Shortest Path
children.top_down_role: The classical shortest augmenting-path organization.

knowledge_statements.title: Sequential Shortest Path
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical successive shortest residual-path augmentation from excess to deficit nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input integral balances \(b\) with \(\sum_v b_v=0\), capacities \(u\), costs \(c\), and a capacity-feasible pseudoflow \(x\) whose residual network has no negative-cost cycle. While some node \(s\) has positive excess and some node \(t\) has deficit, choose such an \(s\), find a minimum-cost residual path \(P\) from \(s\) to a reachable deficit node \(t\), and augment by the minimum of the excess at \(s\), deficit magnitude at \(t\), and residual bottleneck of \(P\). Stop when all imbalances vanish and output \(x\), or report infeasibility if no required path exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly send as much flow as possible along a cheapest residual path from an excess node to a deficit node until balances are satisfied.
assumptions_latex: Balances and capacities are integral.
The initial residual network contains no negative-cost cycle.
Shortest paths are computed exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Successful termination returns a feasible minimum-cost flow.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of path-only termination when the initial capacity-feasible pseudoflow is not residual-cycle optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Take two vertices a,b with zero balances and arcs a\to b and b\to a, each having capacity one and cost -1. At the zero flow all balances vanish, so an algorithm performing only excess-to-deficit augmentations stops with cost 0. Its residual network contains the negative cycle a\to b\to a; sending one unit around that cycle gives a feasible flow of cost -2. Thus balance-only termination is not an optimality certificate unless the initial residual network has no negative-cost cycle or negative cycles are handled separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A balanced initial flow can make path augmentation stop immediately even though a residual negative cycle yields a cheaper circulation.
assumptions_latex: The implementation performs only excess-to-deficit augmentations and stops when all balances vanish.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Balance alone does not certify optimality in the presence of a residual negative-cost cycle.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Balance-scaling variant for minimum-cost flow with integral balances, infinite arc capacities, and conservative costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize $f=0$ and $b'=b$. If $b'=0$, return $f$; otherwise let $b_{\max}=\max_{v\in V(G)}b(v)$ and $\gamma=2^{\lfloor\log b_{\max}\rfloor}$. At scale $\gamma$, repeatedly choose reachable vertices $s,t$ with $b'(s)\geq\gamma$ and $b'(t)\leq-\gamma$, augment $\gamma$ units along a minimum-cost $s$-$t$ path in $G_f$, and update the two residual balances. If no such pair exists, halve $\gamma$; if this occurs at $\gamma=1$ while $b'\neq0$, report that no $b$-flow exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Send power-of-two quantities along shortest residual paths between sufficiently large surplus and deficit vertices, halving the scale when no eligible reachable pair remains; return an optimal flow or report infeasibility at the final scale.
assumptions_latex: u(e)=\infty\quad(e\in E(G))
b:V(G)\to\mathbb{Z},\quad\sum_{v\in V(G)}b(v)=0
c:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}\text{ is conservative}
b_{\max}:=\max_{v\in V(G)}b(v)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: b'=0\Rightarrow f\text{ is returned as a minimum-cost }b\text{-flow};\quad\gamma=1\text{ with no eligible reachable pair and }b'\neq0\Rightarrow\text{ no }b\text{-flow exists}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Successive Shortest-Path Algorithm for Minimum-Cost Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical residual shortest-path augmentation algorithm, including its infeasibility stopping condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize $f=0$ and $b'=b$. While $b'\neq0$, choose $s$ with $b'(s)>0$ and a reachable $t$ with $b'(t)<0$. If no such $t$ exists, report that no $b$-flow exists. Otherwise choose a minimum-cost $s$-$t$ path $P$ in $G_f$, set $\gamma=\min\{\min_{e\in E(P)}u_f(e),b'(s),-b'(t)\}$, augment $f$ along $P$ by $\gamma$, and update $b'(s)\leftarrow b'(s)-\gamma$ and $b'(t)\leftarrow b'(t)+\gamma$. When $b'=0$, return $f$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly send the maximum admissible amount from a residual surplus vertex to a reachable deficit vertex along a shortest residual path; return the resulting minimum-cost flow, or report infeasibility when no required path exists.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a digraph}
u:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}_+
b:V(G)\to\mathbb{R},\quad\sum_{v\in V(G)}b(v)=0
c:E(G)\to\mathbb{R}\text{ is conservative}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: b'=0\Rightarrow f\text{ is returned as a minimum-cost }b\text{-flow};\quad\text{failure of the reachability test implies that no }b\text{-flow exists}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimality invariant underlying successive shortest-path augmentation for minimum-cost flows.

children.title: Potential-Reweighted Residual Shortest Paths
children.top_down_role: Price transformations supporting repeated shortest-path searches.

knowledge_statements.title: Potential-Reweighted Residual Shortest Paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Potential updates for repeated residual shortest-path searches when every residual vertex is reachable from the selected source.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each residual arc \((i,j)\), let \(\bar c_{ij}=c_{ij}-\pi_i+\pi_j\). Suppose all residual reduced costs are nonnegative and every residual-network vertex is reachable from a source \(s\). Let \(d_v\) be the finite shortest reduced-cost distance from \(s\) to \(v\), and define \(\pi'_v=\pi_v-d_v\). Then
\[\bar c'_{ij}=\bar c_{ij}+d_i-d_j\ge0\]
for every residual arc \((i,j)\). Original and reduced costs of any fixed-endpoint path differ only by endpoint potentials, so they have the same minimizing paths; Dijkstra's algorithm is therefore applicable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When all residual reduced costs are nonnegative and every vertex is reachable from the source, subtracting shortest-path distances from the potentials preserves nonnegative reduced costs on every residual arc and preserves shortest-path minimizers.
assumptions_latex: All residual reduced costs before the search are nonnegative.
Every residual-network vertex is reachable from the source \(s\), so every distance \(d_v\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The update \(\pi'_v=\pi_v-d_v\) preserves reduced-cost nonnegativity and shortest-path minimizers.

notation.meaning: Shortest reduced-cost distance from the source.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Safe potential reweighting when some residual vertices are unreachable from the selected source.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \bar c_{ij}=c_{ij}-\pi_i+\pi_j\ge0, choose a source s and reachable target t, and let d(v) be the shortest reduced-cost distance from s, possibly +\infty. Set D=d(t), q(v)=\min\{d(v),D\}, with \min\{+\infty,D\}=D, and \pi'_v=\pi_v-q(v). Then \bar c'_{ij}=\bar c_{ij}+q(i)-q(j)\ge0 for every residual arc, and every arc on an s-t shortest path has zero updated reduced cost. Updating only finite-distance vertices can fail: if d(j)=2, i is unreachable, and an entering residual arc i\to j has \bar c_{ij}=0, leaving \pi_i unchanged while subtracting d(j) at j produces \bar c'_{ij}=-2.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Capping every distance at the target distance safely handles unreachable vertices and makes a shortest source-target path tight; ignoring unreachable vertices can create a negative reduced cost.
assumptions_latex: All residual reduced costs before the update are nonnegative.
The selected target t is reachable from s.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bar c'_{ij}\ge0\text{ for every residual arc, and every arc of an }s\text{-}t\text{ shortest path is tight}.

notation.meaning: Finite reduced-cost distance to the selected target.

children.title: Successive Shortest-Path Complexity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Quantity-dependent and scaled variants of path augmentation.

knowledge_statements.title: Successive Shortest-Path Complexity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantity-dependent bound for integral successive shortest-path augmentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F=\sum_{v:b_v>0}b_v\) be the total integral supply. In successive shortest path, every successful augmentation sends at least one unit and eliminates at least one unit of remaining supply, so there are at most \(F\) augmentations. With nonnegative reduced costs and a binary heap, one residual shortest-path computation costs \(O(m+n\log n)\); hence the running time is
\[O\bigl(F(m+n\log n)\bigr).\]
Because \(F\) may be exponential in the binary encoding length of the balances, this is a pseudopolynomial bound rather than a strongly polynomial one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral successive shortest path uses at most total-supply many augmentations, giving a quantity-dependent pseudopolynomial time bound with heap-based shortest paths.
assumptions_latex: The network has \(n\) nodes and \(m\) residual arcs up to constant factors.
Balances and residual capacities are integral.
Reduced costs are nonnegative for each shortest-path search.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm runs in \(O(F(m+n\log n))\) time under the stated implementation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard integral capacity-scaling regime replacing linear dependence on total supply by logarithmic magnitude dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the standard capacity-scaling successive shortest-path algorithm on integral data of magnitude at most U\ge1, let \Delta range over descending powers of two. In each \Delta-phase the algorithm maintains its \Delta-residual and feasible-potential invariants and performs O(m) shortest-path augmentations before halving \Delta. Hence it performs O(m\log U) shortest-path computations. If each search uses binary-heap Dijkstra on nonnegative reduced costs, the running time is O\!\left(m\log U\,(m+n\log n)\right). The bound is polynomial in the binary encoding length of U but is not strongly polynomial because it depends on \log U.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Standard capacity scaling reduces the number of shortest-path augmentations to O(m log U), giving a weakly polynomial rather than strongly polynomial bound.
assumptions_latex: Capacities and balances are integral and have absolute magnitude at most U.
The standard capacity-scaling residual and feasible-potential invariants are maintained.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Ascent Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Price updates driven by the concave Lagrangian dual of capacitated minimum-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:Ax=b,\ 0\le x\le u\}\), initialize node prices \(\pi\) and choose
\[x(\pi)\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{0\le x\le u}\sum_{(i,j)\in E}(c_{ij}-\pi_i+\pi_j)x_{ij}.\]
The concave dual function is \(g(\pi)=b^{\mathsf T}\pi+\sum_{(i,j)}\min_{0\le z\le u_{ij}}(c_{ij}-\pi_i+\pi_j)z\), and \(b-Ax(\pi)\) is a supergradient. Select an ascent direction from this imbalance, increase prices until a reduced-cost breakpoint is reached, recompute minimizing arcs, and repeat. Stop when a selected \(x(\pi)\) satisfies \(Ax=b\); output \(x(\pi),\pi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dual ascent adjusts node prices using imbalance supergradients, stopping at reduced-cost events. A Lagrangian minimizer that also satisfies flow balance is primal-dual optimal.
assumptions_latex: Arc capacities are finite and nonnegative.
The primal problem is feasible.
Price steps produce nondecreasing dual values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(Ax(\pi)=b\) at termination, then \(x(\pi)\) is primal optimal and \(\pi\) is dual optimal.

notation.meaning: Dual supergradient represented by node imbalance.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact stationarity certificate for the polyhedral node-price dual, including nonunique bound minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let X(\pi)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{0\le x\le u}\{c^{\mathsf T}x+\pi^{\mathsf T}(b-Ax)\} and g(\pi)=\min_{0\le x\le u}\{c^{\mathsf T}x+\pi^{\mathsf T}(b-Ax)\}. Then \partial^+g(\pi)=\{b-Ax:x\in X(\pi)\}. Hence \pi maximizes g if and only if 0\in\partial^+g(\pi), equivalently if and only if some x^*\in X(\pi) satisfies Ax^*=b. Such x^* is primal optimal and \pi is dual optimal. A particular tie-broken minimizer can be imbalanced even when another minimizer in X(\pi) supplies the certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A price is dual optimal exactly when its bound-minimizing face contains a balanced flow; an arbitrarily selected minimizer can remain imbalanced because of ties.
assumptions_latex: The bounded minimum-cost-flow primal is feasible.
All arc capacities are finite, so X(\pi) is nonempty and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \pi\in\operatorname*{argmax}g\iff0\in\partial^+g(\pi)\iff\exists x^*\in X(\pi):Ax^*=b.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose a node \(s\) with positive excess and compute shortest-path labels \(d(v)\) in \(G_x\) using lengths \(\bar c_{ij}\). Select a deficit node \(t\) of minimum finite label, set \(p'_v=p_v+d(v)\) for labeled nodes, and augment \(\delta\) units along an \(s\)-\(t\) shortest path, where \(\delta\) is the minimum of the path residual capacity, the excess at \(s\), and the deficit magnitude at \(t\). Repeat until no imbalance remains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly update potentials by residual shortest-path distances and augment along a shortest path from excess to deficit; feasibility and complementary slackness then yield an optimal flow.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reachability Boundary for the Potential Update
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Qualification of the sequential shortest-path price update when some residual vertices are unreachable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the convention \bar c_{ij}=c_{ij}+p_i-p_j, replacing p_v by p_v+d(v) only for vertices with finite distance from s preserves \bar c\ge0 if every residual vertex is reachable, but it is not valid in general. For a reachable deficit t with D=d(t), the safe update is p'_v=p_v+q(v), where q(v)=\min\{d(v),D\} and q(v)=D when d(v)=+\infty. This preserves nonnegative reduced costs on every residual arc and makes every arc of an s-t shortest path tight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Updating only finite-distance vertices needs an all-reachable condition; capping every label at the chosen target distance is the safe general update.
assumptions_latex: Residual reduced costs are initially nonnegative.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a bound-feasible flow \(x\) and prices \(p\). At each iteration select an imbalanced node or an arc violating the chosen reduced-cost tolerance. Either change one arc flow toward a bound along a reduced-cost-admissible residual direction, or change one node price until a new incident residual arc becomes admissible. Recompute the affected imbalance and reduced costs, and repeat. Stop when \(e=0\) and each arc obeys \(r_a>0\Rightarrow x_a=\ell_a\), \(r_a<0\Rightarrow x_a=u_a\), and \(r_a=0\Rightarrow \ell_a\le x_a\le u_a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relaxation methods alternately modify local flows and node prices, seeking conservation together with arcwise complementary slackness.

children.title: Dual Stalling Regimes
children.top_down_role: Degenerate or weak-progress price configurations in dual-driven methods.

assumptions_latex: The concave flow dual is \(g(p)=\inf_{\ell\le x\le u}\{c^Tx+p^T(Ax-b)\}\).
An implementation supplies an allowed direction \(d\), step interval \([0,\alpha_{\max}]\), and a selected minimizer \(x(p)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A stalled state need not provide a feasible primal flow: \(Ax(p)\ne b\) may hold even though the prescribed dual step makes no progress.

notation.meaning: Direction proposed by the dual-ascent rule.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: operational definition of stalling for restricted dual-ascent rules
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational stalling condition relative to a specified dual-ascent rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The dual iteration is stalled at \(p\) when its prescribed nonzero direction \(d\) satisfies \(g(p+\alpha d)=g(p)\) for every \(\alpha\in[0,\alpha_{\max}]\), or when the rule returns \(d=0\), while its currently selected bound minimizer remains nonconservative: \(Ax(p)\ne b\). The definition is relative to the permitted directions and tie-breaking rule; it does not assert that \(p\) is globally dual optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A dual method stalls when its permitted update cannot improve the dual objective although its associated bound-minimizing flow still violates conservation.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Stalling Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed stalling condition is algorithm- and tie-breaking-dependent and has no citation. Source support is needed to establish that this is a recognized regime for the parent method rather than a newly constructed operational definition.

children.title: Dual Reoptimization Regimes

assumptions_latex: The current prices \(p\) determine the bound-minimizer face \(X(p)=\arg\min_{\ell\le x\le u}(c+A^Tp)^Tx\).
The current dual-ascent rule has stalled while no selected \(x\in X(p)\) is conservative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recomputed pair is either primal-dual optimal, or it exposes a new ascent direction or admissible residual augmentation that leaves the stalled regime.

notation.meaning: Face of bound minimizers at current prices.
Residual network induced by the reselected flow.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: reoptimization over a degenerate dual minimizer face
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic recovery by globally reoptimizing the current dual minimizer face.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On stalling, solve the restricted feasibility problem \(x\in X(p)\) and \(Ax=b\). If it is feasible, output such an \(x\) with \(p\). Otherwise choose a minimizer \(x\in X(p)\), rebuild \(G_x\), and recompute globally the shortest-path, cut, or block direction prescribed by the parent primal-dual method. Move \(p\) to the first breakpoint at which \(X(p)\) changes, reselect \(x\), and restart local relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reoptimization escapes a stall by reconsidering the entire current minimizer face and globally recomputing a residual path, cut, or price direction.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No source supports the claimed face-reoptimization procedure or the conclusion that it necessarily exposes an ascent direction or admissible augmentation. The statement also blends shortest-path, cut, and block variants without fixing their hypotheses.

children.title: Stall-Recovery Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural conditions separating reusable dual states from states requiring substantial repair.

assumptions_latex: A stalled state \((x,p)\) and a set \(\mathcal U(p)\) of admissible dual updates are fixed.
The recovery merit is \(M(x)=\lVert Ax-b\rVert_1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The state is recoverable exactly when an allowed update yields strict dual ascent or reaches a new bound-minimizer face with smaller conservation violation; otherwise it lies on the stall-recovery boundary.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: exact operational boundary induced by allowed recovery steps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algorithm-relative boundary between recoverable and persistent dual stalls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A stalled pair \((x,p)\) is recoverable if some \((d,\alpha)\in\mathcal U(p)\) satisfies either \(g(p+\alpha d)>g(p)\), or \(X(p+\alpha d)\ne X(p)\) and contains \(x'\) with \(M(x')<M(x)\). The stall-recovery boundary consists of stalled pairs for which neither alternative holds. Persistent stalling is therefore possible only when every permitted step is dual-flat and every newly reachable minimizer face has conservation merit at least \(M(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recovery ends precisely where every allowed price step is dual-flat and cannot reach a bound-minimizing flow with less imbalance.
knowledge_statements.title: Stall-Recovery Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The boundary is defined relative to an unspecified update set and parent algorithm, and no source establishes this merit-based characterization. The dual objective and minimizer-face map used in the statement are also not introduced within this record.

knowledge_statements.title: Kilter Classifications
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arcwise linear-cost kilter classification using reduced-cost sign conventions, including fixed arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Arc \(a\) is in kilter for \((x,p)\) if \(\ell_a\le x_a\le u_a\) and one of the following mutually exclusive cases holds: \(\ell_a=u_a=x_a\); \(\ell_a<u_a\), \(x_a=\ell_a\), and \(r_a\ge0\); \(\ell_a<x_a<u_a\) and \(r_a=0\); or \(\ell_a<u_a\), \(x_a=u_a\), and \(r_a\le0\). It is out of kilter otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arc is in kilter when its flow respects its bounds and its reduced-cost sign agrees with whether it is at the lower bound, in the interior, or at the upper bound; a fixed arc is automatically in kilter.
assumptions_latex: The bounded flow problem is \(\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ell\le x\le u\}\).
For each arc \(a\), let \(r_a=c_a+(A^Tp)_a\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An arc is in kilter exactly when its flow and reduced cost satisfy the stated bound-complementarity cases; otherwise it is out of kilter.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x:Ax=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\ne\varnothing\), allowing infinite bounds. Then \(\inf_{x\in P}c^{\mathsf T}x=-\infty\) if and only if there exists \(d\) with \(Ad=0\), \(d_a\ge0\) whenever \(\ell_a\) is finite, \(d_a\le0\) whenever \(u_a\) is finite, and \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\). Equivalently, for any feasible base flow, the residual arcs having infinite residual capacity contain a negative-cost directed cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible instance is unbounded below exactly when it has a negative-cost recession circulation, equivalently an all-infinite-residual-capacity negative cycle.

Arc bounds may be infinite.

children.title: Network Auction Methods
children.top_down_role: Bidding and price competition in network representations.

assumptions_latex: A residual network, node prices \(p\), and tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\) are given.
At least one node has positive excess and can reach a deficit through residual arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each bid either pushes positive flow toward reducing excess or raises a price to create an \(\varepsilon\)-admissible residual arc; termination yields a feasible flow satisfying \(\varepsilon\)-complementary slackness.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: epsilon-auction interpretation on residual networks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic residual-network auction step; specialized auction variants may reverse price signs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Select an excess node \(i\). Among its outgoing residual arcs choose \((i,j)\) of minimum \(r_{ij}\), and let \(r^{(2)}_i\) be the second-smallest value, with \(+\infty\) allowed when no competitor exists. Adjust \(p_i\) so the chosen arc improves relative to its competitor by at least \(\varepsilon\), then push \(\delta=\min\{e_i,-e_j,u^x_{ij}\}\) when \(j\) is deficient, or the corresponding admissible positive amount under the variant's queue rule. Repeat until all node excesses vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Excess nodes bid for residual arcs by changing prices and pushing flow, with each winning bid separated from alternatives by an epsilon margin.

children.title: Epsilon-Relaxation Methods
children.top_down_role: Approximate dual feasibility refined over accuracy scales.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact optimality certificate from sufficiently small residual tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be a feasible circulation on an \(n\)-vertex network with integral arc costs. If some prices \(p\) make \((x,p)\) \(\varepsilon\)-optimal and \(0\le\varepsilon<1/n\), then \(x\) is a minimum-cost circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With integral costs, residual epsilon-optimality below one over the vertex count certifies exact minimum cost.
assumptions_latex: The network has \(n\ge1\) vertices.
Arc costs are integral.
\(x\) is a feasible circulation.
\((x,p)\) is \(\varepsilon\)-optimal.
\(0\le\varepsilon<1/n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in\operatorname*{argmin}\{c^{\mathsf T}y:y\text{ is a feasible circulation}\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Integral-Cost Exactness Threshold

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral-cost witness showing that the strict inequality in the uniform exactness threshold cannot be replaced by equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(n\ge2\), consider a directed \(n\)-cycle of unit-capacity arcs, with one arc of cost \(-1\) and all other arcs of cost \(0\). The zero circulation is feasible and nonoptimal. Prices can be chosen so that every forward residual arc has reduced cost \(-1/n\); hence the zero circulation is \((1/n)\)-optimal despite not being minimum-cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integral-cost negative cycle can make a nonoptimal circulation exactly one-over-n optimal, so the strict uniform threshold is necessary.
assumptions_latex: All cycle arcs have unit capacity.
The zero circulation is the tested flow.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varepsilon=1/n\not\Longrightarrow\text{exact optimality, even with integral costs}.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure at the Uniform Threshold

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximate residual reduced-cost feasibility for a capacity-feasible flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a capacity-feasible flow \(x\), node prices \(p\), and residual reduced costs \(\bar c_{ij}=c^x_{ij}+p_i-p_j\), the pair \((x,p)\) is \(\varepsilon\)-optimal when \[\bar c_{ij}\ge-\varepsilon\qquad\text{for every positive-capacity residual arc }(i,j).\] For \(\varepsilon=0\), this is exact residual reduced-cost optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A flow-price pair is epsilon-optimal when every available residual move has reduced cost at least minus epsilon.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) respects all arc bounds.
Residual arcs carry their signed linear costs.
\(\varepsilon\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{(i,j)\in E_x}\bar c_{ij}\ge-\varepsilon.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual Epsilon-Optimality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Push-relabel refinement of a capacity-feasible epsilon-optimal pseudoflow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a capacity-feasible pseudoflow \(x\), prices \(p\), and excesses \(e=b-Ax\). Saturate residual arcs of negative reduced cost. Repeatedly select a positive-excess node; push on an outgoing negative-reduced-cost residual arc when one exists, and otherwise decrease its price until an outgoing residual arc becomes \(-\varepsilon\)-tight. With the reduced-cost sign convention \(\bar c_{ij}=c^x_{ij}+p_i-p_j\), saturation, pushes, and relabels preserve \(\bar c_{ij}\ge-\varepsilon\). A completed phase has \(e=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epsilon refinement saturates negative arcs and alternates admissible pushes with price relabels until conservation is restored.
assumptions_latex: A feasible circulation exists.
The current pseudoflow respects all arc bounds.
The initial pair is \(\varepsilon\)-optimal.
Residual costs and price signs use the displayed convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: e=0\Longrightarrow x\text{ is a feasible }\varepsilon\text{-optimal circulation}.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Cost Epsilon-Refinement Phase

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance schedule for integral linear minimum-cost circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an \(\varepsilon_0\)-optimal capacity-feasible pseudoflow-price pair and a correct refinement procedure, choose \(\alpha>1\), set \(\varepsilon_{k+1}=\varepsilon_k/\alpha\), and refine the preceding pair to the new tolerance in each phase. Stop after obtaining a feasible \(\varepsilon_k\)-optimal circulation with \(\varepsilon_k<1/|V|\). For integral arc costs, the final circulation is exactly optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Geometric scaling repeatedly invokes epsilon refinement and stops below the integral-cost exactness threshold.
assumptions_latex: Arc costs are integral.
A correct refinement procedure produces a feasible pair at each completed phase.
A feasible circulation exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \varepsilon_k<1/|V|\text{ and feasibility imply exact minimum cost}.
knowledge_statements.title: Geometric Epsilon Scaling

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tolerance reductions needed to cross the integral-cost exactness threshold; excludes refinement work.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varepsilon_k=\varepsilon_0\alpha^{-k}\) with \(\alpha>1\), and let \(K\) be the least nonnegative integer such that \(\varepsilon_K<1/n\). Then \[K=\max\!\left\{0,\left\lfloor\log_\alpha(n\varepsilon_0)\right\rfloor+1\right\}.\] This counts scaling phases only and gives no bound on the work of a refinement phase.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Geometric epsilon scaling uses logarithmically many tolerance reductions to pass below one over the vertex count, independently of the unresolved work per refinement.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon_0>0\).
\(\varepsilon_k=\varepsilon_0\alpha^{-k}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K=\max\{0,\lfloor\log_\alpha(n\varepsilon_0)\rfloor+1\}.

notation.meaning: First phase index with tolerance strictly below \(1/n\).

knowledge_statements.title: Geometric-Scaling Phase Count

assumptions_latex: Residual reduced costs are \(r_{ij}=c_{ij}+p_i-p_j\), and initially \(r_{ij}\ge-\varepsilon\) on every residual arc.
The current flow respects all arc bounds, although it may violate conservation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The iteration maintains \(\varepsilon\)-complementary slackness; if it terminates with conservation, its objective is within the standard \(\varepsilon\)-dependent primal-dual gap, and exactness follows under an appropriate integral-cost threshold.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-arc epsilon-relaxation with optional epsilon scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: While some node \(i\) has positive excess, push flow on an outgoing residual arc satisfying \(r_{ij}\le0\), respecting residual capacity and the chosen imbalance rule. If no such arc exists, let \(m_i=\min_{(i,j)}r_{ij}\) and relabel \(p_i\leftarrow p_i-(m_i+\varepsilon)\), making at least one outgoing residual arc have reduced cost \(-\varepsilon\). Continue until \(e=0\). In an epsilon-scaling implementation, reduce \(\varepsilon\) geometrically and restart relaxation from the preceding flow-price pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Epsilon-relaxation alternates admissible residual pushes with price relabels that preserve approximate complementary slackness, then reduces epsilon across scaling phases.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The local push and relabel rule is mathematically plausible, but no citation supports this precise epsilon-relaxation variant, its primal-dual gap assertion, the integral-cost exactness threshold, or the scaling schedule.

assumptions_latex: The proposal permits an unspecified active-vertex selection rule.
The proposal does not specify current-arc scanning or the cost of finding relabel values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: T_{\mathrm{phase}}=O(n^2m)\text{ and }T_{\mathrm{total}}=O(n^2m\log(nC))\text{ are not established by the stated algorithm}.

children.title: Auction–Shortest-Path Hybrids
children.top_down_role: Hybrid bidding and residual shortest-path organizations.

knowledge_statements.title: Auction–Shortest-Path Hybrids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic residual-path hybrid for capacitated minimum-cost flow under epsilon complementary slackness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a feasible pseudoflow and node prices, select a node with positive excess and construct a residual path toward a node with negative excess. At each current node, traverse a residual arc minimizing reduced cost \(\bar c_{ij}=c_{ij}+p_i-p_j\). If no arc satisfies \(\bar c_{ij}\leq\varepsilon\), change the current node's price until at least one outgoing residual arc becomes epsilon-admissible. Upon reaching a deficit node, augment by the minimum of the source excess, terminal deficit, and residual capacities along the path. Repeat until all imbalances vanish; output the resulting feasible flow and prices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly combine auction-style price changes with shortest reduced-cost residual-path construction, augmenting from excess nodes to deficit nodes until flow balance is attained.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, with finite arc capacities and costs.
\(\varepsilon>0\), and the current pseudoflow satisfies capacity bounds.
\(\sum_{i\in V} b_i=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is feasible when the procedure terminates with zero excess at every node.

children.title: Forward Auction Variants

knowledge_statements.title: Forward Auction Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided auction processing of supply excess in a residual network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A forward variant chooses only nodes having positive excess, sends flow on epsilon-admissible outgoing residual arcs, and otherwise raises or lowers the selected node price according to the adopted reduced-cost convention. Its progress guarantee requires every processed excess to reach some deficit through residual arcs after finitely many price changes. If an excess node lies in a residual set \(S\) from which no deficit is reachable, forward steps confined to \(S\) cannot restore balance; the method must invoke an infeasibility test, an artificial arc, or a complementary reverse phase.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward auction steps alone fail when trapped excess cannot reach any deficit in the residual network; explicit infeasibility or reverse processing is then required.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) obeys arc bounds but may violate node balance.
\(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\) containing positive net excess and no residual path to a deficit is a failure boundary for forward-only processing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the failure-taxonomy container, but the claimed progress guarantee and required remedies depend on the precise forward-auction variant and have no cited support.

children.title: Reverse Auction Variants

knowledge_statements.title: Reverse Auction Variants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided auction processing of demand deficits using reversed residual orientation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A reverse variant chooses only nodes having negative excess, traces admissible residual arcs backward toward positive excess, and changes prices when no admissible predecessor exists. Its progress guarantee requires each processed deficit to be reachable from some excess node in the residual graph after finitely many price changes. If a deficit node belongs to a set \(S\) having no incoming residual path from any excess, reverse steps confined to deficit processing cannot restore balance; the method must report infeasibility, introduce artificial feasibility arcs, or alternate with forward processing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reverse-only auction processing fails when a deficit is unreachable from every excess in the residual network, requiring feasibility handling or a forward phase.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) obeys arc bounds but may violate node balance.
\(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A deficit unreachable from all positive-excess nodes is a failure boundary for reverse-only processing.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits the container, but the reachability condition and proposed remedies depend on the precise reverse-auction convention and lack a source.

knowledge_statements.title: Auction Infeasibility Handling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-cut certificate for a zero-lower-bound capacitated transshipment instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be finite and impose \(x(\delta^+(i))-x(\delta^-(i))=b_i\), \(0\leq x_e\leq u_e\), and \(\sum_{i\in V}b_i=0\). For \(S\subseteq V\), define \(b(S)=\sum_{i\in S}b_i\) and \(u(\delta^+(S))=\sum_{e\in\delta^+(S)}u_e\). If \(b(S)>u(\delta^+(S))\), then no feasible flow exists. Thus such a set \(S\) is an infeasibility certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A node set whose required net export exceeds the total capacity of its outgoing arcs certifies infeasibility of the zero-lower-bound flow instance.

\(0\leq x_e\leq u_e\) with \(u_e\geq0\) for every \(e\in E\).
\(x(\delta^+(i))-x(\delta^-(i))=b_i\) is the balance convention and \(\sum_{i\in V}b_i=0\).

children.title: Price-War Regimes
children.top_down_role: Oscillatory or weak-progress price behavior in auction-based flow methods.

knowledge_statements.title: Price-War Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pseudo-polynomial bidding caused by near-indifference and a remote costly alternative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an assignment auction with \(n\) bidders and \(n\) objects. Each bidder values the first \(n-1\) objects at \(0\) and the last object at \(-M\), where \(M>0\). Under epsilon-sized price increments and an adverse admissible tie rule, bidders repeatedly displace one another among the first \(n-1\) objects until their prices approach the \(M\)-unit disadvantage of the last object. Thus the number of bids can scale as \(\Omega(M/\varepsilon)\). This price-war family precludes a strongly polynomial bound based only on \(n\) for that implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nearly interchangeable preferred objects can provoke repeated displacement until their prices absorb a large cost gap, yielding order M/epsilon bids.
assumptions_latex: \(n\geq2\), \(M>0\), and \(0<\varepsilon<M\).
Bids increase a selected object's price by at least \(\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_{\mathrm{bids}}=\Omega(M/\varepsilon)\) is possible under admissible tie breaking.

notation.meaning: value gap to the unattractive object

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Simplex tableau identities and pivot-update complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the basis-complement identities defining a simplex tableau and the computational cost of updating it after a pivot selected by the specified simplex rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), \(c\in\mathbb R^n\), \(A':=\binom{-I}{A}\), \(b':=\binom0b\), and \(\bar c:=(c^\top,0)\). Let \(B\) consist of \(m\) indices such that \([A\ I]^B\) is nonsingular, let \(J\) be the complementary \(n\) indices, and put \(Q_B:=([A\ I]^B)^{-1}\). Then: (a) \(A'_J\) is nonsingular. (b) For \(x:=(A'_J)^{-1}b'_J\), \((b'-A'x)_J=0\), \((b'-A'x)_B=Q_Bb\), and \(c^\top x=\bar c^B Q_Bb\). (c) If \(y_B=0\) and \(y^\top A'=c^\top\), then \(y^\top=\bar c^B Q_B[A\ I]-\bar c\). (d) If \(i\in J\) and \(w\) satisfies \(A'_iw=-1\) and \(A'_{J\setminus\{i\}}w=0\), then \(A'_Bw=Q_B[A\ I]^i\). (e) For \(T_B:=\begin{pmatrix}Q_B[A\ I]&Q_Bb\\ \bar c^BQ_B[A\ I]-\bar c&c^\top x\end{pmatrix}\), if \(i\) and \(j\) are selected as prescribed by the referenced simplex-algorithm steps and \(B'\) is obtained from \(B\) by replacing \(j\) with \(i\), then \(B'\) and \(T_{B'}\) can be computed from \(B,T_B\) in \(O(m(n+m))\) time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsingular simplex basis determines the complementary system, residuals, objective value, dual vector, and pivot direction through explicit tableau identities. A pivot selected by the stated simplex rules updates the basis and tableau in O(m(n+m)) time.
assumptions_latex: A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n},\quad b\in\mathbb R^m,\quad c\in\mathbb R^n
A':=\binom{-I}{A},\quad b':=\binom0b,\quad \bar c:=(c^\top,0)
[A\ I]^B\text{ is nonsingular},\quad J:=\{1,\ldots,n+m\}\setminus B,\quad Q_B:=([A\ I]^B)^{-1}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A'_J\text{ is nonsingular; the stated primal, dual, residual, direction, and tableau identities hold; and a pivot satisfying the referenced simplex selection rules updates }T_B\text{ in }O(m(n+m))\text{ time}.

knowledge_statements.title: Spanning-Tree Solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tree-basis representation of a bounded network-simplex solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) have connected underlying undirected graph, let \(A\) be its node-arc incidence matrix, and let \(T\subseteq E\) be a spanning tree. Assign each nontree arc \(e\in E\setminus T\) either \(x_e=l_e\) or \(x_e=u_e\). If \(\sum_{i\in V}b_i=0\), then \(Ax=b\) uniquely determines the tree-arc vector \(x_T\). The resulting spanning-tree solution is feasible exactly when \(l_e\leq x_e\leq u_e\) for every \(e\in T\). A tree arc may lie at a bound, in which case the tree solution is degenerate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixing every nontree arc at a bound uniquely determines the tree-arc flows; the tree solution is feasible exactly when all computed tree flows satisfy their bounds.
assumptions_latex: The underlying undirected graph of \(G=(V,E)\) is connected.
\(A\) is the node-arc incidence matrix of \(G\).
\(\sum_{i\in V}b_i=0\).
\(T\subseteq E\) is a spanning tree.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_{E\setminus T}\in\prod_{e\notin T}\{l_e,u_e\}\) uniquely determines \(x_T\), and feasibility is equivalent to \(l_T\leq x_T\leq u_T\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Basic feasible flows are precisely spanning-tree solutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes the basic solutions of the capacitated flow-balance polyhedron by acyclicity of their strictly non-bound support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a minimum-cost-flow instance $(G,u,b,c)$, let
\[
P=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^{E(G)}:0\le x_e\le u(e)\ \forall e\in E(G),\quad \sum_{e\in\delta^+(v)}x_e-\sum_{e\in\delta^-(v)}x_e=b(v)\ \forall v\in V(G)\right\}.
\]
The basic solutions of $P$ are precisely the spanning-tree solutions of $(G,u,b,c)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The basic solutions of the capacity-bounded flow-balance polyhedron are exactly the feasible flows whose strictly non-bound support contains no undirected cycle.
assumptions_latex: (G,u,b,c)\text{ is an instance of the minimum-cost-flow problem}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x:x\text{ is a basic solution of }P\}=\{x\in P:x\text{ is a spanning-tree solution}\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Network-simplex spanning-tree structure, feasibility, and potential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the tree/bound partition, its associated balance flow, feasible and strongly feasible orientations, and its normalized tree potential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $(G,u,b,c)$ be a minimum-cost-flow instance with connected $G$. A spanning-tree structure is $(r,T,L,U)$ such that $r\in V(G)$, $E(G)=T\mathbin{\dot\cup}L\mathbin{\dot\cup}U$, $|T|=|V(G)|-1$, and $(V(G),T)$ is acyclic. Its associated $b$-flow satisfies $f(e)=0$ for $e\in L$, $f(e)=u(e)$ for $e\in U$, and, for $e=(v,w)\in T$ and the component $C_e$ of $(V(G),T\setminus\{e\})$ containing $v$,
\[
f(e)=\sum_{z\in C_e}b(z)+\sum_{a\in U\cap\delta^-(C_e)}u(a)-\sum_{a\in U\cap\delta^+(C_e)}u(a).
\]
The structure is feasible iff $0\le f(e)\le u(e)$ for every $e\in T$. A tree edge $(v,w)$ is downward when $v$ lies on the undirected $r$--$w$ path in $T$, and upward otherwise. The structure is strongly feasible iff $0<f(e)\le u(e)$ on every downward tree edge and $0\le f(e)<u(e)$ on every upward tree edge. Its associated potential is the unique $\pi:V(G)\to\mathbb R$ satisfying $\pi(r)=0$ and $c_\pi(e)=0$ for all $e\in T$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A network-simplex spanning-tree structure partitions the arcs into tree arcs and non-tree arcs fixed at their lower or upper bounds. The balance equations uniquely determine the tree flows. Feasibility imposes the capacity bounds; strong feasibility makes downward tree arcs positive and upward tree arcs strictly below capacity. The associated potential is normalized at the root and makes every tree arc's reduced cost zero.
assumptions_latex: (G,u,b,c)\text{ is a minimum-cost-flow instance}
G\text{ is connected}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (r,T,L,U)\text{ determines the stated associated }b\text{-flow }f\text{ and unique normalized potential }\pi,\text{ with feasibility and strong feasibility characterized by the stated inequalities.}
