children.title: Curvature–Uniqueness Interface
children.top_down_role: Dependence of primal or dual uniqueness on curvature properties.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Curvature Implications Are Not Reversible Without Stronger Hypotheses
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp distinctions among strict convexity, strong convexity, smoothness, and dual curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Strict convexity alone does not imply Lipschitz differentiability of the conjugate: \(f(x)=x^4\) is strictly convex, while \(\nabla f^*(s)\) is not Lipschitz near zero. Strong convexity alone does not imply strict convexity of the conjugate: for \(f(x)=\frac{\mu}{2}x^2+\delta_{[0,\infty)}(x)\), \(f^*(s)=\frac{(\max\{s,0\})^2}{2\mu}\), which is smooth but constant on \(( -\infty,0]\). Incidence gauge directions additionally prevent unnormalized dual uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict curvature, strong curvature, smoothness, and dual uniqueness are distinct; the reciprocal conclusions require the stated quantitative and rank hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Neither strict primal convexity nor strong primal convexity alone supplies all dual curvature and uniqueness conclusions.
knowledge_statements.title: Curvature Implications Are Not Reversible Without Stronger Hypotheses

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional curvature transfer between the primal cost and normalized price dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Phi\) be proper and closed. If \(\Phi\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex, then \(\Phi^*\) is differentiable with \(1/\mu\)-Lipschitz gradient, and \(q(p)=b^Tp-\Phi^*(B^Tp)\) has a gradient with Lipschitz constant at most \(\|B\|^2/\mu\). The primal problem has at most one attained minimizer. Conversely, if \(\Phi\) is differentiable on \(\mathbb R^A\) with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, then \(\Phi^*\) is \(1/L\)-strongly convex. On a normalized potential space \(P\) where \(B^T|_P\) is injective, \(D(p)=\Phi^*(B^Tp)-b^Tp\) is strongly convex with modulus at least \(\sigma_{\min}(B^T|_P)^2/L\), so an attained normalized dual optimum is unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strong primal curvature yields a smooth dual; globally smooth primal costs yield curvature and uniqueness of the normalized dual.
assumptions_latex: All spaces are finite-dimensional.
For the converse, \(\Phi\) is differentiable on the full arc space and \(\nabla\Phi\) is globally \(L\)-Lipschitz.
The normalized space \(P\) removes componentwise incidence gauge freedom.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong primal curvature gives \(\operatorname{Lip}(\nabla q)\le\|B\|^2/\mu\); primal \(L\)-smoothness gives normalized dual strong convexity at least \(\sigma_{\min}(B^T|_P)^2/L\).

Lipschitz constant of the primal gradient

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong primal curvature yields dual smoothness, while sufficiently smooth primal costs yield dual curvature and hence normalized dual uniqueness.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Network-Expansion Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit-capacity reduction for integral separable convex-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a finite directed network with integral node supplies, integral capacities, and marginal increments, perform the following operations. For each arc \(a\), create unit-capacity parallel copies \((a,k)\) of linear cost \(d_{a,k}\), for \(k=1,\ldots,u_a\). Solve the resulting linear minimum-cost-flow problem. If it is feasible, choose an integral optimal expanded flow \(y\) and output
\[
x_a=\sum_{k=1}^{u_a}y_{a,k}
\]
for every original arc. Because the marginal costs are nondecreasing, an optimal integral expanded solution uses the cheapest required copies, so its cost is \(\sum_a(\phi_a(x_a)-\phi_a(0))\). If the expanded problem is infeasible, return its infeasibility certificate; the original integral convex-cost flow problem is then infeasible as well.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For integral supplies and capacities, expand each convex arc into unit-capacity marginal arcs, solve linear minimum-cost flow, and either aggregate an integral optimum or report infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: The directed network is finite, every node supply is integral, and the supplies sum to zero in each weakly connected component.
Every arc has integral capacity \(u_a\), its flow is restricted to \(\{0,\ldots,u_a\}\), and its discretely convex cost \(\phi_a\) is available through nondecreasing marginal increments.
The expanded network size \(\sum_a u_a\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the expanded problem is feasible, aggregation returns an optimal integral convex-cost flow using \(\sum_a u_a\) parallel arcs; otherwise the method returns an infeasibility certificate valid for the original problem.

notation.meaning: Marginal cost of the kth unit on arc a

knowledge_statements.title: Marginal Cycle Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unit-augmentation version for separable discrete-convex integral circulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each arc, give an available forward residual unit cost \(\Delta_a^+(x_a)=\phi_a(x_a+1)-\phi_a(x_a)\) and an available backward residual unit cost \(\Delta_a^-(x_a)=\phi_a(x_a-1)-\phi_a(x_a)\). Repeatedly find a directed cycle \(C\) of negative total marginal cost in \(R_x\), augment one unit around \(C\), and update the affected marginal costs. Stop when no negative directed cycle remains. Discrete convexity makes \(\Delta_a^+(x_a)\) nondecreasing in \(x_a\) and makes \(\Delta_a^-(x_a)\) nonincreasing in \(x_a\); the resulting negative-cycle optimality criterion certifies global optimality of the final feasible circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly augment one flow unit around a negative marginal-cost residual cycle. For an integral separable discrete-convex circulation, absence of such a cycle certifies optimality.
assumptions_latex: The directed network is finite, arc flows and bounds are integral, and each separable arc cost \(\phi_a:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb R\) is discrete convex.
The current circulation \(x\) satisfies flow conservation and all arc bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method terminates at an optimal integral circulation when the marginal residual network contains no negative-cost directed cycle.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Line Search on a Marginal Residual Cycle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiunit variant for an integral discrete-convex circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a directed residual cycle at a feasible integral circulation \(x\), and let \(\bar\delta\) be the largest feasible integer augmentation. The restricted objective \[F_C(\delta)=\sum_a\phi_a\bigl(x_a+\delta(\chi_C)_a\bigr),\qquad \delta\in\{0,\ldots,\bar\delta\},\] is discrete convex. Choosing \(\delta^*\in\arg\min F_C\) and replacing \(x\) by \(x+\delta^*\chi_C\) preserves feasibility and does not increase cost. Marginal costs must be updated as marginal breakpoints are crossed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A chosen residual cycle can be augmented by exact discrete-convex line search, batching unit updates while respecting changing marginal costs.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) is a feasible integral circulation with separable discrete-convex costs.
\(C\) is a directed residual cycle at \(x\).
\(\bar\delta\) is the feasible integer augmentation limit along \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F_C(\delta^*)\le F_C(0), and \(x+\delta^*\chi_C\) is feasible.

notation.meaning: Signed original-arc incidence vector of cycle C

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Successive shortest-path method under a reduced-cost invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain an integral pseudoflow \(x\) and node prices \(p\) such that every available marginal residual arc has nonnegative reduced cost. While the target balance vector is unmet, choose a node requiring one additional unit of net outflow and a node requiring one additional unit of net inflow. If a residual path joins them, compute a minimum reduced-cost path, update prices by shortest-path distances, augment one unit on the resulting tight path, and update the affected forward and backward marginal costs. Discrete convexity preserves nonnegative reduced costs after the marginal update. When all target balances are met, the resulting feasible flow satisfies the marginal reduced-cost optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under nonnegative marginal reduced costs, repeatedly send one unit along a shortest residual path and update prices until the prescribed balances are met.
assumptions_latex: Arc bounds and target balances are integral.
Arc costs are separable and discrete convex.
The initial pseudoflow and prices satisfy nonnegative reduced costs on all available marginal residual arcs.
Each selected excess-to-deficit pair is connected by a residual path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each augmentation preserves the reduced-cost invariant; upon attaining the target balances, the flow is optimal.
knowledge_statements.title: Price-Feasible Unit Marginal-Path Augmentation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Residual Reachability Cut for Unmet Balances
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infeasibility certificate for marginal path augmentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose the current bounded integral pseudoflow has unmet target balances. If no marginal residual path leads from any node requiring additional net outflow to any node requiring additional net inflow, then the set of vertices reachable from the former nodes defines a residual cut across which no admissible correction can carry the required net amount. The target balance equations and arc bounds are therefore infeasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If residual reachability cannot connect remaining excess requirements to deficit requirements, the reachable-set cut certifies infeasibility.
assumptions_latex: The current pseudoflow respects all arc bounds.
Target balances remain unmet.
No required-outflow node reaches a required-inflow node in the residual graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The residual reachable-set cut certifies infeasibility of the target balances under the arc bounds.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F\) units of balance must be installed from a price-feasible starting pseudoflow, the unit marginal-path method performs at most \(F\) augmentations. With a shortest-path routine of cost \(T_{\mathrm{sp}}(n,m)\) per augmentation, its path-search work is \(O(F\,T_{\mathrm{sp}}(n,m))\), apart from marginal and price updates. This is generally pseudopolynomial when \(F\) is binary encoded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unit path method uses at most one shortest-path augmentation per installed flow unit and is generally pseudopolynomial in binary input size.
assumptions_latex: Each augmentation installs one unit of the remaining target balance.
The total number of units to install is \(F<\infty\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-capacity witness against Dijkstra-style search with negative marginal costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider unit-capacity residual arcs \(s\to a,s\to b,a\to b,b\to t\) with marginal costs \(2,1,-3,1\). The path \(s\to a\to b\to t\) costs \(0\), while \(s\to b\to t\) costs \(2\). A label-setting routine that permanently settles \(b\) at distance \(1\) before processing \(a\) can return the latter path and an invalid price update.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative marginal arc can make a settled-label shortest-path search return a nonminimum path even with unit capacities.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Batched price-feasible path augmentation over an interval in which every used marginal cost remains unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a price-feasible integral pseudoflow has a tight residual path \(P\) from a node with remaining outflow requirement to a node with remaining inflow requirement. Let \(\Delta\) be the largest positive integer bounded by both endpoint requirements, every residual capacity on \(P\), and the number of consecutive units for which each residual arc used by \(P\) retains its current marginal cost. Then augmenting \(\Delta\) units on \(P\) is equivalent to \(\Delta\) successive valid unit augmentations along that unchanged tight path. It preserves the bounds and nonnegative reduced marginal costs, and at least one endpoint requirement, residual capacity, or constant-marginal interval becomes tight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tight marginal path can carry a maximal batch while endpoint requirements, residual capacities, and all used marginal costs remain unchanged.

Arc costs are separable and discrete convex.
All available marginal residual arcs initially have nonnegative reduced cost.

knowledge_statements.title: Cycle–Path Selection Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-direction decomposition underlying mixed path-and-cycle algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H_x\) be the marginal residual digraph of a bounded integral pseudoflow \(x\), let \(B_x\) be its node-arc incidence matrix, and let \(d\ge0\) be an integral residual-arc flow respecting all residual capacities. The residual flow \(d\) can be decomposed into incidence vectors of directed residual cycles and directed residual paths, with path endpoints accounting for the nonzero entries of \(B_xd\). Consequently, if \(B_xd=0\), cycle augmentations suffice. If \(B_xd\ne0\), path augmentations transfer imbalance between their endpoints, while cycle components change cost without changing imbalance. A cycle–path selection regime may therefore use paths to restore prescribed balances and cycles to improve cost at fixed balances.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integral residual correction decomposes into imbalance-carrying directed paths and balance-preserving directed cycles, supporting algorithms that use paths for feasibility and cycles for cost improvement.
assumptions_latex: A finite marginal residual digraph \(H_x\) of a bounded integral pseudoflow \(x\) is given.
The vector \(d\) is a nonnegative integral flow on the residual arcs and respects every residual capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Path components account for the imbalance vector \(B_xd\), while cycle components preserve balances; if \(B_xd=0\), cycles alone suffice.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a binary-encoded separable convex-cost flow instance, call a framework polynomial only when its number of cost-oracle evaluations and unit-cost arithmetic operations is bounded by a polynomial in \(|V|\), \(|E|\), and the binary input length \(L\), and every intermediate number has encoding length polynomial in \(L\). A running-time bound polynomial only in the numerical range \(U=\sum_{a\in E}(u_a-\ell_a)\) does not meet this condition. Scaling, aggregated marginal searches, or compact convex optimization can meet the condition only when their termination, oracle complexity, and intermediate encoding lengths are polynomially bounded in \(|V|\), \(|E|\), and \(L\), without constructing all \(U\) marginal units.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex-cost network-flow framework is polynomial only when its work and intermediate encodings are polynomial in the binary input length, rather than merely polynomial in the numerical flow range.
assumptions_latex: Arc bounds, balances, and convex-cost descriptions have finite binary encoding length \(L\).
Marginal values or suitable convex-cost subgradients can be evaluated in time polynomial in \(L\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polynomiality requires oracle use, arithmetic work, and intermediate encoding lengths polynomial in \(|V|\), \(|E|\), and \(L\), independently of the numerical value of \(U\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Evaluation Oracles Do Not Determine Bit Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation boundary for polynomial-time claims about discrete convex-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A bound polynomial in the number of calls to an abstract value, comparison, or marginal-cost oracle does not by itself imply polynomial bit complexity. Such a conclusion additionally requires polynomial-time oracle evaluation, polynomial encoding length for every oracle answer and intermediate number, and a polynomially decodable output representation. Without these requirements, one oracle call may hide superpolynomial computation or return a superpolynomial-length value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polynomially many abstract cost-oracle calls are not a polynomial-time guarantee unless oracle evaluation, numeric encodings, intermediate values, and output decoding are polynomially bounded.
assumptions_latex: Convex costs are accessed through an oracle rather than an explicit unit-marginal list.
Complexity is measured in the binary input model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{poly}(n,m,L)\text{ oracle calls}\not\Longrightarrow\operatorname{poly}(n,m,L)\text{ bit time without oracle and encoding guarantees}.

notation.meaning: Binary length of the explicitly represented input.

children.title: Feasible-Direction Network Methods
children.top_down_role: Continuous descent methods preserving network feasibility.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual-cycle descent with a feasibility-preserving line search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: From a feasible flow \(x^k\), select a directed residual cycle having negative total current marginal cost. Let \(d^k\) be its signed circulation direction and let \(\alpha_{\max}\) be the largest bound-feasible step. Choose \(0<\alpha_k\le\alpha_{\max}\) by exact line search or a sufficient-decrease rule and set \(x^{k+1}=x^k+\alpha_kd^k\). If no negative marginal cycle exists, stop.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method follows a negative marginal residual cycle and line-searches within its residual capacity.
assumptions_latex: The initial flow is feasible.
Arc costs are differentiable and convex.
A positive sufficient-decrease step is selected whenever a negative cycle exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every iterate is feasible, every accepted step decreases the objective, and any finite stopping point is optimal.
knowledge_statements.title: Cycle Feasible-Direction Descent

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Network representation of tangent directions at a bounded feasible flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(F=\{x:Ax=b,\ell\le x\le u\}\) and \(x\in F\), a first-order feasible direction satisfies \(Ad=0\), \(d_a\ge0\) at a nonfixed lower bound, and \(d_a\le0\) at a nonfixed upper bound. Representing positive and negative components by forward and backward residual arcs turns \(d\) into a nonnegative residual circulation, hence a conic combination of directed residual-cycle directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tangent directions of a bounded flow polytope are residual circulations and decompose into directed cycles.
assumptions_latex: The current flow satisfies \(Ax=b\) and \(\ell\le x\le u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every first-order feasible direction is a conic combination of directed residual-cycle directions.
knowledge_statements.title: Feasible Directions as Residual Circulations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonasymptotic convergence of a feasibility-preserving first-order network method.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\{x:Bx=b,\ell\le x\le u\}\) be nonempty and let \(f\) be convex with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. Starting from \(x^0\in F\), define \[x^{k+1}=\Pi_F\!\left(x^k-L^{-1}\nabla f(x^k)\right).\] Every iterate is feasible, and for every minimizer \(x^*\in F\) and \(k\ge1\), \[f(x^k)-f(x^*)\le\frac{L\|x^0-x^*\|^2}{2k}.\] The projection subproblem is a convex quadratic network-flow problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projected gradient preserves flow feasibility and attains the standard one-over-k objective rate for smooth convex costs.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is nonempty and closed.
\(f\) is convex and has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient.
A minimizer exists in \(F\).

notation.meaning: Euclidean projection onto the feasible-flow polytope.

knowledge_statements.title: Projected-Gradient Feasible-Flow Rate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Descent without an adequate step rule need not reach the optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Minimize \(f(x)=x\) over \(F=[0,1]\), start at \(x^0=1\), and choose \(d^k=-1\). With \(\alpha_k=2^{-k-2}\), every iterate is feasible and strictly improves the objective, but \(\sum_{k\ge0}\alpha_k=1/2\), so \(x^k\to1/2\), which is not optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasible descent with summable steps can converge to a nonoptimal point despite strict improvement at every iteration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x^{k+1})<f(x^k)\text{ for every }k,\qquad x^k\to1/2\notin\operatorname*{argmin}_{[0,1]}f.
knowledge_statements.title: Summable-Step Failure

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility-preserving conditional-gradient variant whose direction subproblem is linear minimum-cost flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\{x:Ax=b,\ell\le x\le u\}\) be nonempty and compact, let \(f\) be convex with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient on \(F\), and let \(D=\sup_{x,y\in F}\|x-y\|\). At iteration \(k\), compute \[s^k\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{s\in F}\nabla f(x^k)^{\mathsf T}s\] by a linear minimum-cost-flow subproblem and set \(x^{k+1}=(1-\eta_k)x^k+\eta_k s^k\). With \(\eta_k=2/(k+2)\), every iterate is feasible and, for \(k\ge1\), \[f(x^k)-f(x^*)\le\frac{2LD^2}{k+2}.\] The gap \(g(x)=\max_{s\in F}\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}(x-s)\) satisfies \(f(x)-f(x^*)\le g(x)\), and \(g(x)=0\) exactly at global optima.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conditional gradient solves a linear minimum-cost-flow direction problem, preserves feasibility by convex averaging, and has the standard one-over-k smooth-convex rate and gap certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is nonempty and compact.
\(f\) is convex and has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient on \(F\).
A minimizer \(x^*\in F\) exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x^k)-f(x^*)\le 2LD^2/(k+2)\quad(k\ge1),\qquad f(x)-f(x^*)\le g(x).

notation.meaning: Euclidean diameter of the feasible-flow polytope.

knowledge_statements.title: Network Conditional-Gradient Method

assumptions_latex: The feasible set is \(F=\{x:Ax=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\), and \(F\neq\varnothing\).
The separable objective \(f(x)=\sum_a\phi_a(x_a)\) is convex and differentiable on a neighborhood of \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If the direction subproblem returns \(d=0\), then \(x\) minimizes \(f\) over \(F\); otherwise exact or sufficient-decrease line search produces a nonincreasing objective sequence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order feasible-direction scheme with network-constrained direction subproblems.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Starting from \(x^0\in F\), define \(D(x)=\{d:Ad=0,\ d_a\ge0\text{ if }x_a=\ell_a,\ d_a\le0\text{ if }x_a=u_a\}\). At iteration \(k\), solve a bounded network direction problem minimizing \(\nabla f(x^k)^{\mathsf T}d\) over a normalized subset of \(D(x^k)\). If its optimum is zero, stop. Otherwise choose \(\alpha_k\ge0\) so that \(x^k+\alpha_kd^k\in F\) and a line-search decrease condition holds, then set \(x^{k+1}=x^k+\alpha_kd^k\). Convexity makes the zero-direction condition globally optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimize the objective gradient over feasible network directions, line-search along an improving direction, and stop when no feasible descent direction exists.

children.title: Differentiable Dual Methods
children.top_down_role: Methods exploiting smooth dual network structure.

assumptions_latex: The primal problem minimizes \(\sum_a\phi_a(x_a)\) subject to \(Ax=b\) and \(\ell_a\le x_a\le u_a\).
Each scalar Lagrangian minimizer is unique for every price vector under consideration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The dual is differentiable with \(\nabla g(p)=b-Ax(p)\), so dual gradient or Newton-type updates are driven exactly by primal node imbalance.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth node-price dual for separable convex network flow.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Dualizing \(Ax=b\) with prices \(p\) gives \[g(p)=p^{\mathsf T}b+\sum_a\inf_{\ell_a\le z\le u_a}\bigl(\phi_a(z)-(A^{\mathsf T}p)_az\bigr).\] Let \(x_a(p)\) be the unique scalar minimizer in the corresponding term. Then \(g\) is concave and differentiable, with \(\nabla g(p)=b-Ax(p)\). Hence a dual ascent method updates node prices using the imbalance induced by independently optimized arc flows. A zero gradient yields a primal-feasible Lagrangian minimizer and therefore a primal-dual optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Separable arc minimization defines a smooth price dual whose gradient is node imbalance; dual ascent adjusts prices until the induced arc flow is feasible.
knowledge_statements.title: Differentiable Dual Methods

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Damped Newton iteration exploiting the weighted-Laplacian Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Where the Laplacian Hessian formula applies, compute \(d\) from \[A\operatorname{diag}\!\bigl(\phi_a''(x_a(p))^{-1}\bigr)A^{\mathsf T}d=b-Ax(p)\] with one price gauge per connected component, and set \(p^+=p+\alpha d\), choosing \(0<\alpha\le1\) to increase the dual and remain in the smooth regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth-dual Newton update solves a gauge-fixed weighted Laplacian system driven by node imbalance.
assumptions_latex: The dual is twice differentiable at the current price.
A price gauge is fixed on every connected component.
The step length preserves the smooth regime and produces dual ascent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Newton direction targets zero primal node imbalance through network Laplacian linear algebra.

notation.meaning: dual gradient and primal node imbalance

knowledge_statements.title: Gauge-Fixed Dual Newton Step

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of classical smooth-dual updates when arc minimizers are nonunique.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If an arcwise Lagrangian subproblem has multiple minimizers at \(p\), the induced flow need not be unique and the dual need not be differentiable there. The possible imbalance vectors \(b-Ax\) are supergradients, but no unique gradient or classical Newton Hessian exists without regularization or a selection rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonunique arc minimizers can make the price dual nonsmooth and invalidate ordinary gradient and Newton formulas.
assumptions_latex: At least one scalar Lagrangian arc subproblem has multiple minimizers at \(p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Differentiability and a classical Laplacian Newton system cannot be asserted at \(p\).
knowledge_statements.title: Nonsmooth Dual Boundary

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual Hessian as a Weighted Network Laplacian
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order structure of the smooth node-price dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If every induced arc minimizer is interior and \(\phi_a''(x_a(p))>0\), then \[\nabla^2g(p)=-A\operatorname{diag}\!\bigl(\phi_a''(x_a(p))^{-1}\bigr)A^{\mathsf T}.\] Thus \(-\nabla^2g(p)\) is a weighted graph Laplacian whose nullspace contains the vectors constant on each connected component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The negative smooth-dual Hessian is a weighted network Laplacian with the usual additive price gauge.
assumptions_latex: Every induced arc minimizer is interior.
Each arc cost is twice differentiable with positive second derivative at the induced flow.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: -\nabla^2g(p)\text{ is a positive-semidefinite weighted network Laplacian.}
knowledge_statements.title: Dual Hessian as a Weighted Network Laplacian

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear Convergence of Smooth Dual Gradient Ascent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global rate under uniform smoothness and strong concavity after fixing the price gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix one price gauge on each connected component. Suppose the concave dual \(g\) is \(L\)-smooth and \(\mu\)-strongly concave on a convex invariant region containing a maximizer \(p^*\), where \(0<\mu\le L\). Then \(p^{k+1}=p^k+L^{-1}\nabla g(p^k)\) satisfies \[g(p^*)-g(p^k)\le(1-\mu/L)^k\bigl(g(p^*)-g(p^0)\bigr),\] and \(\nabla g(p^k)=b-Ax(p^k)\) converges to zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform smoothness and strong concavity give linear convergence of gauge-fixed dual gradient ascent and vanishing node imbalance.
assumptions_latex: A price gauge is fixed on each connected component.
\(g\) is \(L\)-smooth and \(\mu\)-strongly concave on an invariant convex region.
The dual maximum is attained in that region.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g(p^*)-g(p^k)\le(1-\mu/L)^k\bigl(g(p^*)-g(p^0)\bigr).

notation.meaning: Strong-concavity constant on the gauge-fixed space.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Convergence of Smooth Dual Gradient Ascent

assumptions_latex: A bounded convex-cost network flow problem is represented by marginal residual costs and node prices.
A tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\) is fixed, and every push respects residual capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: When the procedure reaches feasibility while maintaining \(\varepsilon\)-complementary slackness, its flow is an \(\varepsilon\)-optimal primal solution under the stated relaxation criterion.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain a bounded pseudoflow \(x\), node prices \(p\), and the invariant \(\bar c_{ij}\ge-\varepsilon\) on every marginal residual arc. Select a node with positive excess. If it has a residual outgoing arc attaining the best price-adjusted marginal cost within tolerance \(\varepsilon\), push as much flow as permitted toward that arc's head. Otherwise change the selected node's price until at least one outgoing residual arc becomes admissible. Update the forward and backward marginal costs after each push. Stop when every node has its prescribed balance; optionally reduce \(\varepsilon\) and restart from the current flow and prices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex auction alternates admissible marginal-flow pushes with node repricing, preserving approximate complementary slackness until feasibility and the desired tolerance are reached.

children.top_down_role: Approximate price-optimality organization for separable convex networks.

assumptions_latex: The network is finite with integral arc bounds and integral discrete marginal costs.
The flow \(x\) is feasible, and node prices \(p\) satisfy reduced marginal cost at least \(-\varepsilon\) on every residual arc.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The flow is within the cycle-wise \(\varepsilon\)-relaxation bound; if \(0<\varepsilon<1/|V|\), then \(x\) is exactly optimal.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The pair \((x,p)\) satisfies \(\varepsilon\)-relaxation when \(\bar c_{ij}=c_{ij}+p_i-p_j\ge-\varepsilon\) for every available marginal residual arc \((i,j)\). Price terms telescope on a directed residual cycle, so every simple cycle has marginal cost at least \(-n\varepsilon\). If marginal costs are integral and \(0<\varepsilon<1/n\), every cycle cost is an integer strictly greater than \(-1\), hence nonnegative. The marginal negative-cycle criterion then certifies that the feasible flow \(x\) is exactly optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximate reduced-cost inequalities bound every residual cycle. With integral costs and tolerance below the reciprocal of the vertex count, they certify exact optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Epsilon-Relaxation Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exactness Threshold Requires a Cost Lattice
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary of the reciprocal-vertex epsilon exactness argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Without a positive lattice spacing for residual-cycle marginal costs, no universal positive tolerance certifies exact optimality: for every \(\varepsilon>0\), an epsilon-relaxed feasible flow can have a residual cycle whose cost lies in \((-|V|\varepsilon,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For arbitrary real marginal costs, a negative residual cycle can be too small for any fixed positive epsilon threshold to detect exactly.
assumptions_latex: Residual marginal costs may be arbitrary real numbers.
Epsilon relaxation requires only \(\bar c_{ij}\ge-\varepsilon\) on each residual arc.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No universal \(\varepsilon>0\) certifies exact optimality without a positive cost-lattice spacing or equivalent separation assumption.
knowledge_statements.title: Exactness Threshold Requires a Cost Lattice

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed price refinement using one-unit marginal residual arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integral separable discrete-convex circulation, form the marginal residual network whose arcs represent one-unit changes at current discrete marginal costs. The proposed refinement saturates arcs violating the target tolerance, discharges positive-excess nodes through admissible unit or batched pushes, and changes a node price when no admissible outgoing arc exists. If these operations terminate with all balances restored while preserving \(\bar c_{ij}\ge-\varepsilon\), the result is an \(\varepsilon\)-optimal feasible circulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The proposed convex refinement applies push-relabel operations to changing discrete marginal residual costs.
assumptions_latex: Arc bounds, balances, and flows are integral.
Each arc has nondecreasing discrete marginal costs.
A feasible integral circulation exists.
Residual-cost and price conventions are fixed consistently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: e=0\Longrightarrow x\text{ is a feasible }\varepsilon\text{-optimal discrete-convex circulation}.

children.title: Auction–Relaxation Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Shared price mechanisms and distinctions between the two method families.

assumptions_latex: Auction and relaxation procedures use the same marginal residual network, flow convention, and tolerance \(\varepsilon\).
Auction prices are identified with relaxation node potentials up to the chosen sign convention and an additive constant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under this identification, auction bids are admissible pushes, auction price raises are relaxation relabels, and both maintain the same \(\varepsilon\)-complementary-slackness invariant.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational equivalence under consistent price and reduced-cost conventions.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose signs so that auction prices and relaxation potentials satisfy \(q_i=-p_i\). Then comparing auction net values is equivalent to comparing reduced marginal costs \(c_{ij}+p_i-p_j\). Assigning or transferring flow to an arc whose net value is within \(\varepsilon\) of best is exactly an admissible relaxation push. Raising an auction price until another choice becomes competitive is the corresponding relaxation relabel. Thus both descriptions generate the same flow-price transitions, modulo tie breaking and additive translation of all prices, and preserve identical \(\varepsilon\)-complementary-slackness inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After a sign change in node prices, auction bids and repricing coincide with relaxation pushes and relabels, preserving the same approximate optimality conditions.

children.title: Piecewise-Linear Approximation Methods
children.top_down_role: Controlled approximation by linearized arc costs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction and solution of a convex chordal arc-cost approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose breakpoints on each bounded arc interval, replace each convex arc cost by its chordal piecewise-linear interpolant, solve the resulting convex piecewise-linear flow problem, and return its aggregated flow. The interpolant is convex and overestimates the original arc cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace each convex arc cost by a chordal piecewise-linear overestimate and solve the resulting piecewise-linear network flow.
assumptions_latex: Each approximated arc interval is bounded.
Each arc cost is finite and convex on that interval.
The piecewise-linear approximation problem attains an optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constructed instance is a convex piecewise-linear network-flow problem on the original feasible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Chordal Piecewise-Linear Approximation

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive accuracy of chordal interpolation under bounded curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(0\le\phi_a''(z)\le M_a\) and the largest breakpoint spacing on arc \(a\) is \(h_a\), its chordal interpolant satisfies \(0\le\widehat\phi_a(z)-\phi_a(z)\le M_ah_a^2/8\). Therefore an exact minimizer \(\widehat x\) of the approximating flow satisfies \[f(\widehat x)-f(x^*)\le\sum_a M_ah_a^2/8.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bounded curvature converts breakpoint spacing into an explicit additive objective guarantee.
assumptions_latex: Each arc cost is twice differentiable and convex on its bounded interval.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform chordal approximation with a curvature-based additive error bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Interpolate each \(\phi_a\) linearly between consecutive breakpoints to obtain \(\widehat\phi_a\), and solve the resulting piecewise-linear convex network-flow problem. The chord interpolation bound gives \(0\le\widehat\phi_a(z)-\phi_a(z)\le M_ah_a^2/8\) throughout the arc interval. Hence, with \(\widehat f(x)=\sum_a\widehat\phi_a(x_a)\), every feasible \(x\) satisfies \(0\le\widehat f(x)-f(x)\le\sum_aM_ah_a^2/8\). If \(\hat x\) minimizes \(\widehat f\) and \(x^*\) minimizes \(f\), then \(f(\hat x)-f(x^*)\le\sum_aM_ah_a^2/8\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Chordal arc-cost approximations reduce the problem to piecewise-linear flow and yield an explicit additive error controlled by curvature and breakpoint spacing.

children.title: Interior-Point Network Methods

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible-start logarithmic-barrier method for bounded convex network flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite bounds and \(\mu>0\), minimize \[F_\mu(x)=\sum_a\phi_a(x_a)-\mu\sum_a\bigl(\log(x_a-\ell_a)+\log(u_a-x_a)\bigr)\] subject to \(Ax=b\). Starting from a strictly feasible flow, use damped equality-constrained Newton steps that preserve \(\ell<x<u\); after meeting an inner residual tolerance, reduce \(\mu\) and warm-start the next barrier problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The method follows the bound-barrier central path with feasibility-preserving Newton steps and decreasing barrier parameters.
assumptions_latex: All arc bounds are finite.
A strictly feasible flow exists.
Each arc cost is convex and twice differentiable on the open interval.
Each barrier subproblem is solved to the prescribed residual tolerance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: As \(\mu\downarrow0\) and inner residuals vanish, the produced feasible objective values approach the optimum under attainment.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal Log-Barrier Path Following

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Barrier-parameter stopping bound with two finite bounds per arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At an exact central-path point for a differentiable convex objective, the lower- and upper-bound multipliers satisfy complementarity products equal to \(\mu\). With two finite bounds per arc, the resulting primal-dual gap is \(2|A|\mu\). Approximate central points require their feasibility and stationarity residual errors to be added to this bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two logarithmic bound barriers per arc give a central-path primal-dual gap of two times the arc count times the barrier parameter.
assumptions_latex: All arc bounds are finite and strict feasibility holds.
The optimum is finite and attained.
The objective is differentiable at the central-path point.
The stated equality applies to an exact central-path point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x_\mu)-f^*\le 2|A|\mu.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Initialization boundary of the direct primal barrier formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(\{x:Ax=b,\ell<x<u\}=\varnothing\), the direct primal logarithmic barrier has no feasible point even when the closed-bound problem is feasible. Initialization then requires a phase-one embedding, facial reduction, or a primal-dual self-dual formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed-bound feasibility is insufficient for a direct primal log-barrier method; strict feasibility or an embedding is required.
assumptions_latex: The closed-bound problem is feasible.
No balance-feasible flow satisfies every finite bound strictly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The direct primal logarithmic-barrier path is empty.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Barrier Newton System and Network Schur Complement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Network linear algebra of a primal barrier step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With \(H=\nabla^2F_\mu(x)\) positive diagonal, the equality-constrained Newton equations have coefficient matrix \[\begin{bmatrix}H&A^{\mathsf T}\\A&0\end{bmatrix}.\] Eliminating the arc direction yields a node system with coefficient \(AH^{-1}A^{\mathsf T}\), a weighted graph Laplacian; after fixing one multiplier gauge per connected component, the arc direction follows by back-substitution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminating arc directions from the barrier KKT equations yields a weighted Laplacian system in node multipliers.
assumptions_latex: The current flow is strictly inside every bound.
The barrier Hessian is positive diagonal.
Redundant balance rows are removed or multiplier gauges are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each Newton direction reduces to a weighted-Laplacian solve and arcwise back-substitution.
knowledge_statements.title: Barrier Newton System and Network Schur Complement

assumptions_latex: The feasible set \(\{x:Ax=b,\ \ell<x<u\}\) contains a strictly feasible point.
Every arc cost is convex and twice continuously differentiable on its open bounded interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Following approximate minimizers of the barrier problems as \(\mu\downarrow0\) yields primal solutions approaching the optimal convex-cost flow value.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal equality-constrained logarithmic-barrier path-following framework.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mu>0\), minimize over \(Ax=b\) the barrier objective \[F_\mu(x)=\sum_a\phi_a(x_a)-\mu\sum_a\bigl(\log(x_a-\ell_a)+\log(u_a-x_a)\bigr).\] Starting from a strictly feasible point, compute damped Newton directions in the null space of \(A\), equivalently by solving the associated weighted network KKT system, and use a step preserving \(\ell<x<u\). Once the Newton residual meets the prescribed inner tolerance, reduce \(\mu\) and warm-start the next barrier problem. Stop when the barrier duality-gap bound and residual tolerances are at most the requested accuracy, and output the current feasible flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A network interior-point method follows logarithmic-barrier minimizers using feasibility-preserving Newton steps and reduces the barrier parameter until the target optimality gap is reached.
knowledge_statements.title: Interior-Point Network Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hardness of the Unrestricted Nonconvex Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case complexity boundary supplied by the fixed-charge subclass.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The separable nonconvex-cost flow class contains fixed-charge network flow, whose arc costs may have the form \(\phi_a(0)=0\) and \(\phi_a(x)=F_a+c_ax\) for \(0<x\le u_a\), with \(F_a>0\). Consequently, solving unrestricted separable nonconvex-cost flow is NP-hard under standard binary encodings.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separable network flow in which convexity fails on at least one arc; coupled objectives and side constraints are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\min\{\sum_{a\in A}\phi_a(x_a):Bx=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\), the arc-cost regime is nonconvex if some \(\phi_a\) is not convex on its feasible interval. Equivalently, for some arc \(a\), points \(s,t\in[\ell_a,u_a]\), and \(\lambda\in(0,1)\), \[\phi_a(\lambda s+(1-\lambda)t)>\lambda\phi_a(s)+(1-\lambda)\phi_a(t).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A separable flow has nonconvex arc costs when at least one arc cost violates the convex chord inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(Bx=b\) and \(\ell\le x\le u\) are the underlying network constraints.
The objective is arc-separable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At least one arc cost violates convexity on its feasible interval.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Arc-Cost Regime

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural feature lost when a differentiable arc cost is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If a differentiable function \(\phi:I\to\mathbb R\) is nonconvex on an interval \(I\), then \(\phi'\) is not nondecreasing on \(I\). Thus there exist \(s<t\) in \(I\) with \(\phi'(s)>\phi'(t)\), and residual marginal costs derived from this arc need not be monotone as its flow increases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differentiable nonconvex arc cost has nonmonotone marginal costs, so convex-flow monotone-marginal reasoning no longer applies.
assumptions_latex: \(I\subseteq\mathbb R\) is an interval.
\(\phi\) is differentiable but not convex on \(I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi'\) is not nondecreasing on \(I\).

Nonconvex Arc Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A two-parallel-arc example where arcwise nonconvexity separates local and global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider two parallel arcs from source to sink carrying one unit in total. Let the first-arc flow be \(x\in[0,1]\), the second-arc flow be \(1-x\), and the total cost be \(h(x)=x^2-3x^3+x^4\). The function \(h\) is nonconvex on \([0,1]\). Moreover, \(x=0\) is a strict one-sided local minimizer because \(h(x)>h(0)=0\) for every sufficiently small \(x>0\), whereas \(h(1)=-1<h(0)\). Thus local marginal or residual optimality cannot, without convexity, certify global optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonconvex arc cost can admit a locally optimal feasible flow whose cost exceeds that of a distant feasible flow.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x=0\) is locally minimizing but not globally minimizing.

notation.meaning: flow on the first parallel arc

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global Convex Optimality Certificate for Coupled Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Replacement for arc-local reduced-cost certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\{x:Bx=b,\ell\le x\le u\}\), let \(F\) be proper closed convex, and assume a standard relative-interior qualification for \(F+\delta_P\). A feasible \(x^*\) is optimal exactly when \[0\in\partial F(x^*)+N_P(x^*).\] Equivalently, there exist node multipliers \(p\) and nonnegative bound multipliers \(\lambda,\mu\) such that \[0\in\partial F(x^*)+B^{\mathsf T}p-\lambda+\mu,\] with \(\lambda_a(x_a^*-\ell_a)=0\) and \(\mu_a(u_a-x_a^*)=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coupled convex flow retains a global subgradient/KKT certificate, although it generally lacks independent arc-local reduced costs.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper, closed, and convex.
A relative-interior qualification ensures the displayed multiplier form.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in P}F(x)\iff0\in\partial F(x^*)+N_P(x^*).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete convex objective with a nonzero mixed derivative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On an open set in \(\mathbb R^2\), let \(F(x_1,x_2)=(x_1+x_2)^2\). Its Hessian is positive semidefinite, so \(F\) is convex, but \(\partial^2F/(\partial x_1\partial x_2)=2\). Hence it cannot equal \(\phi_1(x_1)+\phi_2(x_2)\) there for twice-differentiable scalar functions \(\phi_1,\phi_2\), whose mixed derivative would be zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A shared-load quadratic is convex but not decomposable into independent arc costs.
assumptions_latex: \((x_1,x_2)\) ranges over a nonempty open set.
Any asserted scalar decomposition is twice differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\ne\phi_1+\phi_2\text{ on the open set}.
knowledge_statements.title: Shared-Load Quadratic Coupling

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Flow with Coupled Arc Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex network-flow model without an arcwise-separable objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A coupled convex-cost flow problem has the form \[\min\{F(x):Bx=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\},\] where \(F:\mathbb R^A\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper convex but need not satisfy \(F(x)=\sum_{a\in A}\phi_a(x_a)\). Feasibility retains network structure, while objective values and marginal changes may involve several arcs jointly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coupled convex-cost flow preserves network feasibility but permits a jointly dependent convex objective.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper and convex.
The feasible set is defined by network conservation and arc bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ need not decompose into independent scalar arc costs}.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Flow with Coupled Arc Costs

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of independent scalar subproblems after dualizing conservation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Dualizing \(Bx=b\) with node prices \(p\) yields \[\inf_{\ell\le x\le u}\bigl(F(x)-(B^{\mathsf T}p)^{\mathsf T}x\bigr).\] Additive arc separability makes this infimum split into scalar arc subproblems. For a genuinely coupled \(F\), the split generally fails, and the price-induced flow must be obtained from a coupled convex problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Node prices do not generally split a coupled objective into independent arc minimizations.
assumptions_latex: Conservation is dualized by node prices.
\(F\) is genuinely nonseparable on the feasible box.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Arcwise scalar Lagrangian minimization is not valid in general}.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Arcwise Lagrangian Decomposition

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Loss of Fixed Arc-Local Residual Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional derivatives of a coupled objective depend on the whole current flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(F\) is differentiable, the first-order cost of a feasible circulation direction \(d\) at \(x\) is \(\nabla F(x)^{\mathsf T}d\). For nonseparable \(F\), \(\partial F(x)/\partial x_a\) may depend on coordinates \(x_b\) with \(b\ne a\). Thus a residual arc cannot generally be assigned an exact marginal-cost function determined solely by its own flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under coupling, an arc's marginal cost can depend on other arc flows, invalidating independent arc-local residual costs.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is differentiable near the current flow.
\(F\) is not arc-separable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \partial_aF(x)\text{ may depend on }x_b\text{ for }b\ne a.
knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Fixed Arc-Local Residual Costs
Coupled Arc Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex coupling can invalidate an exact decomposition into independent arc costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On two arc variables \((x_1,x_2)\in\mathbb R^2\), let \(F(x_1,x_2)=(x_1-x_2)^2\). This cost is convex but cannot be represented on any open set as \(F(x_1,x_2)=\phi_1(x_1)+\phi_2(x_2)\): its mixed derivative is \(\partial^2F/(\partial x_1\partial x_2)=-2\), while every twice-differentiable separable representation has zero mixed derivative. Consequently, the exact marginal cost of changing one arc depends on the other arc flow, so fixed arc-local residual costs do not represent the coupled objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even a convex objective may lose arc separability, making each arc’s exact marginal cost depend on flows elsewhere.
assumptions_latex: \((x_1,x_2)\) ranges over an open subset of \(\mathbb R^2\).
\(\phi_1\) and \(\phi_2\) are twice differentiable if such a decomposition is asserted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\neq\phi_1+\phi_2\) on every nonempty open set.
review_flags: No supplied locator specifically supports the separability boundary.

children.title: Side-Constrained Convex Flows

knowledge_statements.scope_note: KKT certificate showing how genuine side constraints enlarge the node-potential certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose each \(\phi_a\) is proper, closed, and convex, the side-constrained problem has a finite feasible point, and a convex constraint qualification ensuring KKT necessity holds. A feasible finite-cost flow \(x^\star\) is optimal if and only if there exist node potentials \(\pi\), equality multipliers \(\lambda\), and inequality multipliers \(\mu\ge0\) such that \[0\in\partial\phi_a(x_a^\star)+(B^{\mathsf T}\pi+C^{\mathsf T}\lambda+D^{\mathsf T}\mu)_a+N_{[\ell_a,u_a]}(x_a^\star)\quad(a\in A),\] and \(\mu_i((Dx^\star)_i-q_i)=0\) for every side inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under a suitable constraint qualification, side constraints require additional KKT multipliers; node potentials alone generally do not certify optimality.
assumptions_latex: Each arc cost is proper, closed, and convex.
The problem has a finite feasible point.
A constraint qualification ensuring KKT necessity holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Optimality is equivalent to primal feasibility, stationarity, dual feasibility, and complementary slackness with side-constraint multipliers.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A separable convex-cost flow augmented by constraints not expressible solely as node balances and individual arc bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A side-constrained convex flow has the form \[\min_x\sum_{a\in A}\phi_a(x_a)\quad\text{subject to}\quad Bx=b,\quad \ell\le x\le u,\quad Cx=d,\quad Dx\le q,\] where every \(\phi_a\) is convex and at least one row of \(C\) or \(D\) is nonredundant and is neither a node-balance equation nor a single-arc bound. The model remains convex, but its constraint system is not purely an incidence system with box bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Side-Constrained Convex Flow
Side-Constrained Convex Flows
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An additional linear constraint can destroy the integral network-flow structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider two parallel source-to-sink arcs with continuous flows \(x_1,x_2\geq0\), unit demand \(x_1+x_2=1\), and any convex objective, for example the zero function. Adding the side constraint \(x_1=x_2\) leaves the unique feasible flow \((x_1,x_2)=(1/2,1/2)\). Hence, although the underlying network and its demand have integral data, the side-constrained feasible set has no integral point. Pure network-flow integrality and algorithms relying on the unaugmented incidence structure therefore do not transfer automatically.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A side constraint can force fractional flows despite integral network data, eliminating the usual network-flow integrality guarantee.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x_1,x_2)=(1/2,1/2)\) is the unique feasible flow.

knowledge_statements.title: Continuous Convex-Flow Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separable convex-cost flow with real-valued arc variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a directed graph with node-arc incidence matrix \(B\), let \(b\in\mathbb R^V\), and let \(\ell,u\in(\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty,+\infty\})^A\) satisfy \(\ell_a\leq u_a\) for every \(a\in A\). The continuous convex-flow problem is
\[\min_{x\in\mathbb R^A}\left\{\sum_{a\in A}\phi_a(x_a):Bx=b,\ \ell_a\leq x_a\leq u_a\text{ for every }a\in A\right\}.\]
Each \(\phi_a:[\ell_a,u_a]\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Feasible flows and perturbations are real-valued; no integrality restriction is imposed on \(x\), even when \(b,\ell,u\) are integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuous convex flow minimizes separable convex arc costs over real-valued flows satisfying conservation equations and arc bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,A)\) is a directed graph and \(B\) is its node-arc incidence matrix.
\(b\in\mathbb R^V\) and \(\ell_a\leq u_a\) for every \(a\in A\).
\(\phi_a\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on \([\ell_a,u_a]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is optimized over a convex subset of \(\mathbb R^A\).

notation.meaning: directed graph with node set V and arc set A

children.title: Integral Convex-Flow Regime
children.top_down_role: Structural behavior of convex flows restricted to integral variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Integral Convex-Flow Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separable discrete-convex cost flow with integer arc variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,A)\) be a directed graph with node-arc incidence matrix \(B\), let \(b\in\mathbb Z^V\), and let \(\ell,u\in\mathbb Z^A\) satisfy \(\ell_a\leq u_a\) for every \(a\in A\). The integral convex-flow problem is
\[\min_{x\in\mathbb Z^A}\left\{\sum_{a\in A}\phi_a(x_a):Bx=b,\ \ell_a\leq x_a\leq u_a\text{ for every }a\in A\right\}.\]
For every \(a\in A\), the function \(\phi_a\) is defined on \([\ell_a,u_a]\cap\mathbb Z\), and its forward differences \(\Delta\phi_a(k)=\phi_a(k+1)-\phi_a(k)\) are nondecreasing wherever they are defined. Thus convexity is interpreted discretely, and feasible augmentations change flow by integral amounts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integral convex flow minimizes separable costs with nondecreasing discrete marginal costs over integer-valued flows satisfying conservation equations and arc bounds.

knowledge_statements.title: Continuous–Integral Transfer Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous convex optima need not themselves be feasible integral flows.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Take two parallel arcs carrying total demand one, with \(x_1+x_2=1\), \(x_1,x_2\geq0\), and objective \(x_1^2+x_2^2\). Over real flows, strict convexity gives the unique optimum \((x_1,x_2)=(1/2,1/2)\) with value \(1/2\). Under the additional restriction \((x_1,x_2)\in\mathbb Z^2\), the only feasible flows are \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\), each with value \(1\). Thus network integrality does not imply that a nonlinear continuous convex optimum is integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly convex continuous flow may have a unique fractional optimum even though integral feasible flows exist.

children.title: Generalized-Flow Feasibility

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized-Flow Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility with arc gains and lower-bound node requirements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let each directed arc \(a=(i,j)\) have gain \(\gamma_a>0\), capacity \(u_a\geq0\), and sent flow \(x_a\). Define node excess by
\[e_v(x)=\sum_{a=(i,v)}\gamma_a x_a-\sum_{a=(v,j)}x_a.\]
For a requirement vector \(b\in\mathbb R^V\), a generalized flow is feasible when \(0\leq x_a\leq u_a\) for every arc and \(e_v(x)\geq b_v\) for every node. An arc sending \(x_a\) units consumes that amount at its tail and delivers \(\gamma_a x_a\) at its head.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generalized-flow feasibility requires capacities and gain-adjusted node excesses meeting all prescribed lower bounds.

\(u_a\geq0\)

children.title: Generalized Circulation

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Circulation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Gain-adjusted balance equalities, including the zero-demand circulation case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a directed gain network, a generalized circulation with prescribed balance vector \(b\in\mathbb R^V\) is a vector \(x\) satisfying \(\ell_a\leq x_a\leq u_a\) and
\[\sum_{a=(i,v)}\gamma_a x_a-\sum_{a=(v,j)}x_a=b_v\qquad\text{for every }v\in V.\]
The pure generalized-circulation case has \(b=0\). Unlike ordinary circulation, the total amount arriving along an arc may differ from the amount sent, so the equations need not reduce to ordinary flow conservation unless all gains equal one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized circulation satisfies capacity bounds and gain-adjusted balance equations at every node; pure circulation uses zero balances.

children.title: Generalized-Flow Maximization

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized-Flow Maximization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum gain-adjusted delivery to a designated sink under finite capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(t\in V\) be a designated sink, let \(s_v\geq0\) be available external supply at each \(v\neq t\), and define \(e_v(x)\) by gain-adjusted inflow minus sent outflow. The generalized-flow maximization problem is
\[\max\left\{e_t(x):0\leq x_a\leq u_a,\ e_v(x)\geq-s_v\text{ for every }v\neq t\right\}.\]
Its objective measures the quantity delivered to \(t\) after applying all traversed arc gains; finite capacities prevent unlimited use of amplifying arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generalized-flow maximization sends available supplies through gain arcs to maximize gain-adjusted excess delivered at a chosen sink.

\(s_v\geq0\) for \(v\neq t\).
\(0\leq u_a<\infty\)

children.title: Minimum-Cost Generalized Flow

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cost Generalized Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-cost optimization subject to gain-adjusted balance equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given arc costs \(c_a\in\mathbb R\), gains \(\gamma_a>0\), bounds \(\ell_a\leq u_a\), and prescribed balances \(b_v\), the minimum-cost generalized-flow problem is
\[\min_x\left\{\sum_{a\in A}c_ax_a:\ell_a\leq x_a\leq u_a,\ \sum_{a=(i,v)}\gamma_ax_a-\sum_{a=(v,j)}x_a=b_v\text{ for every }v\in V\right\}.\]
Costs are charged per unit sent on an arc, while the receiving node obtains the gain-scaled quantity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimum-cost generalized flow minimizes sending costs while satisfying capacities and gain-adjusted node balances.

\(\ell_a\leq u_a\)
\(c_a,b_v\in\mathbb R\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sparse-Column LP Representation of Minimum-Cost Generalized Flow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality-form nonnegative linear programs whose columns contain at most two nonzero coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) have \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\), and suppose \(|\operatorname{supp}(a_j)|\le 2\) for every column \(a_j\). The problem \(\min\{c^\top x:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}\) admits a generalized-network representation: rows are nodes, each two-entry column is a link between the corresponding nodes, each one-entry column is a link incident to its corresponding node, and its nonzero coefficients are incidence multipliers. Thus \(Ax=b\) is precisely the system of weighted nodal-balance equations \(\sum_{j:\,p\in L_j}A_{pj}x_j=b_p\) for every node \(p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a full-row-rank equality-form nonnegative LP has at most two nonzero coefficients in every column, its rows can be regarded as nodes and its nonzero columns as links. The column coefficients serve as endpoint multipliers, so the equality constraints are weighted nodal-flow balances. With the linear objective, this is a minimum-cost generalized-flow or gain-network representation.

children.title: Generalized Residual Networks

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence between residual vectors and bound-preserving changes under tail-based units.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z_e^+\) and \(z_e^-\) be nonnegative amounts on the forward and reverse residual copies of an original arc \(e\), within their respective residual capacities. Define \[\Delta x_e=z_e^+-\frac{z_e^-}{\gamma_e}.\] Then \(0\leq x+\Delta x\leq u\), and, writing \(A_{\gamma_x}\) for the generalized incidence matrix of the residual arcs, \[A_\gamma\Delta x=A_{\gamma_x}z.\] For linear costs, \[c^{\mathsf T}\Delta x=\sum_e c_ez_e^+-\sum_e\frac{c_e}{\gamma_e}z_e^-,\] which is the residual-vector cost. Conversely, every bound-preserving change \(\Delta x\) has such a representation by using only the forward copy when \(\Delta x_e\geq0\) and only the reverse copy when \(\Delta x_e<0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual vectors encode exactly all bound-preserving arc changes, with matching generalized imbalance and objective change.

Every gain \(\gamma_e\) is positive.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gauge Invariance of Generalized Node Labels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common rescaling and logarithmic translation of a positive node labeling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any positive labeling \(\mu\in\mathbb R_{>0}^{V}\) and scalar \(a>0\), set \(\mu'_i=a\mu_i\). Then \[\gamma_{ij}^{\mu'}=\gamma_{ij}\frac{a\mu_i}{a\mu_j}=\gamma_{ij}^{\mu}.\] Equivalently, for \(p_i=\log\mu_i\), replacing \(p\) by \(p+(\log a)\mathbf 1\) preserves every label difference, represented gain, and tight arc. Thus one normalization such as \(\mu_r=1\) or \(p_r=0\) may be imposed without changing the represented gains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Common positive rescaling changes no represented gain; in logarithmic coordinates it is translation by a constant, so one reference label may be normalized.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma^{a\mu}=\gamma^{\mu}\), and common-scalar normalization preserves all represented-gain inequalities and equalities.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and every \(\gamma_e>0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative labels and their logarithmic additive representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A generalized node-label representation assigns \(\mu_i\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}\) to every \(i\in V\). For an arc \((i,j)\), its represented gain is \[\gamma_{ij}^{\mu}:=\gamma_{ij}\frac{\mu_i}{\mu_j}.\] Equivalently, setting \(p_i:=\log\mu_i\) and \(\ell_{ij}:=-\log\gamma_{ij}\) gives \[\log\gamma_{ij}^{\mu}=p_i-p_j-\ell_{ij}.\] Thus the multiplicative condition \(\gamma_{ij}^{\mu}\leq1\) is the additive difference inequality \(p_i-p_j\leq\ell_{ij}\), while equality identifies an arc tight under the labeling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive node labels rescale each gain by the tail label divided by the head label; logarithms convert this into a difference-constraint representation.

u}(R_{\mu}(x,\gamma))=R_{\mu\odot
u}(x,\gamma),\] where \((\mu\odot

Capacities transform as \(u_e^{\mu}=u_e/\mu_i\), and linear costs as \(c_e^{\mu}=c_e\mu_i\), preserving \(c^{\mathsf T}x\). For every directed cycle \(C\), cancellation of node labels yields \(\prod_{e\in C}\gamma_e^{\mu}=\prod_{e\in C}\gamma_e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relabeling changes node units, flows, gains, capacities, and costs consistently while preserving balances, objective values, and every directed cycle-gain product.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Relabeling Transformations

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The diagonal relabeling formulas are internally consistent, but their exact generalized-incidence and cost conventions need specialized support.

children.title: Label Feasibility Regimes
children.top_down_role: Compatibility boundaries for node labels within generalized residual networks.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction of a nonamplifying label or a gain-cycle obstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(\ell_{ij}=-\log\gamma_{ij}\). Form a difference-constraint graph having an arc \(j\to i\) of length \(\ell_{ij}\) for every original arc \(i\to j\), and add a source with zero-length arcs to all vertices. Bellman--Ford either returns a negative directed cycle, corresponding to an original directed cycle \(C\) with \(\prod_{e\in C}\gamma_e>1\), or returns distances \(p\) satisfying \(p_i-p_j\leq\ell_{ij}\). In the latter case \(\mu_i=e^{p_i}\) is gain-feasible. In a real-arithmetic model this requires \(O(|V||E|)\) relaxation evaluations on the augmented graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The logarithmic difference-constraint algorithm either constructs a feasible positive label or returns an amplifying directed cycle.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite.
Every gain satisfies \(\gamma_e>0\).
Logarithms and exact comparisons are available in the stated real-arithmetic complexity model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns either \(\mu>0\) with \(\gamma_{ij}\mu_i\leq\mu_j\) for every arc or a directed cycle \(C\) with \(\Gamma(C)>1\).

notation.meaning: negative logarithm of the arc gain

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Label Construction by Difference Constraints
Label Feasibility Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility of labels that make all represented gains nonamplifying.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A positive label \(\mu\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{V}\) is gain-feasible when \[\gamma_{ij}\mu_i\leq\mu_j\qquad\text{for every }(i,j)\in E.\] Such a label exists if and only if every directed cycle \(C\) satisfies \[\Gamma(C):=\prod_{e\in C}\gamma_e\leq1.\] Under logarithms, this is the feasibility criterion for the difference constraints \(p_i-p_j\leq-\log\gamma_{ij}\). A cycle with \(\Gamma(C)>1\) is therefore a finite, directly checkable obstruction to this label regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Labels making every rescaled gain at most one exist exactly when every directed cycle has gain product at most one.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed graph.
Every arc gain satisfies \(\gamma_e>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A feasible positive label exists exactly when no directed cycle has gain product greater than one.

notation.meaning: multiplicative gain of directed cycle C

children.title: Generalized Feasibility Obstructions
children.top_down_role: Label and gain-cycle obstructions to feasibility.

knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Feasibility Obstructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-capacity Farkas separation certificate for generalized balance feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The bounded generalized-flow system \(A_\gamma x=b\), \(0\leq x\leq u\), is infeasible if and only if there exists a vector \(y\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\) satisfying \[y^{\mathsf T}b>\sum_{e\in E}u_e\bigl[(A_\gamma^{\mathsf T}y)_e\bigr]_+.\] Such a vector is a finite, directly checkable generalized feasibility obstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded generalized-flow balance system is infeasible exactly when a node vector values the demand more highly than every capacity-bounded generalized arc flow can be valued.
assumptions_latex: \(A_\gamma\) is the generalized incidence matrix of a finite network.
The feasibility system is \(A_\gamma x=b\) with finite bounds \(0\leq x\leq u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed strict inequality is a verifiable certificate that the bounded generalized-flow system is infeasible, and such a certificate exists whenever the system is infeasible.

children.title: Generalized Optimality Certificates
children.top_down_role: Gain-aware replacements for ordinary cut and reduced-cost certificates.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit dual program underlying the gain-aware reduced-cost certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:A_\gamma x=b,\ 0\leq x\leq u\},\] with finite \(u\), an equivalent dual is \[\max_{\pi\in\mathbb R^V,\ q\geq0}\ b^{\mathsf T}\pi-u^{\mathsf T}q\quad\text{subject to}\quad A_\gamma^{\mathsf T}\pi-q\leq c.\] Writing \(r=c-A_\gamma^{\mathsf T}\pi\), the gap for primal- and dual-feasible points is \[c^{\mathsf T}x-(b^{\mathsf T}\pi-u^{\mathsf T}q)=x^{\mathsf T}(r+q)+(u-x)^{\mathsf T}q\geq0.\] Equality is equivalent to \(x_e(r_e+q_e)=0\) and \((u_e-x_e)q_e=0\) for every arc, and eliminating \(q\) gives the immutable seed's reduced-cost sign conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The bounded generalized-flow LP has a node-potential and upper-bound-multiplier dual; zero primal-dual gap is equivalent to the gain-aware reduced-cost certificate.
assumptions_latex: \(A_\gamma x=b\) is finite-dimensional.
Every upper bound \(u_e\) is finite.
The primal is feasible and has a finite optimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Primal and dual feasibility imply weak duality, while zero gap is necessary and sufficient for mutual optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Generalized-Flow Linear-Programming Dual

assumptions_latex: \(x\) is feasible for \(\min\{c^{\mathsf T}x:A_\gamma x=b,\ 0\leq x\leq u\}\).
All capacities are finite and all data are real.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The flow \(x\) is optimal if and only if a node potential satisfying the displayed gain-aware sign conditions exists.

notation.meaning: gain-aware reduced cost of arc e

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-cost, bounded generalized-flow optimality via LP reduced costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A gain-aware optimality certificate for a feasible flow \(x\) is a vector \(\pi\in\mathbb{R}^{V}\). For each arc \(e=(i,j)\), define \[r_e:=c_e-(A_\gamma^{\mathsf T}\pi)_e=c_e+\pi_i-\gamma_e\pi_j.\] The certificate conditions are \[x_e=0\Rightarrow r_e\geq0,\qquad 0<x_e<u_e\Rightarrow r_e=0,\qquad x_e=u_e\Rightarrow r_e\leq0.\] A feasible \(x\) is globally optimal if and only if such \(\pi\) exists. These conditions are linear-programming complementary slackness expressed through the generalized incidence columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible generalized flow is optimal exactly when node potentials give nonnegative reduced costs at lower bounds, zero inside bounds, and nonpositive costs at upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Optimality Certificates

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reduced-cost signs are the correct bounded-LP optimality conditions and the certificate content kind fits, but the exact generalized-flow formulation lacks a source.
