children.title: Augmented-Forest Structures
children.top_down_role: Forest and extra-arc representations for generalized-flow bases.

assumptions_latex: \(A_\gamma\) is the generalized incidence matrix on \(V\).
Candidate basis columns consist of arc columns and selected node-unit columns.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected square matrix is nonsingular exactly when every component has one nonsingular augmentation of its forest.

notation.meaning: oriented multiplicative gain around cycle C

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized-incidence bases represented by forests with one augmentation per component.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An augmented forest consists of an undirected forest \(F\) of selected arc columns together with exactly one augmentation in each connected component: either one node-unit column, or one additional arc that creates a unique cycle \(C\). In the second case orient the traversal of \(C\), using \(\gamma_e\) when traversing an arc forward and \(\gamma_e^{-1}\) when traversing it backward, and require \(\Gamma(C)\neq1\). The square matrix formed from the columns indexed by \(F\cup Q\) is nonsingular if and only if every component has exactly one such augmentation and each augmented cycle satisfies this nonunit-gain condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized-flow basis is represented by forest components, each augmented by one root column or by one extra arc forming a nonunit-gain cycle.
knowledge_statements.title: Augmented-Forest Structures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The asserted augmented-forest nonsingularity characterization depends on the precise extended matrix containing node-unit columns and on specialized terminology; neither is sourced or fully specified.

children.title: Augmented-Forest Primal-Dual Representation Pair
children.top_down_role: Primal and dual information induced by augmented forests.

children.title: Augmented-Forest Flows
children.top_down_role: Primal flow information induced by augmented-forest structures.

assumptions_latex: \(B\) is the nonsingular basis matrix represented by an augmented forest.
Nonbasic arc variables are fixed at specified lower or upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The augmented-forest flow is the unique basic solution obtained by solving the generalized balance equations on the forest and its augmentations.

notation.meaning: generalized right-hand side after fixing nonbasic variables

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal basic solution associated with a nonsingular augmented forest.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix every nonbasic variable \(x_N\) at one of its bounds and set \(\widehat b:=b-A_Nx_N\). The augmented-forest flow is the unique vector \(x_B\) satisfying \[Bx_B=\widehat b,\qquad x_B=B^{-1}\widehat b.\] On a rooted-tree component, its entries can be determined by eliminating leaves toward the augmenting node column. On a unicyclic component, tree elimination leaves one scalar cycle equation; its coefficient is nonzero precisely because \(\Gamma(C)\neq1\). The resulting full vector \(x=(x_B,x_N)\) is primal feasible exactly when every basic component also obeys its prescribed bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After nonbasic flows are fixed, the augmented forest uniquely determines all basic flows; feasibility additionally requires those values to respect their bounds.
knowledge_statements.title: Augmented-Forest Flows

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The linear-algebraic basic-flow representation is plausible, but its augmented-forest interpretation and elimination claims depend on the unsourced basis convention.

children.title: Augmented-Forest Potentials
children.top_down_role: Dual price information induced by augmented-forest structures.

assumptions_latex: \(B\) is a nonsingular augmented-forest basis matrix.
\(c_B\) contains the objective coefficients of its basic columns.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The augmented forest determines a unique node-potential vector satisfying zero reduced cost on every basic column.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual basic solution induced by augmented-forest columns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The augmented-forest potential is the unique vector \(\pi\) solving \[B^{\mathsf T}\pi=c_B,
\qquad \pi=B^{-\mathsf T}c_B.\] Hence every basic arc \(e=(i,j)\) has zero reduced cost \(c_e+\pi_i-\gamma_e\pi_j=0\). A selected node-unit column fixes the potential at its augmented node to that column's cost. In a unicyclic component, propagating the arc equations around the unique cycle determines the remaining scalar potential because \(\Gamma(C)\neq1\). Reduced costs of nonbasic arcs are then obtained from the same gain-aware formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Basic costs and the augmented forest uniquely determine node potentials, making every basic reduced cost zero and defining reduced costs on nonbasic arcs.
knowledge_statements.title: Augmented-Forest Potentials

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dual equation is correct for a square nonsingular basis, but the node-unit and unicyclic augmented-forest interpretations require specialized evidence.

children.title: Flow–Potential Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Compatibility between forest-induced primal and dual information.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Corrects the overlapping lower- and upper-bound implications when an arc has equal bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a minimization problem with reduced cost r_e, the lower-bound rule r_e\ge0 and upper-bound rule r_e\le0 apply only to nonfixed variables. If \ell_e=u_e, the variable admits no feasible local displacement and bound complementarity imposes no sign restriction on r_e. Thus the disjoint rule is r_e\ge0 at a nonfixed lower bound, r_e=0 in the strict interior, r_e\le0 at a nonfixed upper bound, and no sign condition for a fixed arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed arc has no reduced-cost sign requirement; lower-, interior-, and upper-bound tests apply only to nonfixed arcs with disjoint bound statuses.
assumptions_latex: x_e\in[\ell_e,u_e].
r_e\text{ is the reduced cost in a minimization formulation}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \ell_e=u_e\Longrightarrow r_e\text{ is unrestricted by bound complementarity}.

notation.meaning: Gain-aware reduced cost of arc e.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Arc Exception to Bound-Sign Tests

assumptions_latex: \(x\) is the augmented-forest basic flow and \(\pi\) its associated potential.
The model is a bounded linear-cost generalized flow with finite capacities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Primal bounds together with the gain-aware reduced-cost signs are equivalent to compatibility and certify optimality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual compatibility for a bounded augmented-forest basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An augmented-forest flow-potential pair \((x,\pi)\) is compatible when \(A_\gamma x=b\), \(0\leq x\leq u\), and, for every arc \(e=(i,j)\), \[r_e:=c_e+\pi_i-\gamma_e\pi_j\] satisfies \[x_e=0\Rightarrow r_e\geq0,
\qquad 0<x_e<u_e\Rightarrow r_e=0,
\qquad x_e=u_e\Rightarrow r_e\leq0.\] The basis equations already imply \(r_e=0\) for every basic arc \(e\in B\). Therefore compatibility is checked by primal bounds on basic flows and the appropriate reduced-cost signs on nonbasic arcs; when both hold, \((x,\pi)\) is a primal-dual optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An augmented-forest flow and potential are compatible when the flow respects balances and bounds and every reduced cost has the complementary sign required by its bound status.
knowledge_statements.title: Flow–Potential Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compatibility conditions match bounded-LP complementary slackness when lower and upper bounds are distinct. As written, finite capacities permit \(u_e=0\), where the displayed implications overlap and incorrectly force zero reduced cost; the source or assumptions must resolve this boundary case.

children.title: Augmented-Forest Basis Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Correspondence between generalized network structures and bases.

children.title: Good Augmented-Forest Structures
children.top_down_role: Augmented forests possessing the structural features needed for basis interpretations.

assumptions_latex: The augmented directed graph is \(\bar G=(V,\bar E)\), and every arc \(a\in\bar E\) has gain \(\gamma_a>0\).
An augmented forest \(F\subseteq\bar E\) has exactly one undirected cycle in each weakly connected component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is good if and only if \(\Gamma(C)\ne 1\) for the unique cycle \(C\) of every component.

notation.meaning: Gain product around an oriented cycle, using reciprocal gains against its orientation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the unicyclic-component interpretation of an augmented forest; the project-specific convention requires confirmation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an oriented traversal of a cycle \(C\), define \(\Gamma(C)=\prod_{a\in C}\gamma_a^{\sigma_a}\), where \(\sigma_a=1\) when the traversal follows arc \(a\) and \(\sigma_a=-1\) otherwise. An augmented forest \(F\) is called good when every weak component of \((V,F)\) is unicyclic and its unique cycle \(C\) satisfies \(\Gamma(C)\ne1\). Equivalently, the generalized-incidence columns indexed by each component of \(F\) are linearly independent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A unicyclic augmented forest is good when the gain product around every component’s unique cycle is not one, equivalently making its generalized-incidence columns independent.
knowledge_statements.title: Good Augmented-Forest Structures

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is plausible under the stated full generalized-incidence convention, but no inspectable source establishes the project-specific meaning of an augmented forest, the term “good,” or the claimed linear-independence equivalence.

children.title: Linear-Programming Basis Structures
children.top_down_role: Basis geometry associated with generalized network-flow formulations.

assumptions_latex: The generalized-flow polyhedron is \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^{E}:A_\gamma x=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\).
The generalized incidence matrix \(A_\gamma\) has full row rank \(r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A basis is an arc set \(B\subseteq E\) with \(|B|=r\) and \(\det A_{\gamma,B}\ne0\).

notation.meaning: Generalized incidence matrix with tail coefficient minus one and head coefficient equal to the arc gain.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded-variable linear-programming basis specialized to a generalized-incidence matrix.

source_refs.locator: 5.10 Methods for linear programming p. 67
source_refs.source_title: Combinatorial Optimization: Polyhedra and Efficiency

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A_\gamma\in\mathbb R^{r\times E}\) have full row rank. A linear-programming basis is a set \(B\subseteq E\) of \(r\) arcs such that the square matrix \(A_{\gamma,B}\) is nonsingular. After every nonbasic variable \(x_a\), \(a\notin B\), is fixed at either \(\ell_a\) or \(u_a\), the basic vector is uniquely determined by \(A_{\gamma,B}x_B=b-A_{\gamma,E\setminus B}x_{E\setminus B}\). The basis is feasible precisely when \(\ell_B\le x_B\le u_B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basis selects a nonsingular square set of generalized-incidence columns; fixing all other variables at bounds uniquely determines the basic variables.
knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Programming Basis Structures

source_witnesses.locator: 5.10 Methods for linear programming p. 67
source_witnesses.source_title: Combinatorial Optimization: Polyhedra and Efficiency

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded-variable LP geometry specialized to the generalized-incidence formulation; it does not characterize independent sets as augmented forests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let P=\{x\in\mathbb R^E:A_\gamma x=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}, let \operatorname{rank}(A_\gamma)=r, and define I(x)=\{a\in E:\ell_a<x_a<u_a\}. A feasible x is a vertex of P if and only if the columns A_{\gamma,I(x)} are linearly independent. Equivalently, I(x) extends to a size-r basis B, all variables outside B are at bounds, and A_{\gamma,B} uniquely determines x_B.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible bounded generalized flow is a vertex exactly when the columns belonging to its strictly non-bound arcs are independent; equivalently, those columns can be extended to a feasible LP basis.
assumptions_latex: P=\{x:A_\gamma x=b,\ \ell\le x\le u\}\ne\varnothing.
\operatorname{rank}(A_\gamma)=r.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\in\operatorname{vert}(P)\iff A_{\gamma,I(x)}\text{ has linearly independent columns}.

notation.meaning: Variables strictly between their bounds at x.

knowledge_statements.title: Vertex Characterization by Free-Column Independence

children.title: Forest–Basis Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Structural correspondence between good augmented forests and linear-programming bases.

assumptions_latex: For each arc \(a=(i,j)\), its column has entries \(-1\) at \(i\), \(\gamma_a>0\) at \(j\), and zero elsewhere.
The selected set \(B\) contains exactly \(|V|\) arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(A_{\gamma,B}\) is nonsingular exactly when every component of \((V,B)\) is unicyclic and has cycle gain different from \(1\).

notation.meaning: Generalized-incidence submatrix formed by columns indexed by the selected arcs.
Oriented gain product of a cycle.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-row generalized-incidence convention without deleting a balance row.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\subseteq E\) satisfy \(|B|=|V|\). Then \(A_{\gamma,B}\) is nonsingular if and only if every weak component of \((V,B)\) contains equally many vertices and arcs and its unique undirected cycle \(C\) has oriented gain product \(\Gamma(C)\ne1\). Thus the linear-programming bases are exactly the good augmented forests under this matrix convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the full generalized-incidence convention, bases correspond exactly to unicyclic components whose unique cycle has gain product unequal to one.
knowledge_statements.title: Forest–Basis Correspondence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The correspondence is plausible for the stated full square generalized-incidence convention, but its validity depends critically on the retained-row and augmented-arc conventions. No source supports those hypotheses or the exact equivalence.

children.title: Degenerate Basis Regimes
children.top_down_role: Geometric regimes where the forest-to-basis interpretation loses uniqueness or regularity.

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Basis Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded-variable simplex degeneracy, independent of the particular forest representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A feasible bounded-variable basis \(B\) is degenerate if and only if at least one basic variable satisfies \(x_a=\ell_a\) or \(x_a=u_a\). In a degenerate regime, a valid simplex pivot may have step length zero, in which case the basis changes while the represented feasible point and its objective value remain unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible bounded-variable basis is degenerate exactly when at least one basic variable is at a bound. Degeneracy can permit a zero-step pivot that changes the basis without changing the feasible point or objective value.
assumptions_latex: A feasible bounded-variable basis \(B\) determines \(x_B=A_{\gamma,B}^{-1}(b-A_{\gamma,E\setminus B}x_{E\setminus B})\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The basis is degenerate if and only if \(x_a\in\{\ell_a,u_a\}\) for at least one \(a\in B\).

children.title: Generalized Network Simplex
children.top_down_role: Simplex pivoting specialized to gain networks.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded-variable simplex variant within generalized network simplex; the augmented-forest basis is unchanged when the entering variable alone limits the step.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a nonbasic variable x_a enter from one of its bounds and let d satisfy A_\gamma d=0 with d_a\in\{1,-1\}. Define \theta^*=\sup\{\theta\ge0:\ell\le x+\theta d\le u\}. If x_a reaches its opposite bound before every basic variable reaches a bound, update x\leftarrow x+\theta^*d and change only the nonbasic bound status of a; the basis B and its augmented-forest representation remain unchanged. If a basic variable is simultaneously limiting, an admissible tie rule may instead perform a basis exchange.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the entering arc reaches its opposite bound before any basic arc limits the step, generalized network simplex performs a bound flip and retains the augmented-forest basis.
assumptions_latex: B\text{ is a feasible bounded-variable basis}.
a\notin B\text{ is selected to move away from its current bound}.
d_B=-A_{\gamma,B}^{-1}A_{\gamma,a}d_a.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: a\text{ alone limits the step}\Longrightarrow B'=B\text{ and only the bound status of }a\text{ changes}.

notation.meaning: Maximum primal step preserving all variable bounds.
Feasible basis direction induced by the entering arc.

knowledge_statements.title: Entering-Variable Bound Flip

assumptions_latex: The bounded generalized-flow linear program has a feasible augmented-forest basis.
Entering and leaving choices obey a deterministic anti-cycling rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The method terminates when every nonbasic arc satisfies its bound-compatible reduced-cost sign condition.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal bounded-variable simplex with bases represented by good augmented forests.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize with a feasible good augmented-forest basis \(B\). Compute node potentials from \(A_{\gamma,B}^{\mathsf T}\pi=c_B\) and reduced costs \(\bar c_a=c_a-A_{\gamma,a}^{\mathsf T}\pi\). If every nonbasic arc has the sign required by the bound at which it is fixed, output the current flow. Otherwise choose a violating entering arc, solve \(A_{\gamma,B}d_B=-A_{\gamma,a}d_a\), increase \(\theta\ge0\) until a variable first reaches a bound, exchange the corresponding leaving arc with the entering arc, and repeat.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The generalized network simplex performs bounded-variable simplex pivots while representing each basis by a gain-aware augmented forest.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Network Simplex

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The generic bounded-variable simplex outline fits the container, but the augmented-forest pivot mechanics, reduced-cost sign convention, and termination claim require a source specifying the generalized-network variant and anti-cycling rule.

children.title: Generalized-Flow Improvement Algorithm Family
children.top_down_role: Path, preflow, relaxation, and scaling methods for gain networks.

children.title: Generalized Augmenting-Path Methods
children.top_down_role: Path-based improvement with gain-adjusted quantities.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single residual-path augmentation with every residual capacity measured in the corresponding arc's tail units; no global stopping theorem is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=(a_1,\ldots,a_k)\) be a residual path, with gain \(g_i>0\) and tail-unit residual capacity \(r_i>0\) on \(a_i\). Put \(q_0=1\) and \(q_i=\prod_{h=1}^{i}g_h\). An input \(\delta\) at the path origin sends \(q_{i-1}\delta\) through \(a_i\), so feasibility is equivalent to \(q_{i-1}\delta\le r_i\) for all \(i\). Therefore \(\delta^*=\min_i r_i/q_{i-1}\) is the largest feasible input, and the delivered amount at the path endpoint is \(q_k\delta^*\). Internal gain-adjusted imbalances cancel.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cumulative gains determine how much flow each path arc carries; the maximum input is the minimum residual capacity divided by the preceding prefix gain.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a directed residual path.
Every residual gain and capacity is positive.
Residual capacities are measured in arc-tail units.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta^*=\min_{1\le i\le k}\frac{r_i}{q_{i-1}},\qquad \text{endpoint delivery}=q_k\delta^*.

notation.meaning: product of the first i residual gains, with q_0=1
tail-unit residual capacity of the ith path arc
maximum feasible input at the path origin

knowledge_statements.title: Gain-Adjusted Residual-Path Augmentation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Path-Only Stopping Can Miss a Flow-Generating Cycle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counterexample to absence of a residual source-to-sink path being a general optimality certificate for generalized-flow maximization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider vertices \(s,v,w,t\) and arcs \(sv,vt,vw,wv\) with gains \(1,1,2,1\), respectively. Let \(u_{sv}=1\), and let the other capacities be at least \(2\). The flow \(x_{sv}=x_{vt}=1\), \(x_{vw}=x_{wv}=0\) balances \(v,w\) and delivers one unit to \(t\). Its residual network has no \(s\)-to-\(t\) path because \(sv\) is saturated. Nevertheless, for every sufficiently small \(\varepsilon>0\), setting \(x_{vw}=\varepsilon\), \(x_{wv}=2\varepsilon\), and increasing \(x_{vt}\) by \(\varepsilon\) preserves internal balances and increases delivery to \(t\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A saturated source arc may eliminate all residual source-to-sink paths while a gain-greater-than-one cycle can still generate additional sink flow.
assumptions_latex: The source may supply the displayed unit and the sink may absorb flow.
The nonsource arcs have sufficient residual capacity for the stated perturbation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nexists\text{ residual }s\text{-}t\text{ path}\quad\not\Rightarrow\quad x\text{ is optimal}.

notation.meaning: positive perturbation sent on arc vw

knowledge_statements.title: Path-Only Stopping Can Miss a Flow-Generating Cycle

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Forward and Reverse Residual Arcs in Tail Units
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual convention for one capacitated generalized arc; costs and global optimality conditions are outside this statement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an original arc \(ij\) with gain \(\gamma_{ij}>0\), capacity \(u_{ij}\), and flow \(0\le x_{ij}\le u_{ij}\), the forward residual arc \(ij\) has gain \(\gamma_{ij}\) and tail-unit capacity \(u_{ij}-x_{ij}\). If \(x_{ij}>0\), the reverse residual arc \(ji\) has gain \(\gamma_{ij}^{-1}\) and tail-unit capacity \(\gamma_{ij}x_{ij}\). Sending \(\eta\) tail units on the reverse arc cancels \(\eta/\gamma_{ij}\) units of original flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reverse residual arc has reciprocal gain and head-unit capacity sufficient to cancel the current original flow.
assumptions_latex: \(0\le x_{ij}\le u_{ij}\).
Residual capacities are measured at the residual arc's tail.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r^+_{ij}=u_{ij}-x_{ij},\quad \gamma^+_{ij}=\gamma_{ij},\qquad r^-_{ji}=\gamma_{ij}x_{ij},\quad \gamma^-_{ji}=\gamma_{ij}^{-1}.

notation.meaning: forward residual capacity in units at i
reverse residual capacity in units at j

knowledge_statements.title: Forward and Reverse Residual Arcs in Tail Units

assumptions_latex: A feasible residual generalized network contains an \(s\)-to-\(t\) residual path \(P=(a_1,\ldots,a_k)\).
Each residual arc \(a_i\) has gain \(g_i>0\) and residual capacity \(r_i>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maximum path augmentation is \(\delta^*=\min_{1\le i\le k}r_i/q_{i-1}\), delivering \(q_k\delta^*\) at \(t\).

notation.meaning: Residual capacity of the ith path arc measured at its tail.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-path augmentation with capacities measured in each residual arc’s tail units.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(q_0=1\) and \(q_i=\prod_{h=1}^{i}g_h\). For an input amount \(\delta\ge0\), send \(q_{i-1}\delta\) through arc \(a_i\); gain conservation then passes \(q_i\delta\) to the next vertex. Feasibility requires \(q_{i-1}\delta\le r_i\) for every \(i\). Choose \(\delta^*=\min_i r_i/q_{i-1}\), augment the residual flow accordingly, update forward and reverse residual capacities, and stop when no improving residual \(s\)-to-\(t\) path remains.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An augmenting path scales flow by cumulative gains; its bottleneck is the smallest residual capacity divided by the gain accumulated before that arc.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Augmenting-Path Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The gain-adjusted bottleneck formula is plausible when residual capacities are measured in tail units. A source is required for the residual reverse-arc convention and for the claim that absence of an improving source-to-sink path is a sufficient stopping condition for the intended problem.

children.title: Fat-Path Methods
children.top_down_role: Augmentation through paths carrying substantial relabeled flow.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tail-Unit Fatness of a Residual Path
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One explicit and internally consistent fatness convention; other normalizations must be converted before comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix positive node labels \(\mu_i\). For a residual arc \(ij\) whose residual capacity \(r_{ij}\) is measured in tail units, define \(\widehat r_{ij}=r_{ij}/\mu_i\). The labeled bottleneck of a residual path \(P\) is \(\operatorname{fat}_{\mu}(P)=\min_{ij\in P}\widehat r_{ij}\). The path is \(\Delta\)-fat exactly when \(\operatorname{fat}_{\mu}(P)\ge\Delta\), equivalently when every arc of \(P\) can accept at least \(\Delta\) labeled tail units.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the tail-unit convention, a path is Delta-fat when every residual arc has at least Delta capacity after division by its tail label.
assumptions_latex: Residual capacities are measured in each arc's tail units.
Every node label is positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is }\Delta\text{-fat}\iff\min_{ij\in P}r_{ij}/\mu_i\ge\Delta.

notation.meaning: residual capacity in labeled tail units
tail-unit labeled bottleneck of path P

knowledge_statements.title: Tail-Unit Fatness of a Residual Path

assumptions_latex: Positive labels \(\mu_i\) define relabeled residual capacities \(\hat r_{ij}=r_{ij}/\mu_i\).
A scaling threshold \(\Delta>0\) is fixed during the phase.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A residual path \(P\) is \(\Delta\)-fat when \(\min_{(i,j)\in P}\hat r_{ij}\ge\Delta\).

notation.meaning: Positive node label used to measure flow in relabeled units.
Residual capacity in relabeled tail units.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic relabeled-capacity formulation; exact fatness normalization varies among generalized-flow algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given labels \(\mu_i>0\), form \(\hat r_{ij}=r_{ij}/\mu_i\). During a \(\Delta\)-phase, search for an improving residual path \(P\) satisfying \(\hat r_{ij}\ge\Delta\) on every arc. Augment by the largest gain-adjusted amount permitted by \(P\), update residual capacities, and repeat while such a path exists. When none exists, reduce \(\Delta\) according to the prescribed scaling schedule; output when the terminal threshold guarantees the required feasibility or optimality tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fat-path method augments only on paths whose residual arcs all carry at least a threshold amount in relabeled flow units.
knowledge_statements.title: Fat-Path Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Fat-path definitions and relabeling normalizations vary across generalized-flow algorithms. Without a named algorithm or source, neither the stated normalization nor the terminal accuracy or optimality claim is reliable.

children.title: Price-Imbalance Algorithm Family
children.top_down_role: Local price and imbalance methods adapted to gains.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: Relaxation Methods for Minimum Cost Ordinary and Generalized Network Flow Problems
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: Relaxation Methods for Minimum Cost Ordinary and Generalized Network Flow Problems

children.title: Generalized Relaxation Methods
children.top_down_role: Local price-based improvement methods adapted to gain networks.

assumptions_latex: A generalized preflow and node prices \(p\) are maintained.
Residual reduced costs are \(\bar c_{ij}=c_{ij}+p_i-\gamma_{ij}p_j\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Each iteration either pushes flow on an admissible residual arc or changes a price until an admissible arc appears.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local push-or-price-update template for costed generalized-flow relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize a generalized preflow and prices satisfying the selected reduced-cost tolerance. Choose an active vertex \(i\) with positive imbalance \(e_i\). If a residual arc \((i,j)\) is admissible under \(\bar c_{ij}=c_{ij}+p_i-\gamma_{ij}p_j\), push the largest amount allowed by its residual capacity and the active imbalance, accounting for gain at \(j\). Otherwise change \(p_i\) to the nearest value that makes some residual arc admissible while preserving the global tolerance. Stop when no vertex is active.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generalized relaxation alternates gain-aware pushes from imbalanced vertices with local price changes that create admissible residual arcs.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Relaxation Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic role fits the leaf, but the reduced-cost sign, active-imbalance convention, price-update direction, and preserved global tolerance depend on an unstated relaxation variant.

children.title: Generalized Preflow Methods
children.top_down_role: Imbalance-based generalized-flow methods using preflow states.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit excess-oriented convention; formulations using deficit signs are equivalent only after reversing the inequalities and active-node terminology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a capacity-feasible generalized flow \(x\), define \(e_i=b_i+\sum_{(j,i)}\gamma_{ji}x_{ji}-\sum_{(i,j)}x_{ij}\). Given an exceptional terminal set \(T\), an excess-oriented generalized preflow satisfies \(e_i\ge0\) for every \(i\in V\setminus T\); equality is not required during the method.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the stated sign convention, a generalized preflow is capacity feasible and has no deficit outside the exceptional terminal set.
assumptions_latex: All arc gains are positive.
\(x\) satisfies the arc-capacity bounds.
The imbalance sign convention is exactly the displayed formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x\text{ is a generalized preflow}\iff e_i\ge0\quad(i\in V\setminus T).

notation.meaning: gain-adjusted excess at node i under the stated convention

knowledge_statements.title: Excess-Oriented Generalized Preflow

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gain-Adjusted Imbalance Transfer by a Push
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local imbalance algebra for a residual push; admissibility and global progress require a separately specified algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the excess convention, pushing a tail amount \(\delta\ge0\) on a residual arc \(ij\) of gain \(\gamma_{ij}>0\) changes only the endpoint imbalances: \(e_i' = e_i-\delta\) and \(e_j'=e_j+\gamma_{ij}\delta\). Thus a legal push consumes \(\delta\) units of tail excess and creates \(\gamma_{ij}\delta\) units of head excess, subject to residual capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A residual push removes its tail amount from the tail excess and adds the gain-scaled amount to the head excess.
assumptions_latex: The displayed excess convention is used.
The push amount does not exceed the tail-unit residual capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: e_i'=e_i-\delta,\qquad e_j'=e_j+\gamma_{ij}\delta.

notation.meaning: pushed amount measured at the residual arc tail

knowledge_statements.title: Gain-Adjusted Imbalance Transfer by a Push

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact-Balance Recovery from an Excess-Oriented Preflow
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility recovery under the accepted excess convention; this does not certify objective optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) be an excess-oriented generalized preflow with exceptional terminal set \(T\). If \(e_i=0\) for every \(i\notin T\), then every ordinary node satisfies its generalized balance equation. If the prescribed terminal conditions also hold on \(T\), the same capacity-feasible vector \(x\) is a feasible generalized flow.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized preflow is a feasible generalized flow once all ordinary excesses vanish and the exceptional terminals satisfy their prescribed conditions.
assumptions_latex: The accepted excess-oriented imbalance convention is used.
\(x\) is capacity feasible.
\(e_i=0\) for every \(i\in V\setminus T\).
All prescribed terminal conditions hold on \(T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: e_i=0\ (i\notin T)\ \land\ \text{terminal conditions on }T\quad\Rightarrow\quad x\text{ is a feasible generalized flow}.

notation.meaning: gain-adjusted excess under the accepted convention

knowledge_statements.title: Exact-Balance Recovery from an Excess-Oriented Preflow

assumptions_latex: For flow \(x\), node imbalance is \(e_i=b_i+\sum_{ji}\gamma_{ji}x_{ji}-\sum_{ij}x_{ij}\).
A designated set \(T\subseteq V\) may absorb surplus; all other nodes must not have deficits.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A generalized preflow satisfies \(e_i\ge0\) for every \(i\in V\setminus T\).

notation.meaning: Net gain-adjusted imbalance at node i.
Set of nodes permitted to absorb surplus or violate the ordinary conservation target.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Excess-oriented preflow convention; source-oriented formulations may reverse the imbalance sign.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a capacitated gain network, define \(e_i=b_i+\sum_{(j,i)}\gamma_{ji}x_{ji}-\sum_{(i,j)}x_{ij}\). A generalized preflow is a capacity-feasible vector \(x\) satisfying \(e_i\ge0\) at every nonterminal node \(i\in V\setminus T\); equality is not required during the algorithm. A preflow method repeatedly selects a node with disposable excess, pushes flow through residual arcs with gain-adjusted updates, and terminates or converts to a feasible generalized flow when the required imbalances vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A generalized preflow respects capacities but allows gain-adjusted excess at nonterminal nodes; push operations move that excess through residual arcs.
knowledge_statements.title: Generalized Preflow Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sign and terminal conventions are essential and currently unsupported. Moreover, the record is primarily a definition even though the terminal container names a method family; a source is needed before choosing between a definition and an algorithmic treatment.

children.title: Price–Imbalance Coordination
children.top_down_role: Interaction between local price information and node imbalance management.

assumptions_latex: The algorithm maintains imbalances \(e_i\) and prices \(p_i\).
For every residual arc, \(\bar c_{ij}=c_{ij}+p_i-\gamma_{ij}p_j\ge-\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An active imbalance is moved only on admissible arcs, while relabeling preserves \(\varepsilon\)-optimality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epsilon-optimal price convention for gain-adjusted residual costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain the joint invariant that residual reduced costs obey \(\bar c_{ij}\ge-\varepsilon\) and that only vertices with nonzero imbalance require processing. An admissible push transfers imbalance along an arc whose reduced cost is at the active boundary, with the receiving imbalance multiplied by \(\gamma_{ij}\). If no such arc leaves an active vertex, change its price only as far as needed to create one, without violating any residual reduced-cost inequality. Thus price updates expose directions and pushes reduce or relocate imbalance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prices identify admissible gain-aware directions, while pushes reduce or relocate imbalance without violating the maintained approximate reduced-cost conditions.
knowledge_statements.title: Price–Imbalance Coordination

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The coordination principle is plausible, but admissibility at the active boundary and preservation of all residual reduced-cost inequalities depend on the exact price convention and algorithm. These are not sourced.

children.title: Continuous-Scaling Contraction Calculus
children.top_down_role: Relabeling, scaling, and contraction in strongly polynomial generalized flow.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: A Strongly Polynomial Algorithm for Generalized Flow Maximization
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: A Strongly Polynomial Algorithm for Generalized Flow Maximization

children.title: Continuous-Scaling Framework
children.top_down_role: Scale management in strongly polynomial generalized-flow methods.

assumptions_latex: A scale parameter \(\Delta>0\) controls admissible imbalance or residual-capacity error.
Each phase preserves a specified \(\Delta\)-feasibility and approximate-optimality invariant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The framework produces solutions at scales \(\Delta_k\downarrow0\), with each phase warm-started from the preceding phase.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Abstract continuous-scaling template; the intended named algorithm and invariants require authoritative identification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(\Delta_0>0\) and \(0<\rho<1\). At phase \(k\), starting from the preceding flow and labels, apply gain-aware augmentations, pushes, and relabelings until the prescribed \(\Delta_k\)-feasibility and approximate-optimality conditions hold. Contract every arc certified abundant by the phase invariant, transfer the flow and labels to the contracted instance, and set \(\Delta_{k+1}=\rho\Delta_k\). Continue until \(\Delta_k\) is below the required tolerance, then expand contractions and recover a solution in the original network.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Continuous scaling repeatedly tightens an error scale, reuses the preceding solution, and contracts arcs whose status is certified stable at the current scale.
knowledge_statements.title: Continuous-Scaling Framework

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is too abstract to identify a mathematically determinate continuous-scaling algorithm. The phase invariant, contraction certificate, recovery rule, and stopping guarantee require an authoritative source and a named variant.

children.title: Gain-Aware Contraction
children.top_down_role: Network contraction based on persistent gain-aware structure.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic normalization used before contraction; it does not itself assert that contraction preserves feasibility or optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For positive node factors \(\alpha_i\), define \(\gamma'_{ij}=\gamma_{ij}\alpha_i/\alpha_j\). If \(a=(p,q)\) and \(\alpha_q=\gamma_a\alpha_p\), then \(\gamma'_a=1\). For every directed walk \(W\) from \(s\) to \(t\), \(\prod_{ij\in W}\gamma'_{ij}=(\alpha_s/\alpha_t)\prod_{ij\in W}\gamma_{ij}\); all internal scaling factors telescope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive node-unit scaling can normalize a selected arc to unit gain, and transformed walk gains differ only by the endpoint unit conversion.
assumptions_latex: Every arc gain is positive.
The node factors satisfy \(\alpha_i>0\).
For the selected arc \(a=(p,q)\), \(\alpha_q=\gamma_a\alpha_p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma'_a=1\) and transformed walk-gain products telescope by endpoint factors.

notation.meaning: positive scaling factor for node i

knowledge_statements.title: Gain Normalization by Node-Unit Scaling

assumptions_latex: An arc \(a=(p,q)\) with gain \(\gamma_a>0\) has been certified contractible.
Positive node scaling factors satisfy \(\alpha_q=\gamma_a\alpha_p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: After relabeling, \(\gamma'_a=1\), so \(p\) and \(q\) may be identified while preserving gains of projected walks.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic normalization underlying contraction; algorithmic validity additionally requires an abundance or persistence certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Relabel node units by positive factors \(\alpha_i\) and transform every gain by \(\gamma'_{ij}=\gamma_{ij}\alpha_i/\alpha_j\). Choosing \(\alpha_q=\gamma_a\alpha_p\) gives \(\gamma'_a=1\). The endpoints of \(a
g=(p,q)\) can then be identified in the relabeled network, with each incident arc retaining its transformed gain. Products of transformed gains along projected walks agree with those before identification. This algebraic contraction is algorithmically valid only when a separate certificate ensures that fixing or preserving \(a\) cannot exclude an admissible optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Normalize a contractible arc to unit gain by rescaling node units, then identify its endpoints while retaining transformed gains on incident arcs.
knowledge_statements.title: Gain-Aware Contraction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The gain-normalization formula is algebraically plausible, but endpoint identification does not by itself establish preservation of the generalized-flow instance or its optima. A source must provide the contractibility certificate and flow, balance, capacity, and expansion formulas. The statement also contains a malformed line break in the arc designation.

children.title: Relabeling Within Scaling Phases
children.top_down_role: Role of gain-aware price changes during continuous scaling.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary Condition for a Common-Factor Relabel
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact fitting-label condition for multiplying the labels of one vertex set by a common factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\gamma_{ij}^{\mu}=\gamma_{ij}\mu_i/\mu_j\le1\) on every residual arc, let \(S\subseteq V\), and set \(\mu'_i=\alpha\mu_i\) for \(i\in S\) and \(\mu'_i=\mu_i\) otherwise, where \(\alpha\ge1\). Gains on arcs internal or external to \(S\) are unchanged, gains entering \(S\) are divided by \(\alpha\), and gains leaving \(S\) are multiplied by \(\alpha\). Hence fitting is preserved exactly when \(\alpha\gamma_{ij}^{\mu}\le1\) for every residual arc \(i\in S,j\notin S\). If such arcs exist, the largest permissible factor is \(\alpha^*=\min_{i\in S,j\notin S}1/\gamma_{ij}^{\mu}\), and at least one leaving arc becomes tight at \(\alpha^*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scaling all labels in a set upward preserves fitting precisely until a residual arc leaving the set becomes tight.
assumptions_latex: \(\mu_i>0\) and \(\gamma_{ij}^{\mu}\le1\) on every residual arc.
\(\alpha\ge1\) multiplies exactly the labels in \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fitting is preserved iff \(\alpha\le\min_{i\in S,j\notin S}1/\gamma_{ij}^{\mu}\), with the minimum interpreted only when a leaving residual arc exists.
knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Condition for a Common-Factor Relabel

assumptions_latex: The generalized-flow instance has directed residual graph \(G_f=(V,E_f)\), positive residual gains \(\gamma_{ij}\), and positive labels \(\mu_i\).
The relabeled gain and excess are \(\gamma_{ij}^{\mu}=\gamma_{ij}\mu_i/\mu_j\) and \(e_i^{\mu}=e_i/\mu_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_{ij}^{\mu'}\le 1\) for every residual arc after the relabeling, and every arc newly declared admissible satisfies \(\gamma_{ij}^{\mu'}=1\).

notation.meaning: residual gain after applying node labels

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: fitting-label invariants are standard in generalized-flow scaling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fitting-label update inside one continuous-scaling phase.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a phase tolerance \(\Delta>0\), retain labels of inactive vertices and multiply labels on a selected active set \(S\subseteq V\) by a common factor \(\alpha\ge 1\). Choose the smallest \(\alpha\) at which either an arc crossing the boundary of \(S\) becomes tight, meaning \(\gamma_{ij}^{\mu'}=1\), or the phase reaches its prescribed event threshold. The selected set and direction of scaling must ensure that no residual relabeled gain exceeds one. Replace \(\mu\) by \(\mu'\), recompute relabeled excesses, and continue augmentation or contraction. Stop the phase when its scaling termination test is met.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Scale labels on the active set until a residual arc becomes tight or another phase event occurs, while preserving the fitting-label inequalities.
knowledge_statements.title: Relabeling Within Scaling Phases

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The selected set, scaling direction, and event threshold are not defined sufficiently to establish the claimed fitting-label invariant. An authoritative continuous-scaling generalized-flow source is needed to determine the correct update and hypotheses.

children.title: Contraction Validity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Structural conditions limiting safe generalized-network contraction.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tightness Alone Does Not Justify Contraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimal unit-gain instance showing that endpoint identification can erase a binding transfer capacity even when the selected arc is relabel-tight.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p\) supply two units, let \(q\) demand two units, and let the only arc be \(a=(p,q)\) with \(\gamma_a=1\) and capacity \(u_a=1\). With equal positive labels, \(\gamma_a^\mu=1\), but the original instance is infeasible. Naively identifying \(p\) and \(q\) and aggregating their opposite balances produces a zero-balance singleton instance, for which the zero flow is feasible. Thus relabeled tightness without a capacity-aware projection and lifting rule does not preserve feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tight unit-gain arc of insufficient capacity can join opposite-balance vertices; naively contracting it erases the transfer requirement and changes infeasibility into feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(p\) has supply \(2\) and \(q\) has demand \(2\).
The sole arc \(a=(p,q)\) has \(\gamma_a=1\), \(u_a=1\), and is tight under equal positive labels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_a^\mu=1\) does not imply that endpoint identification preserves feasibility.

notation.meaning: gain of the selected arc in relabeled units

knowledge_statements.title: Tightness Alone Does Not Justify Contraction

assumptions_latex: An arc \(ij\) is tight under \(\mu>0\), so \(\gamma_{ij}\mu_i/\mu_j=1\).
The proposed contraction identifies \(i\) and \(j\) and transforms all incident gains, bounds, and node balances consistently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Tightness alone does not imply that contracting \(ij\) preserves feasibility or the optimum; contraction is valid only with a recoverable flow correspondence in both directions.

notation.meaning: gain on the directed arc from i to j

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: contractions require a bidirectional lifting correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between tightness and equivalence-preserving contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A gain-aware contraction of a tight arc \(ij\) is valid only if every feasible contracted flow can be lifted to an original feasible flow and every original feasible flow projects to a contracted flow with the same objective value. This requires consistent rescaling of arcs incident to the merged vertex and preservation of finite capacities, lower bounds, supplies, and demands. Contraction is not justified merely by \(\gamma_{ij}^{\mu}=1\): it can fail when the arc cannot carry the amount required by a lift, when a fixed balance is discarded, or when transformed parallel arcs acquire incompatible bounds. In any such case, feasibility or the optimum may change.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tight arc may be contracted only when flows project and lift with all bounds, balances, gains, and objective values preserved.
knowledge_statements.title: Contraction Validity Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind fits, but the asserted projection-and-lifting requirements and transformed-bound conditions need a specialized contraction theorem or construction supporting their necessity and sufficiency.

children.title: Generalized-Flow Complexity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Approximate, exact, weakly polynomial, and strongly polynomial regimes.

children.title: Approximate Generalized Flow
children.top_down_role: Approximation based on relabeled imbalance and multiplicative accuracy.

assumptions_latex: The instance has nonnegative arc flows \(f\), positive gains \(\gamma\), positive labels \(\mu\), and distinguished sink \(t\).
The optimum sink inflow \(\mathrm{OPT}>0\), and \(0<\varepsilon<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((f,\mu)\) is an \(\varepsilon\)-approximate generalized flow when \(d_{\mu}(f)\le\varepsilon\), \(\gamma_{ij}^{\mu}\le 1+\varepsilon\) on every residual arc, and \(e_t(f)\ge(1-\varepsilon)\mathrm{OPT}\).

notation.meaning: node excess induced by the generalized flow
maximum relabeled deficit outside the sink

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: combines relabeled feasibility error with multiplicative objective error
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One explicit relabeled-imbalance and multiplicative-objective convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each nonsink vertex \(i\), let \(e_i(f)\) be generalized inflow minus outflow and prescribed demand, and define \(d_{\mu}(f)=\max_{i\ne t}(-e_i(f)/\mu_i)_+\). For every residual arc \(ij\), define \(\gamma_{ij}^{\mu}=\gamma_{ij}\mu_i/\mu_j\). The pair \((f,\mu)\) is called \(\varepsilon\)-approximate under this convention if \(d_{\mu}(f)\le\varepsilon\), every residual arc satisfies \(\gamma_{ij}^{\mu}\le1+\varepsilon\), and its sink value satisfies \(e_t(f)\ge(1-\varepsilon)\mathrm{OPT}\). The normalization of \(\mu\) must be fixed, since otherwise the deficit bound is scale-dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximation bounds normalized node deficits and residual gain violations by epsilon while achieving at least a one-minus-epsilon fraction of optimum sink flow.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximate Generalized Flow

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The proposed approximation convention combines three distinct errors and uses a scale-dependent absolute deficit threshold. A source is needed to establish the intended normalization, dimensions, residual-arc condition, and relation to OPT.

children.title: Approximation-to-Exact Conversion
children.top_down_role: Exact recovery from sufficiently refined approximate structure.

assumptions_latex: All gains, capacities, and balances are rational with total encoding length \(L\).
An exact optimal solution is uniquely determined by a recoverable active constraint basis \(B\).
The approximation is accurate enough to identify \(B\) without ambiguity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Solving the rational linear system indexed by \(B\) and verifying all constraints yields an exact optimal generalized flow.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: rational basis recovery is a standard approximation-to-exact mechanism
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact recovery by active-basis identification and rational reconstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Compute an approximate solution \(\widehat f\) at a precision sufficient to separate active constraints from inactive ones. Select a full-rank candidate basis \(B\) consisting of generalized balance equalities and arc-bound equalities indicated by \(\widehat f\). Solve the corresponding rational linear system exactly to obtain \(f^*\). Accept \(f^*\) only after checking every capacity and balance constraint and an exact optimality certificate, such as feasible dual labels with zero primal-dual gap. If the basis is ambiguous or verification fails, refine the approximation and repeat. The output is the verified rational flow \(f^*\), not the rounded coordinates of \(\widehat f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Identify an optimal active basis from a sufficiently precise approximation, solve that basis exactly, and verify primal and dual optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Approximation-to-Exact Conversion

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithmic role fits, but no separation bound or generalized-flow theorem shows how much precision identifies the optimal basis. The uniqueness and recoverability assumptions do not supply an inspectable threshold.

children.title: Weakly Polynomial Generalized-Flow Methods
children.top_down_role: Algorithms retaining encoded gain dependence.

assumptions_latex: The generalized-flow data are rational and encoded in binary.
Arithmetic on numbers of polynomial encoding length is charged polynomial bit complexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A weakly polynomial generalized-flow method has running time \(\operatorname{poly}(|V|,|E|,L)\), with permitted dependence on the encoding length \(L\) of gains and other numerical data.

notation.meaning: total binary encoding length of numerical input

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bit-complexity characterization, not a particular generalized-flow algorithm.

source_refs.locator: Polynomial and Strongly Polynomial Computations p. 32
source_refs.source_title: Geometric Algorithms and Combinatorial Optimization

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L\) denote the total binary encoding length of all rational gains, capacities, supplies, and demands. A generalized-flow algorithm is weakly polynomial if its bit-operation count is bounded by \(\operatorname{poly}(|V|,|E|,L)\), and every intermediate number has encoding length polynomial in the input length. Thus logarithmic dependence on gain magnitudes, denominators, capacity magnitudes, or a requested rational accuracy is allowed through \(L\). This classification does not imply a bound on the number of arithmetic operations depending only on \(|V|\) and \(|E|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weakly polynomial methods run in polynomial bit time but may retain polynomial dependence on the encoded gains, capacities, and balances.
knowledge_statements.title: Weakly Polynomial Generalized-Flow Methods

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weakly Polynomial Solution by Rational Linear Programming
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic exact bit-polynomial solvability through the rational linear formulation, without claiming a specialized combinatorial or strongly polynomial algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The generalized-flow constraints and linear objective form a rational linear program whose encoded size is polynomial in \(|V|+|E|+L\). Hence an exact polynomial-time rational linear-programming algorithm can return an optimum or correctly report infeasibility or unboundedness using \(\operatorname{poly}(|V|,|E|,L)\) bit operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The rational linear-program formulation gives a generic weakly polynomial exact method for generalized flow.
assumptions_latex: All gains, capacities, balances, and objective coefficients are rational and binary encoded.
An exact bit-polynomial rational linear-programming method is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Generalized flow is solvable in }\operatorname{poly}(|V|,|E|,L)\text{ bit time.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A generalized-flow algorithm is strongly polynomial when the number of arithmetic operations and comparisons is bounded by a polynomial in \(|V|+|E|\), independently of the magnitudes and encoding lengths of gains, capacities, supplies, and demands. children.title: Flow-Generating Cycles
children.top_down_role: Amplifying cycles and their feasibility or boundedness effects.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic balance effect of a capacity-feasible scaled adjustment around a residual cycle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=(v_0v_1,\ldots,v_{k-1}v_0)\) be a directed residual cycle with gain product \(\Gamma(C)>0\). Choose \(\delta>0\) small enough for the recursively gain-scaled arc adjustment to respect all residual capacities. Every vertex other than \(v_0\) has zero net balance change, whereas the balance change at \(v_0\) is \((\Gamma(C)-1)\delta\). Thus products greater than, equal to, or less than one respectively generate excess, preserve balance, or create a deficit at the base vertex; feasibility in the last case additionally requires that the deficit be supplied.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scaled residual-cycle adjustment generates, preserves, or consumes flow according as its gain product is greater than, equal to, or less than one.
assumptions_latex: Every arc of \(C\) has positive residual capacity.
The initial adjustment \(\delta\) is small enough that all recursively scaled arc adjustments respect residual capacities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Delta b(v_0)=(\Gamma(C)-1)\delta,\qquad \Delta b(v)=0\ \text{for }v\in V(C)\setminus\{v_0\}.

notation.meaning: product of residual gains around the cycle
change in generalized balance at vertex v

knowledge_statements.title: Gain-Product Trichotomy for Residual Cycles

assumptions_latex: A directed residual cycle is \(C=(v_0v_1,\ldots,v_{k-1}v_0)\) with positive residual capacities.
Its gain product is \(\Gamma(C)=\prod_{r=0}^{k-1}\gamma_{v_rv_{r+1}}\), with indices modulo \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\Gamma(C)>1\), a sufficiently small traversal creates excess \((\Gamma(C)-1)\delta>0\) at \(v_0\) while preserving balance at the other cycle vertices.

notation.meaning: product of gains around the cycle
amount sent on the first cycle arc

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: follows from the generalized conservation equations around a cycle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Residual amplifying cycles in a capacitated generalized network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(\delta>0\) small enough that every residual capacity on \(C\) can carry the recursively scaled traversal. Send \(\delta\) on \(v_0v_1\), then send \(\gamma_{v_0v_1}\delta\) on \(v_1v_2\), and continue similarly. Each intermediate vertex receives exactly the amount it sends, while \(v_0\) sends \(\delta\) and receives \(\Gamma(C)\delta\). Hence a cycle with \(\Gamma(C)>1\) generates \((\Gamma(C)-1)\delta\) units of excess at \(v_0\). With finite capacities the generated amount is bounded by a residual bottleneck; without an effective bound, repeated circulation can imply unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Traversing a residual cycle whose gain product exceeds one returns more flow than was injected, creating excess subject to residual capacities.
knowledge_statements.title: Flow-Generating Cycles

children.title: Failure of Ordinary Cut Certificates
children.top_down_role: Loss of direct max-flow–min-cut structure under gains.

assumptions_latex: The network has arcs \(sv\) and \(vt\), with capacities \(1\) and \(2\), respectively.
The corresponding gains are \(2\) and \(1\), and there are no other arcs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The maximum delivered flow is \(2\), whereas the ordinary unweighted capacity of cut \(\{s\}\) is \(1\); thus the ordinary max-flow--min-cut equality fails.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: explicit two-arc counterexample is directly checkable
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Counterexample to using unweighted ordinary cut capacity under gains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Send one unit on \(sv\). Because \(\gamma_{sv}=2\), vertex \(v\) receives two units and can send two units on \(vt\), whose gain is one. Thus two units reach \(t\), and this is optimal because arc \(sv\) is saturated. The ordinary cut \(S=\{s\}\), evaluated by summing capacities of arcs leaving \(S\) without gain weights or labels, has capacity one. Therefore its capacity is smaller than the achievable sink flow. Generalized flows consequently require gain-aware dual labels or other generalized certificates; ordinary cut capacity is not a valid universal upper bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A unit-capacity arc of gain two can deliver two sink units across an ordinary cut of capacity one, invalidating the ordinary cut certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Ordinary Cut Certificates

children.title: Gain-Arithmetic Stability Boundary
children.top_down_role: Arithmetic growth and stability issues from repeated gains.

children.title: Gain Conditioning
children.top_down_role: Sensitivity caused by the magnitude and composition of network gains.

knowledge_statements.title: Gain Conditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A path-product conditioning measure for positive gains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a directed walk \(P\) of length \(\ell=|P|\le h\), define \(\Gamma(P)=\prod_{e\in P}\gamma_e\). If \(0<\gamma_{\min}\le\gamma_e\le\gamma_{\max}\) on every relevant arc, then \(\gamma_{\min}^{\ell}\le\Gamma(P)\le\gamma_{\max}^{\ell}\). Consequently, for any two relevant walks \(P\) and \(Q\) having the same length \(\ell\le h\), \(\Gamma(P)/\Gamma(Q)\le(\gamma_{\max}/\gamma_{\min})^{\ell}\le\kappa_h\), where \(\kappa_h=(\gamma_{\max}/\gamma_{\min})^h\). A large value of \(\kappa_h\) indicates that equal-length transfer factors may have a large multiplicative spread.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a walk of actual length ell, its gain product lies between the ell-th powers of the minimum and maximum gains; equal-length products can differ by at most the corresponding gain ratio raised to ell.
assumptions_latex: Every relevant directed walk \(P\) has positive arc gains.
The walk length is \(\ell=|P|\le h\), and \(0<\gamma_{\min}\le\gamma_e\le\gamma_{\max}\) for every relevant arc \(e\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_{\min}^{\ell}\le\Gamma(P)\le\gamma_{\max}^{\ell}\), and the multiplicative spread between products of equal-length relevant walks is at most \((\gamma_{\max}/\gamma_{\min})^{\ell}\le\kappa_h\).

notation.meaning: product of gains along a walk
equal-length gain-spread bound at horizon h

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: product bounds follow directly from uniform gain bounds

children.title: Arithmetic Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Exactness or stability issues caused by gain-dependent arithmetic growth.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rounding Error in Sequential Gain Products
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward error from sequential floating-point multiplication, complementing the immutable input-perturbation bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\Gamma(P)=\prod_{i=1}^{k}\gamma_i\) is evaluated by sequential floating-point multiplication with unit roundoff \(u\), no overflow or underflow, and \(\operatorname{fl}(ab)=ab(1+\varepsilon)\) with \(|\varepsilon|\le u\). If \((k-1)u<1\), then \(\widehat\Gamma(P)=\Gamma(P)(1+\theta_{k-1})\), where \(|\theta_{k-1}|\le (k-1)u/(1-(k-1)u)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sequential multiplication of k exact gains has a bounded relative rounding error when overflow and underflow are absent.
assumptions_latex: The input gains are represented exactly before multiplication.
Each multiplication satisfies the stated relative-error model with unit roundoff \(u\).
No intermediate result overflows or underflows.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left|\frac{\widehat\Gamma(P)}{\Gamma(P)}-1\right|\le \frac{(k-1)u}{1-(k-1)u}.

notation.meaning: number of gains in the path product

knowledge_statements.title: Rounding Error in Sequential Gain Products
Arithmetic Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward relative-error bound for products of positive gains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a finite directed path, let \(\widehat\gamma_e=\gamma_e(1+\delta_e)\), and suppose \(|\delta_e|\le\eta<1\) for every \(e\in P\). Then \(\widehat\Gamma(P)/\Gamma(P)=\prod_{e\in P}(1+\delta_e)\). Since \(|\log(1+\delta_e)|\le\eta/(1-\eta)\), the logarithmic product error is at most \(|P|\eta/(1-\eta)\), and hence \[\left|\frac{\widehat\Gamma(P)}{\Gamma(P)}-1\right|\le \exp\!\left(\frac{|P|\eta}{1-\eta}\right)-1.\] This bound accounts for perturbations in the stored gains but not for additional rounding during multiplication.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform relative errors in the individual gains accumulate linearly in log space, giving an exponential upper bound on the relative error of the path product.
assumptions_latex: A finite directed path \(P\) has gains \(\gamma_e>0\), with stored gains \(\widehat\gamma_e=\gamma_e(1+\delta_e)\).
For every \(e\in P\), \(|\delta_e|\le\eta<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\left|\widehat\Gamma(P)/\Gamma(P)-1\right|\le \exp\!\left(|P|\eta/(1-\eta)\right)-1\).

children.title: Repeated-Gain Amplification
children.top_down_role: Numeric growth arising from repeated traversal of gain-bearing structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Repeated-Gain Amplification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact amplification along a homogeneous gain path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\ge0\) enter a directed path of \(k\) arcs, each having gain \(g>1\), and suppose no capacity bound obstructs the traversal. Generalized conservation passes \(gx\) beyond the first arc, \(g^2x\) beyond the second, and ultimately \(g^kx\) to the endpoint. Therefore an absolute input perturbation \(\Delta x\) produces endpoint perturbation \(g^k\Delta x\). If the common gain is instead changed from \(g\) to \(g(1+\eta)\), with \(\eta>-1\), the relative change in the endpoint amount is \((1+\eta)^k-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Applying a gain greater than one along k consecutive arcs multiplies both the flow and any absolute input perturbation by g to the k-th power.
assumptions_latex: A directed path consists of \(k\) arcs, each with gain \(g>1\).
An input amount \(x\ge0\) can traverse the path without meeting a capacity bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The delivered amount is \(g^kx\), and an input perturbation \(\Delta x\) produces output perturbation \(g^k\Delta x\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct composition of generalized-flow transfer factors

children.title: Conditioning–Precision Boundary
children.top_down_role: Interaction between gain conditioning and the precision required for reliable computation.

knowledge_statements.title: Conditioning–Precision Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Precision needed to classify a cycle as amplifying or attenuating.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(\widehat\Gamma=\Gamma(1+\theta)\) with \(|\theta|\le\rho<1\). Then the exact cycle product satisfies \[\Gamma\in\left[\frac{\widehat\Gamma}{1+\rho},\frac{\widehat\Gamma}{1-\rho}\right].\] The error bound certifies \(\Gamma>1\) exactly when \(\widehat\Gamma>1+\rho\), and it certifies \(\Gamma<1\) exactly when \(\widehat\Gamma<1-\rho\). If \(1-\rho\le\widehat\Gamma\le1+\rho\), the interval contains one, so the available relative-error guarantee alone cannot certify whether the cycle attenuates or amplifies.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A computed cycle product certifies amplification only above one plus the relative-error bound and attenuation only below one minus that bound; values in between remain unresolved.
assumptions_latex: A cycle has exact gain product \(\Gamma>0\), while computation returns \(\widehat\Gamma=\Gamma(1+\theta)\).
The total relative product error satisfies \(|\theta|\le\rho<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sign of \(\Gamma-1\) is certified precisely when \(\widehat\Gamma>1+\rho\) or \(\widehat\Gamma<1-\rho\); otherwise the relative-error interval contains \(1\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: interval separation gives the stated precision boundary

children.title: Paired Residual-Arc Storage

knowledge_statements.title: Paired Residual-Arc Storage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Array representation for coupled forward and reverse arcs of a residual network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every stored residual arc \(a=(u,v)\), store an index \(\operatorname{rev}(a)\) for the opposite arc \(\bar a=(v,u)\), with \(\operatorname{rev}(\bar a)=a\), costs \(c_{\bar a}=-c_a\), and nonnegative residual capacities \(r_a,r_{\bar a}\). Sending \(\delta\) units through \(a\), where \(0\leq\delta\leq r_a\), is represented by the coupled update \[r_a\leftarrow r_a-\delta,\qquad r_{\bar a}\leftarrow r_{\bar a}+\delta.\] Thus one constant-time update preserves the paired representation of cancellation and augmentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each residual arc stores its reverse index. Augmenting decreases the forward residual capacity and equally increases the reverse capacity while opposite costs remain negatives.
assumptions_latex: \(0\leq\delta\leq r_a\).
Each arc has a distinct stored reverse record.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rev}(\operatorname{rev}(a))=a\) and the paired residual update takes \(O(1)\) time.

children.title: Heap-Based Shortest-Path Engines
children.top_down_role: Priority-queue organizations for sparse residual networks.

knowledge_statements.title: Heap-Based Shortest-Path Engines
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dijkstra engine for sparse residual graphs having nonnegative reduced arc lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite residual digraph \(G_r=(V,A_r)\), a source \(s\in V\), and lengths \(\ell_a\geq 0\), initialize \(d(s)=0\) and \(d(v)=+\infty\) for every \(v\in V\setminus\{s\}\), and insert \(s\) into a min-priority queue. Repeatedly extract an unsettled vertex \(u\) of minimum key, mark it settled, and, for every arc \(a=(u,v)\in A_r\) with unsettled endpoint \(v\), replace \(d(v)\) by \(d(u)+\ell_a\) and perform an insertion or decrease-key whenever this value is smaller. When the queue is empty, \(d(v)\) equals the shortest-path distance from \(s\) to \(v\), with \(+\infty\) for unreachable vertices. With a binary heap, the running time is \(O((|V|+|A_r|)\log |V|)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary-heap Dijkstra computes all residual shortest-path distances under nonnegative lengths, using logarithmic priority-queue time per extraction or successful relaxation.
assumptions_latex: \(G_r=(V,A_r)\) is finite.
\(s\in V\).
\(\ell_a\geq 0\) for every \(a\in A_r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(v\in V\), the final label is \(d(v)=\operatorname{dist}_{G_r,\ell}(s,v)\), and the running time is \(O((|V|+|A_r|)\log |V|)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Bucket-Based Shortest-Path Engines
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dial-style shortest-path engine for bounded nonnegative integer residual lengths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_r=(V,A_r)\) have integer lengths \(0\leq\ell_a\leq C\). Initialize Dijkstra labels and place each finite label \(k\) in bucket \(B_k\). Scan bucket indices upward, extracting vertices from the first nonempty bucket and relaxing their outgoing arcs; a decreased integer label is moved to its corresponding bucket. Because every simple shortest path has length at most \((|V|-1)C\), buckets through that index suffice. Stale entries may be discarded by comparing their key with the current label. The algorithm returns exact distances in \(O(|A_r|+|V|C)\) time and \(O(|A_r|+|V|C)\) storage with a direct bucket array.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dial’s algorithm replaces a heap with integer-indexed buckets and computes exact distances in time linear in the arcs plus the scanned key range.
assumptions_latex: \(G_r\) is finite.
\(\ell_a\in\{0,1,\ldots,C\}\) for every \(a\in A_r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Shortest-path distances are computed in \(O(|A_r|+|V|C)\) time.

knowledge_statements.title: Radix-Based Shortest-Path Engines
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotone radix-heap implementation of Dijkstra for bounded integer keys.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_r=(V,A_r)\) have integer lengths \(0\leq\ell_a\leq C\), and run Dijkstra using a radix heap whose extracted keys never decrease. Initialize the queue with key \(0\) for \(s\); perform ordinary relaxations and insert or decrease each improved integer key. Radix buckets group keys by the most significant bit at which they differ from the last extracted key, and redistribution follows each extraction from the first nonempty bucket. Since every finite simple-path key is at most \(U=(|V|-1)C\), the engine uses \(O(|V|+\log(U+1))\) queue storage and \(O(|A_r|+(|A_r|+|V|)\log(U+1))\) time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A radix heap exploits monotone bounded integer distance keys, replacing comparison-heap costs by logarithmic dependence on the attainable key range.
assumptions_latex: \(G_r\) is finite.
\(\ell_a\in\{0,1,\ldots,C\}\) for every \(a\in A_r\).
Extracted priority keys are monotone nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact distances are obtained with logarithmic dependence on \(U=(|V|-1)C\).

knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Key Suitability Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which integer-priority shortest-path engines preserve correctness and offer useful bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An integer-key engine is directly applicable when every residual length used by the shortest-path search belongs to \(\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\), additions cannot overflow the key type, and the queue supports all attainable tentative distances. If \(0\leq\ell_a\leq C\), finite simple-path distances lie in \([0,(|V|-1)C]\). Bucket scanning is attractive when \(|V|C\) is moderate; radix organization is attractive when this range is large but its bit length is moderate. Scaling rational lengths by a common denominator is exact only when the products and accumulated path lengths remain representable integers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integer queues suit nonnegative, exactly representable keys with a controlled value range; bucket and radix structures favor different range sizes.
assumptions_latex: Residual shortest-path lengths are nonnegative.
Keys and path-length sums are represented without overflow.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: All attainable finite keys lie in \(\{0,\ldots,(|V|-1)C\}\) when \(0\leq\ell_a\leq C\).

knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Distance Reuse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact label repair after residual-arc insertions or nonnegative length decreases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(d\) contains exact distances from \(s\) in \(G=(V,A)\) with nonnegative lengths. Form \(G'\) only by inserting arcs or decreasing lengths, so every stored predecessor path remains present with unchanged or smaller length. Retain all labels, and for each changed arc \((u,v)\) with \(d(u)+\ell'_{uv}<d(v)\), set \(d(v)\leftarrow d(u)+\ell'_{uv}\) and queue \(v\). Repeatedly extract a minimum-label queued vertex and relax its outgoing arcs under \(\ell'\). Stop when no queued vertex remains. The repaired labels are the exact distances in \(G'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: After only arc insertions or length decreases, retain old distances, seed violated changed arcs, and propagate improvements to recover exact new distances.
assumptions_latex: Old labels are exact source distances.
All old arcs remain and no old arc length increases.
All new lengths are nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At termination, \(d(v)=\operatorname{dist}_{G',\ell'}(s,v)\) for every \(v\in V\).

notation.meaning: reused distance label from source s

knowledge_statements.title: Incremental Potential Reuse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility criterion and shortest-distance update for reused node potentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For residual costs \(c_{uv}\), define reduced cost \(c^\pi_{uv}=c_{uv}+\pi(u)-\pi(v)\). A stored potential \(\pi\) may be reused after a residual change precisely when \(c^\pi_{uv}\geq0\) for every currently residual arc. If \(d\) is the vector of shortest distances from a source under these reduced costs, then the update \(\pi'(v)=\pi(v)+d(v)\) satisfies \[c^{\pi'}_{uv}=c^\pi_{uv}+d(u)-d(v)\geq0\] for every arc whose endpoints have finite distance. Hence the updated potential remains dual feasible on the reached residual subgraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A potential is reusable exactly while all current reduced costs are nonnegative; adding reduced-cost distances produces another feasible potential on reached vertices.
assumptions_latex: Every considered residual arc has finite cost.
\(c^\pi_{uv}\geq0\) before the shortest-path computation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi'=\pi+d\) is feasible on arcs joining vertices with finite distance labels.

children.title: Residual-Change Invalidation
children.top_down_role: Residual modifications that limit or invalidate cached information.

knowledge_statements.title: Residual-Change Invalidation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conservative invalidation predicates for cached distances and feasible potentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d\), a predecessor tree \(T\), and a feasible potential \(\pi\) be cached for a residual graph. Invalidate the distance cache if a tree arc is deleted or its length increases, or if an inserted or shortened arc \((u,v)\) violates \(d(v)\leq d(u)+\ell'_{uv}\). Invalidate the potential cache if any inserted or recosted residual arc satisfies \(c_{uv}+\pi(u)-\pi(v)<0\). Changes not meeting these predicates leave the corresponding certificate valid; otherwise the affected labels or potentials must be recomputed or repaired before reuse.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Residual changes invalidate cached distances when they break stored paths or Bellman inequalities, and invalidate potentials when they create a negative reduced-cost arc.
assumptions_latex: Cached distances have a valid predecessor tree.
The cached potential was feasible before the change.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Reuse is permitted only if the applicable distance and potential invalidation predicates are false.
