children.title: Reuse Consistency Checks
children.top_down_role: Validation of cached distances or potentials before continued use.

knowledge_statements.title: Reuse Consistency Checks
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Locally checkable certificates for exact cached distances and feasible potentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_r=(V,A_r)\) be a finite residual digraph with arc lengths \(\ell_{uv}\), source \(s\in V\), and labels \(d:V\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\). The labels certify exact shortest distances when \(d(s)=0\), every vertex \(v\neq s\) with \(d(v)<+\infty\) has a stored predecessor arc \((p(v),v)\in A_r\) satisfying \(d(v)=d(p(v))+\ell_{p(v)v}\), every such predecessor chain terminates at \(s\), and every arc \((u,v)\in A_r\) obeys \(d(v)\leq d(u)+\ell_{uv}\) under extended-real arithmetic. A potential \(\pi:V\to\mathbb R\) certifies dual feasibility for residual costs \(c_{uv}\) when every \((u,v)\in A_r\) obeys \(c_{uv}+\pi(u)-\pi(v)\geq0\). The arc conditions and predecessor structure can be checked in \(O(|V|+|A_r|)\) time.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bellman inequalities together with tight predecessor chains to the source certify exact finite distances and force unreachable labels to be infinite; nonnegative reduced costs certify potential feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(G_r=(V,A_r)\) is finite.
\(s\in V\).
All finite labels, lengths, costs, and potentials are exactly comparable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If all stated checks pass, then \(d(v)=\operatorname{dist}_{G_r,\ell}(s,v)\) for every \(v\in V\), and \(\pi\) is feasible on every residual arc.

notation.meaning: stored predecessor of a finite-labeled non-source vertex

children.title: Active-Arc Management
children.top_down_role: Selection and storage of residual arcs currently eligible for local processing.

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Arc Management
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certified filtering of residual arcs against an algorithm-dependent eligibility threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each residual arc \(a\), maintain a valid lower bound \(L_a\leq c_a^\pi\) and an eligibility threshold \(\tau\). Define the active set by \(A_{\mathrm{act}}=\{a:r_a>0,\ L_a<\tau\}\). Search or discharge operations inspect only \(A_{\mathrm{act}}\). Whenever residual capacity, cost, potential, or \(\tau\) changes, update the corresponding bounds before the next inspection; insert an arc when its new bound falls below \(\tau\), and remove it when its residual capacity becomes zero. Since every inactive residual arc satisfies \(c_a^\pi\geq L_a\geq\tau\), filtering cannot omit an arc whose reduced cost is below \(\tau\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maintain only arcs that may cross the current reduced-cost threshold, using certified lower bounds and immediate updates after relevant state changes.
assumptions_latex: \(L_a\leq c_a^\pi\) for every residual arc.
Eligibility means \(c_a^\pi<\tau\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every eligible residual arc belongs to \(A_{\mathrm{act}}\).

notation.meaning: certified lower bound on reduced cost

children.title: Admissible-Graph Management
children.top_down_role: Maintenance of residual subgraphs satisfying the current admissibility criterion.

knowledge_statements.title: Admissible-Graph Management
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dynamic zero-reduced-cost subgraph under a feasible potential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G_r=(V,A_r)\) be a residual digraph with residual capacities \(r_a\), costs \(c_a\), and a feasible potential \(\pi:V\to\mathbb R\). For an arc \(a=(u,v)\), define \(c^{\pi}_a=c_a+\pi(u)-\pi(v)\), and assume \(c^{\pi}_a\geq0\) for every \(a\in A_r\). The admissible graph is \(G_0=(V,A_0)\), where \[A_0=\{a\in A_r:r_a>0,\ c^{\pi}_a=0\}.\] Store membership flags and adjacency lists for \(A_0\). After an augmentation, reclassify the forward and reverse arcs whose residual status changed; after a potential update, reclassify every arc whose reduced cost may have changed. Every directed path in \(G_0\) has total reduced cost \(0\) and is therefore a shortest path between its endpoints with respect to the nonnegative residual reduced costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The admissible graph contains exactly the positive-capacity residual arcs of zero reduced cost; while potential feasibility holds, every path in this graph is reduced-cost shortest between its endpoints.
assumptions_latex: \(G_r=(V,A_r)\) is a residual digraph.
\(c^{\pi}_a\geq0\) for every \(a\in A_r\).
Membership tests use exact reduced-cost equality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every directed path in \(G_0\) has reduced cost \(0\) and is shortest between its endpoints under \(c^{\pi}\).

notation.meaning: reduced cost of residual arc a under potential pi

children.title: Active-Set Refresh Regimes
children.top_down_role: Conditions governing localized refresh or global reconstruction of active structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Active-Set Refresh Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Event-driven and periodic rebuilding rules for certified active residual structures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain an active structure \(S\), a dirty set \(D\) of arcs whose capacity, cost, endpoint potential, or eligibility bound changed, and a refresh limit \(K\). Before using \(S\), incrementally reclassify every arc in \(D\) and clear \(D\). Perform a full scan of \(A_r\) after at most \(K\) incremental refreshes, whenever a global potential or threshold change lacks valid per-arc bounds, or whenever a consistency check finds a membership error. Output the rebuilt set \(S=\{a\in A_r:P(a)\}\) for the chosen eligibility predicate \(P\). No search may use \(S\) while an unprocessed change can alter \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Refresh changed arcs before use, and periodically or conditionally rebuild the entire active set when local membership certificates are insufficient.
assumptions_latex: Every state change marks all arcs whose eligibility may change.
\(P(a)\) is deterministically checkable from current residual state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Whenever \(S\) is used, \(S=\{a\in A_r:P(a)\}\).

children.title: Global Price Updates
children.top_down_role: Periodic restoration of globally consistent price information.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Price Updates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact shortest-path price refresh under the stated reduced-cost sign convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the residual network have vertex set \(V\), residual-arc costs \(c(u,v)\), and prices \(p:V\to\mathbb R\), with reduced costs \(c_p(u,v)=c(u,v)+p(u)-p(v)\). From a specified nonempty source set, compute exact shortest-path distances \(d(v)\) using residual-arc lengths \(c_p\). Define \(p'(v)=p(v)+d(v)\) for every reachable vertex and \(p'(v)=p(v)\) otherwise. Output \(p'\) and the distance labels. For every residual arc \((u,v)\) whose endpoints are reachable, the output satisfies \(c_{p'}(u,v)\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compute exact shortest reduced-cost distances from a specified source set and add them to reachable-node prices; all residual arcs between reachable vertices then have nonnegative updated reduced cost.
assumptions_latex: The residual network is finite, and the designated source set is nonempty.
The residual network contains no negative reduced-cost cycle reachable from the source set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The updated prices satisfy \(c_{p'}(u,v)\ge0\) on every residual arc \((u,v)\) whose endpoints are reachable.

notation.meaning: reduced cost of residual arc (u,v) under price p
shortest-path distance from the designated source set using reduced costs

children.title: Global Distance Updates
children.top_down_role: Periodic recomputation of global residual-distance information.

knowledge_statements.title: Global Distance Updates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reverse multi-source shortest-path refresh on the current residual network.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\subseteq V\) be a nonempty target set. Initialize \(d(t)=0\) for \(t\in T\) and \(d(v)=+\infty\) otherwise. Run a shortest-path algorithm from all vertices of \(T\) on the reversal of the current residual graph, using reversed-arc length \(w(u,v)\) for each original residual arc \((u,v)\). Output \(d(v)=\min\{\sum_{a\in P}w(a):P\text{ is a residual path from }v\text{ to }T\}\), with \(d(v)=+\infty\) when no such path exists. The output satisfies \(d(t)=0\) for every \(t\in T\) and \(d(u)\le w(u,v)+d(v)\) for every residual arc \((u,v)\), using extended-real arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recompute every vertex's exact residual distance to a nonempty target set, assigning infinity when no target is reachable; the resulting labels satisfy every residual-arc triangle inequality.
assumptions_latex: The residual graph is finite, and \(T\subseteq V\) is nonempty.
Residual arc lengths are nonnegative, or more generally no negative-length cycle can occur on a residual walk leading to \(T\).
The selected shortest-path method is valid for the residual arc lengths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The refreshed labels are exact extended-real distances to \(T\) and satisfy \(d(u)\le w(u,v)+d(v)\) on every residual arc \((u,v)\).

notation.meaning: distance from v to the target set

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At iteration \(k\), invoke a global metric refresh under a threshold regime precisely when \(S_k\ge\tau\), or under a periodic regime precisely when \(q_k\ge Q\), where \(Q\ge1\). After refreshing, reset \(S_k=0\) and \(q_k=0\); otherwise perform the next local update and increase the selected statistics. For a hybrid regime, the trigger predicate is \((S_k\ge\tau)\lor(q_k\ge Q)\). The policy must evaluate the predicate before using any metric whose validity depends on the refresh.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Refresh globally when accumulated stale work, elapsed local operations, or either quantity in a hybrid policy reaches its configured threshold.

children.title: Local–Global Refresh Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Cost and information-quality tradeoffs between localized maintenance and global restoration.

knowledge_statements.title: Local–Global Refresh Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operation-count crossover between accumulated local work and one global refresh.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be the finite index set of local-refresh events between two global refreshes, and let \(v_i\) be the vertex refreshed at event \(i\in K\). Define \(D_K=\sum_{i\in K}\deg_R(v_i)\). If event \(i\) costs at most \(a\deg_R(v_i)+b\), then the accumulated local-refresh work is at most \(aD_K+b|K|\). Consequently, \(aD_K+b|K|\le G(n,m)\) is the regime in which the stated local-work guarantee is no larger than the stated global-refresh guarantee. If the inequality is reversed, the global refresh has the smaller declared upper bound. This comparison concerns refresh work only and does not compare realized costs or downstream iteration counts.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compare the declared degree-weighted upper bound for all local-refresh events with the declared bound for one global refresh; this compares work guarantees, not realized runtime or later iteration counts.
assumptions_latex: Each local refresh event touching vertex \(v\) costs at most \(a\deg_R(v)+b\), where \(a,b\ge0\).
A global refresh costs at most \(G(n,m)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The declared local-refresh bound is no larger than the declared global-refresh bound whenever \(aD_K+b|K|\le G(n,m)\).

notation.meaning: finite index set of local-refresh events before the next global refresh
sum of current residual degrees over local-refresh events

children.title: Layout Conversion Costs
children.top_down_role: Memory and traversal consequences of changing network representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Layout Conversion Costs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case construction costs for converting adjacency and matrix layouts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: To convert sparse adjacency storage to a dense matrix, initialize \(n^2\) matrix entries and insert or aggregate \(m\) stored arc records, requiring \(\Theta(n^2+m)\) time and \(\Theta(n^2+m)\) destination space when per-pair containers retain parallel arcs; the space becomes \(\Theta(n^2)\) when each ordered pair has one fixed-size aggregate record. To convert an unindexed dense representation to sparse storage, inspect all \(n^2\) entries and emit all \(m\) represented arcs, requiring \(\Theta(n^2+m)\) time and \(\Theta(n+m)\) destination space. When each matrix entry contains at most one arc record, \(m\le n^2\) and the conversion time simplifies to \(\Theta(n^2)\). An occupancy index permits enumeration in \(O(n+m)\) time but adds storage and update overhead.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conversion must account for quadratic matrix initialization or inspection and for all emitted arc records; with at most one record per ordered pair, dense-to-sparse time simplifies to quadratic.
assumptions_latex: The source representation contains \(n\) vertices and \(m\) explicitly stored arc records.
Allocation, initialization, inspection, and emission of one fixed-size record or storage word take constant time.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: General sparse-to-dense and unindexed dense-to-sparse conversion take \(\Theta(n^2+m)\) time; with at most one fixed-size record per ordered pair, the dense-to-sparse bound is \(\Theta(n^2)\).

notation.meaning: number of explicitly represented arc records

children.title: Primal Feasibility Validation
children.top_down_role: Checks of balances, bounds, and residual consistency.

assumptions_latex: The directed network is finite and uses the balance convention \(\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_a=b_v\).
Every arc has finite declared bounds \(l_a\le u_a\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Passing the displayed balance, bound, and residual-capacity checks certifies primal feasibility and residual consistency.

notation.meaning: node supply under the stated convention

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact primal certificate for bounded linear minimum-cost flow.

source_refs.locator: 1.2.1 The Minimum Cost Flow Problem p. 9
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A flow \(x\) passes primal validation exactly when \(l_a\le x_a\le u_a\) for every \(a\in A\) and \(\sum_{a\in\delta^+(v)}x_a-\sum_{a\in\delta^-(v)}x_a=b_v\) for every \(v\in V\). Residual consistency additionally requires forward residual capacity \(r_a^+=u_a-x_a\ge0\) and reverse residual capacity \(r_a^-=x_a-l_a\ge0\), with stored reverse-arc links mutually consistent. These equalities and inequalities are directly checkable in \(O(n+m)\) arithmetic operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Check every arc bound, every node balance, and both residual capacities; these linear-time checks certify primal feasibility and residual consistency.
knowledge_statements.title: Primal Feasibility Validation

children.title: Price-Reduced-Cost Validation System
children.top_down_role: Checks of prices and residual cost compatibility.

children.title: Dual-Price Validation
children.top_down_role: Checks that supplied node prices meet the relevant dual compatibility conditions.

assumptions_latex: A finite bounded minimum-cost-flow instance and candidate prices are given.
One reference vertex is fixed in each weakly connected component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The checks validate that prices are finite, normalized, and induce the reported reduced costs consistently.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Syntactic and algebraic validation of node prices before optimality checks.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 6. Dual Ascent Methods for Min-Cost Flow p. 213
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Validate a reported price vector by checking \(p_v\in\mathbb R\) for every \(v\), imposing the normalization \(p_r=0\) at one chosen reference vertex \(r\) in each weakly connected component, and recomputing every reported reduced cost as \(\bar c_{uv}=c_{uv}+p_u-p_v\). Since adding a constant to all prices in one component leaves every reduced cost unchanged, normalization removes only this indeterminacy. Passing these checks certifies price representation and reduced-cost arithmetic, not optimality by itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Ensure prices are finite and componentwise normalized, then recompute every reduced cost from costs and price differences.
knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Price Validation

source_witnesses.locator: Chapter 6. Dual Ascent Methods for Min-Cost Flow p. 213
source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

children.title: Reduced-Cost Validation
children.top_down_role: Checks of residual reduced-cost signs and arc-status compatibility.

assumptions_latex: The candidate flow satisfies all primal balance and bound constraints.
Reduced costs use \(\bar c_{uv}=c_{uv}+p_u-p_v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sign checks are equivalent to nonnegative reduced cost on every positive-capacity residual arc and certify optimality of the feasible flow.

notation.meaning: reduced cost of original arc a
residual capacity of a residual arc

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact reduced-cost optimality certificate for bounded linear minimum-cost flow.

source_refs.locator: Chapter 7. Primal-Dual Algorithms for Min-Cost Flow p. 137
source_refs.source_title: Combinatorial Optimization: Algorithms and Complexity

source_refs.locator: Chapter 6. Dual Ascent Methods for Min-Cost Flow p. 213
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each original arc \(a\), check \(\bar c_a\ge0\) when \(x_a<u_a\), because its forward residual arc exists, and check \(\bar c_a\le0\) when \(x_a>l_a\), because its reverse residual arc has reduced cost \(-\bar c_a\). Consequently, \(l_a<x_a<u_a\) requires \(\bar c_a=0\). Equivalently, every residual arc \(e\) with \(r_e>0\) must have nonnegative reduced cost. Together with primal feasibility, these checks certify minimum cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Check the reduced-cost sign required by each available residual direction; interior-flow arcs must have zero reduced cost, certifying optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Reduced-Cost Validation

children.title: Price–Residual Consistency
children.top_down_role: Cross-checks linking dual prices to the current residual network.

assumptions_latex: The network is finite and directed, with arc bounds \(l_a\le x_a\le u_a\), linear costs \(c_a\), and node prices \(\pi_v\).
The candidate flow \(x\) satisfies its prescribed node balances exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The price-flow pair is consistent exactly when \(x_a<u_a\Rightarrow \bar c_a\ge 0\) and \(x_a>l_a\Rightarrow \bar c_a\le 0\) for every arc \(a=(i,j)\).

notation.meaning: Reduced cost of original arc a=(i,j).
Residual network induced by the candidate flow and bounds.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-cost bounded flows with the stated reduced-cost sign convention.

source_refs.locator: 3.3.2 A Price-Based Max-Flow Algorithm p. 139
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each original arc \(a=(i,j)\), put \(\bar c_a=c_a+\pi_i-\pi_j\). The residual network contains a forward residual arc of cost \(\bar c_a\) when \(x_a<u_a\), and a reverse residual arc of cost \(-\bar c_a\) when \(x_a>l_a\). A price-residual consistency certificate is valid precisely when every residual arc has nonnegative reduced cost; equivalently, \(x_a<u_a\Rightarrow \bar c_a\ge0\) and \(x_a>l_a\Rightarrow \bar c_a\le0\) for all \(a\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prices and a feasible flow are consistent when every available residual move has nonnegative reduced cost, including reverse moves on arcs carrying flow.
knowledge_statements.title: Price–Residual Consistency

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3.2 A Price-Based Max-Flow Algorithm p. 139
source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate and sign convention are mathematically coherent, but the cited price-based max-flow section does not clearly support the bounded linear-cost residual optimality conditions stated here. A direct min-cost-flow optimality or reduced-cost locator is required.

children.title: Tolerance-Sensitive Validation
children.top_down_role: Validation behavior when reduced costs are assessed with numeric tolerances.

assumptions_latex: All reported flows, costs, prices, balances, and bounds are finite floating-point values.
Nonnegative absolute and relative tolerances and all comparison scales are fixed before validation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The candidate passes only if every primal and reduced-cost violation is no larger than its declared mixed absolute-relative tolerance.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A declared mixed-tolerance policy; it does not assert exact feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\tau(s)=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}s\), where \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}},\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}\ge0\). Given declared nonnegative scales \(s_v,s_a^x,s_a^c\), validation requires \(|(Ax-b)_v|\le\tau(s_v)\), \(l_a-\tau(s_a^x)\le x_a\le u_a+\tau(s_a^x)\), \(x_a<u_a-\tau(s_a^x)\Rightarrow\bar c_a\ge-\tau(s_a^c)\), and \(x_a>l_a+\tau(s_a^x)\Rightarrow\bar c_a\le\tau(s_a^c)\). NaN, infinity, negative tolerances, or undeclared scales invalidate the certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Validation uses declared absolute-relative tolerances for balances, bounds, and reduced-cost signs; nonfinite data or unspecified scales cause rejection.
knowledge_statements.title: Tolerance-Sensitive Validation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The mixed-tolerance policy is internally precise and fits the validation leaf, but its particular scales, strict interior tests, and rejection rules are implementation-sensitive and have no cited source.

children.title: Optimization Pathology Validation System
children.top_down_role: Checks of cut obstructions and improving recession structures.

children.title: Infeasibility-Certificate Validation
children.top_down_role: Checks of cut or balance obstructions certifying absence of feasible flow.

knowledge_statements.title: Infeasibility-Certificate Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Farkas certificate after an exact standard-form conversion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Convert the stated lower bounds, upper bounds, and balance equations without relaxation into \(Mz=d\), \(z\ge0\). A proposed multiplier \(y\) is a valid infeasibility certificate when exact evaluation gives \(M^{\mathsf T}y\ge0\) componentwise and \(d^{\mathsf T}y<0\). Validation must also verify the exact equivalence of the standard-form conversion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact Farkas multiplier validates infeasibility when it is nonnegative on every standard-form column but has negative pairing with the right-hand side, provided the conversion is verified exactly.
assumptions_latex: The bounded network-flow constraints have been converted exactly to \(Mz=d\) with \(z\ge0\).
All certificate comparisons are performed in exact arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A vector \(y\) satisfying \(M^{\mathsf T}y\ge0\) and \(d^{\mathsf T}y<0\) certifies that the network constraints are infeasible.

notation.meaning: Exact standard-form feasibility system equivalent to the bounded flow system.

children.title: Unboundedness-Certificate Validation
children.top_down_role: Checks of improving recession structures certifying an unbounded objective.

knowledge_statements.title: Unboundedness-Certificate Validation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear-cost minimization with possibly infinite arc bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pair \((x,d)\) validates unboundedness below when \(Ax=b\), \(l\le x\le u\), \(Ad=0\), and \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\). Bound compatibility requires \(d_a\ge0\) whenever \(l_a\) is finite and \(d_a\le0\) whenever \(u_a\) is finite; consequently, \(d_a=0\) when both bounds are finite. All feasibility, bound-compatibility, and objective-direction checks are performed exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible flow plus an exactly checked, bound-compatible, balance-preserving direction of negative cost is a certificate of unboundedness below.
assumptions_latex: The linear-cost network-flow problem has a verified feasible flow \(x\).
The direction \(d\) and all input data are checked in exact arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(d\) is a feasible recession direction and \(c^{\mathsf T}d<0\), then \(x+td\) is feasible for every \(t\ge0\) and the minimization problem is unbounded below.

notation.meaning: Node-arc incidence matrix under the chosen balance convention.

children.title: Cut-Obstruction Checks
children.top_down_role: Independent examination of cut-based feasibility obstructions.

assumptions_latex: For every arc \(a\), the lower and upper bounds satisfy \(l_a\le u_a\) and are finite.
The balance convention is net outflow \(b_v\), so feasible flows satisfy \(Ax=b\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any set \(S\subseteq V\) with \(b(S)>u(\delta^+(S))-l(\delta^-(S))\) certifies infeasibility.

notation.meaning: Arcs leaving and entering S, respectively.
Total prescribed net outflow in S.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-capacity bounded transshipment under the net-outflow convention.

source_refs.locator: 3.1.2 The Max-Flow/Min-Cut Theorem p. 121
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

source_refs.locator: Section 8.1. Max-Flow-Min-Cut Theorem p. 178
source_refs.source_title: Combinatorial Optimization: Theory and Algorithms

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a proposed vertex set \(S\subseteq V\), compute \(b(S)=\sum_{v\in S}b_v\), \(u(\delta^+(S))=\sum_{a\in\delta^+(S)}u_a\), and \(l(\delta^-(S))=\sum_{a\in\delta^-(S)}l_a\). Every feasible bounded flow must obey \(b(S)\le u(\delta^+(S))-l(\delta^-(S))\). Therefore a strict violation is a cut-obstruction certificate. The validator checks set membership, cut incidence, all three exact sums, and the strict inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex set is an infeasibility witness when its required net outflow exceeds outgoing upper capacity minus mandatory incoming lower flow.
knowledge_statements.title: Cut-Obstruction Checks

children.title: Recession-Structure Checks
children.top_down_role: Independent examination of residual structures supporting unlimited improvement.

assumptions_latex: The feasible region is \(P=\{x:Ax=b,\ l\le x\le u\}\), where either bound may be infinite.
At least one feasible point exists when the recession structure is used to diagnose objective unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recession cone consists exactly of balance-preserving directions satisfying the sign restrictions induced by finite bounds.

notation.meaning: Recession cone of the feasible flow polyhedron.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral recession structure for bounded and one-sided-bounded arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The recession cone is \[\operatorname{rec}(P)=\{d:Ad=0,\ d_a\ge0\text{ if }l_a> -\infty,\ d_a\le0\text{ if }u_a<+\infty\}.\] Thus an arc with two finite bounds has \(d_a=0\); an arc unbounded above only may have \(d_a\ge0\); an arc unbounded below only may have \(d_a\le0\); and a doubly unbounded arc is unrestricted apart from \(Ad=0\). Exact validation checks these conditions componentwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recession directions preserve all balances and obey the signs forced by finite lower or upper bounds; doubly bounded arcs cannot change.
knowledge_statements.title: Recession-Structure Checks

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The recession-cone representation and finite-bound sign restrictions are mathematically correct and fit the leaf, but no inspectable source is supplied for the formula.

children.title: Integrality Validation
children.top_down_role: Checks distinguishing exact integral solutions from numerical near-integrality.

assumptions_latex: Each arc variable is required by the model to belong to \(\mathbb Z\).
The candidate values and model data have an exact representation available to the validator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The candidate passes integrality validation exactly when every arc value is an integer and all flow constraints hold exactly.

notation.meaning: Distance from a scalar to the nearest integer.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact validation of integer-constrained arc flows.

source_refs.locator: 1.2 Network Flow Models - Examples p. 8
source_refs.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an integer-constrained bounded flow model, exact integrality validation requires \(x_a\in\mathbb Z\) for every arc \(a\), together with exact satisfaction of \(Ax=b\) and \(l\le x\le u\). A floating-point condition such as \(\operatorname{dist}(x_a,\mathbb Z)\le\varepsilon\) establishes only near-integrality and is not an exact certificate unless each accepted value is first reconstructed as a specified integer and every constraint is then re-evaluated exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact validation reconstructs integer arc values and rechecks every constraint exactly; merely being within a floating-point tolerance of integers is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.title: Integrality Validation

source_witnesses.locator: 1.2 Network Flow Models - Examples p. 8
source_witnesses.source_title: Network Optimization: Continuous and Discrete Models

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The exact-integrality condition is precise and correctly distinguishes exact validation from near-integrality, but the cited introductory network-model section does not clearly support the numerical-validation and reconstruction claims.

children.title: Numerical Arithmetic Regimes
children.top_down_role: Exact, rationally scaled, and inexact computation in specialized flow solvers.

children.title: Exact Arithmetic Representation Family
children.top_down_role: Exact computation and normalization for discrete network data.

children.title: Exact Integer Arithmetic
children.top_down_role: Exact computation for integral capacities, costs, balances, or potentials.

assumptions_latex: Every input and intermediate value is represented as a signed integer of unbounded mathematical precision.
Arithmetic operations either complete exactly or report resource exhaustion without returning a mathematical result.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Integer addition, subtraction, multiplication, comparison, and Euclidean division return their exact mathematical values, with division producing unique quotient and remainder under the stated convention.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Mathematical semantics of arbitrary-precision signed-integer operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Exact integer arithmetic represents each value as an element of \(\mathbb Z\), without rounding, overflow, or saturation. For \(a,b\in\mathbb Z\), addition, subtraction, multiplication, sign, absolute value, and comparison return their ordinary integer results. For Euclidean division with \(b\ne0\), the implementation returns integers \(q,r\) satisfying \(a=bq+r\) and \(0\le r<|b|\). Resource limits may cause explicit failure, but may not replace an exact result by a rounded or wrapped value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact integer arithmetic implements ordinary unbounded integers without rounding or overflow and must report resource failure instead of returning an altered value.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Integer Arithmetic

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition gives coherent arbitrary-precision integer semantics and fits the exact-arithmetic leaf, but the standard-field rationale is not a substitute for the required inspectable source.

children.title: Exact Rational Arithmetic
children.top_down_role: Exact computation for rationally represented network data.

assumptions_latex: Every rational operand is represented by integers \(p,q\) with \(q\ne0\).
All underlying integer operations are exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated cross-product formulas implement the field operations and comparisons of \(\mathbb Q\) without rounding.

notation.meaning: Rational number represented by numerator p and nonzero denominator q.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale:rational field operations by integer cross-products
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact fraction arithmetic over arbitrary-precision integers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p/q,r/s\in\mathbb Q\) with \(q,s\ne0\), exact arithmetic uses \(p/q+r/s=(ps+rq)/(qs)\), \((p/q)(r/s)=pr/(qs)\), and \((p/q)/(r/s)=ps/(qr)\) when \(r\ne0\). Equality is decided by \(ps=rq\); order is decided by sign-corrected cross multiplication. Each result may be divided by common factors and its denominator made positive, but no rounding is permitted. Division by zero and resource exhaustion are reported explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rational values use integer numerator-denominator pairs; field operations and comparisons use exact cross-products, with no rounding and explicit division-by-zero failure.
knowledge_statements.title: Exact Rational Arithmetic

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation and exact field-operation formulas are correct, including the need for sign-aware comparison, but no source with a specific locator is provided.

children.title: Rational Normalization
children.top_down_role: Scaling and canonical representation choices for rational network quantities.

assumptions_latex: The input pair \((p,q)\) consists of integers with \(q\ne0\).
Greatest-common-divisor and sign operations are exact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Normalization returns the unique pair \((p',q')\) representing \(p/q\) with \(q'>0\) and \(\gcd(|p'|,q')=1\).

notation.meaning: Positive greatest common divisor of numerator magnitude and denominator magnitude.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical normalization of one exact rational number.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \((p,q)\in\mathbb Z^2\) with \(q\ne0\), set \(g=\gcd(|p|,|q|)\), \(p_0=p/g\), and \(q_0=q/g\). If \(q_0<0\), output \((p',q')=(-p_0,-q_0)\); otherwise output \((p',q')=(p_0,q_0)\). The output satisfies \(p'/q'=p/q\), \(q'>0\), and \(\gcd(|p'|,q')=1\). For \(p=0\), the unique normalized output is \((0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Divide numerator and denominator by their gcd, move any sign to the numerator, and represent zero uniquely as zero over one.
knowledge_statements.title: Rational Normalization

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The normalization algorithm is complete, handles signs and zero correctly, and has the proper content kind, but it lacks a cited source with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Bit-Length Growth
children.top_down_role: Growth of exact numeric representations during solver execution.

assumptions_latex: For nonzero integers, bit length is \(\ell(z)=\lfloor\log_2|z|\rfloor+1\), with \(\ell(0)=1\).
Arithmetic is performed by exact arbitrary-precision integer operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Addition increases maximum operand length by at most one bit, multiplication has at most the sum of operand lengths, and normalization cannot increase numerator or denominator length.

notation.meaning: Binary bit length of an integer.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Value-size bounds, excluding machine-time bounds for arithmetic algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For integers \(a,b\), \(\ell(a+b)\le\max\{\ell(a),\ell(b)\}+1\) and, when \(ab\ne0\), \(\ell(ab)\le\ell(a)+\ell(b)\). Consequently, unreduced rational addition \(p/q+r/s\) forms a denominator of length at most \(\ell(q)+\ell(s)\) and a numerator of length at most \(\max\{\ell(p)+\ell(s),\ell(r)+\ell(q)\}+1\). Dividing numerator and denominator by their gcd cannot increase either length. Repeated operations can nevertheless cause cumulative bit-length growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact addition and multiplication have elementary operand-length bounds; gcd normalization never enlarges a fraction, though repeated rational operations may still grow representations.
knowledge_statements.title: Bit-Length Growth

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated value-size inequalities are correct under the supplied bit-length convention and the complexity-bound kind fits the leaf, but no source is cited.

children.title: Floating-Point Tolerance Regimes
children.top_down_role: Tolerance-sensitive feasibility and price comparisons.

assumptions_latex: All candidate values are finite floating-point numbers and each validation scale is nonnegative and declared.
The absolute and relative tolerances satisfy \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}},\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A comparison at scale \(s\) is accepted exactly when its signed or absolute violation does not exceed \(\tau(s)=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}s\).

notation.meaning: Mixed absolute-relative tolerance at declared scale s.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Declared mixed tolerances for feasibility and price comparisons.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A floating-point tolerance regime fixes \(\tau(s)=\varepsilon_{\mathrm{abs}}+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rel}}s\) before inspecting a candidate and assigns a declared scale \(s\ge0\) to every comparison. An equality residual \(r\) passes when \(|r|\le\tau(s)\); an inequality \(g\le0\) passes when \(g\le\tau(s)\). Bound, balance, and reduced-cost tests must use their specified scales consistently. Passing establishes tolerance-feasibility only, not exact feasibility, and nonfinite operands invalidate the comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A floating-point regime fixes absolute-relative tolerances and scales in advance, applies them consistently, rejects nonfinite values, and reports only tolerance-feasibility.
knowledge_statements.title: Floating-Point Tolerance Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The principle accurately distinguishes tolerance-feasibility from exact feasibility and requires declared scales, but the mixed absolute-relative regime and nonfinite-value policy are implementation-sensitive and unsupported by a cited source.

children.title: Numeric Range Failure Family
children.top_down_role: Arithmetic failures from large costs, potentials, capacities, or gains.

children.title: Integer Overflow Failures
children.top_down_role: Range failures involving integral costs, capacities, balances, or potentials.

knowledge_statements.title: Integer Overflow Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Machine-integer failure boundary for exact network-flow arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the implementation represent integers only in the interval \([L,U]\cap\mathbb Z\). For integer arc costs \(c_e\), flows \(x_e\), node balances \(b_v\), and potentials \(p_v\), define the required intermediate set
\[
\mathcal I=\{c_ex_e:e\in E\}\cup\left\{\sum_{e\in E}c_ex_e\right\}\cup\left\{\sum_{e\in\delta^+(v)}x_e-\sum_{e\in\delta^-(v)}x_e:v\in V\right\}\cup\{c_e+p_u-p_v:e=(u,v)\in E\}.
\]
An integer-overflow failure occurs whenever an exact value in \(\mathcal I\) lies outside \([L,U]\), even if every input datum and every stored flow lies inside that interval. Consequently, correctness requires checked arithmetic or a representation whose range contains every required intermediate value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Overflow occurs when any exact product, sum, balance, or reduced-cost intermediate exceeds the machine-integer range, even though all inputs and flows are individually representable.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed network with integer data.
\(L<U\) are the minimum and maximum representable machine integers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal I\nsubseteq[L,U]\) implies that unchecked machine-integer evaluation need not equal exact network-flow arithmetic.

notation.meaning: arcs leaving and entering node v
node potential used in reduced costs
set of exact intermediate integer values required by the computation

review_flags: implementation-specific arithmetic claim lacks a supporting numerical-analysis or solver-verification locator

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind fits the terminal container, and the statement is internally coherent. However, no source is cited for the machine-integer semantics, required-intermediate characterization, or correctness consequence; the inventory sources do not specifically support numerical overflow behavior.

children.title: Floating-Point Range Failures
children.top_down_role: Overflow, underflow, or scale loss in inexact solver state.

knowledge_statements.title: Floating-Point Range Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exponent-range failures in floating-point network-flow computations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a floating-point format have largest finite magnitude \(F_{\max}\) and smallest positive normal magnitude \(F_{\min}\). For the exact real intermediate values \(y\) required by a network-flow computation, overflow occurs when \(|y|>F_{\max}\); normal-range underflow occurs when \(0<|y|<F_{\min}\). The computed value may then become an infinity, a subnormal number, or zero, according to the arithmetic regime. If such a value is used in a residual-capacity test, reduced-cost sign test, objective accumulation, or stopping test, the floating-point execution need not follow the corresponding exact-arithmetic decision path.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A range failure occurs when an exact intermediate is too large or too small for the format, potentially changing feasibility, reduced-cost, objective, or stopping decisions.
assumptions_latex: The implementation uses a finite-exponent floating-point format.
Network-flow decisions depend on computed arithmetic intermediates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|y|>F_{\max}\) or \(0<|y|<F_{\min}\) permits a range-induced departure from the exact-arithmetic execution.

notation.meaning: an exact real intermediate required by the solver

review_flags: floating-point range semantics require a supporting arithmetic-standard or numerical-verification locator

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure_boundary kind fits the terminal container. The range thresholds and possible control-flow consequences require a specific floating-point standard or authoritative numerical-arithmetic source, particularly because overflow and underflow outcomes depend on format, rounding, subnormal support, and arithmetic regime.

children.title: Potential-Growth Failures
children.top_down_role: Dynamic-range pressure caused by large accumulated price potentials.

knowledge_statements.title: Potential-Growth Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Range failure caused by growth of stored node potentials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the directed path \(v_0,v_1,\ldots,v_{n-1}\) with arc cost \(C>0\) on every arc \((v_{i-1},v_i)\). With normalization \(p_{v_0}=0\), shortest-path labels—and hence a potential vector that stores these labels—satisfy \(p_{v_i}=iC\). Thus an implementation whose potential type represents only magnitudes at most \(M\) fails whenever \((n-1)C>M\), although every individual arc cost is representable when \(C\le M\). More generally, repeated potential updates \(p^{k+1}=p^k+d^k\) require bounds on accumulated labels, not merely on input costs or single updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Potentials can grow with path length or repeated updates; representable arc costs do not guarantee representable labels or accumulated potentials.
assumptions_latex: \(n\ge2\), \(C>0\), and the potential representation has magnitude limit \(M\).
Potentials store shortest-path labels or cumulative label updates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\le M<(n-1)C\) gives representable arc costs but an unrepresentable potential \(p_{v_{n-1}}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Gain-Induced Range Amplification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplicative range amplification along generalized-flow paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In a generalized flow, let traversing arc \(e_i\) multiply incoming flow by a positive gain \(\gamma_i\). Along a directed path \(P=(e_1,\ldots,e_k)\), an initial amount \(x_0>0\) becomes
\[
x_k=x_0\prod_{i=1}^{k}\gamma_i.
\]
For a numeric format with finite upper magnitude \(M\) and positive lower threshold \(m\), range failure occurs if \(x_k>M\) or \(0<x_k<m\). In particular, constant gain \(\gamma>1\) produces exponential amplification \(x_k=x_0\gamma^k\), while \(0<\gamma<1\) produces exponential attenuation. Hence individually representable gains and initial flows do not ensure representability after path propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generalized-flow gains multiply along paths, so representable local data can produce exponentially large or small propagated flows.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a directed path and every gain satisfies \(\gamma_i>0\).
The numeric representation has finite thresholds \(0<m<M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_0\prod_{i=1}^{k}\gamma_i\notin[m,M]\) causes overflow or lower-range loss during gain propagation.
